entries.greek: ἄνδρʼ ἀπαμύνασθαι, ὅτε τις πρότερος χαλεπήνῃ.
entries.english: to defend yourself, when someone else starts the quarrel.
entries.reading: You need not go looking for conflict, but you should be ready to answer it if it comes to you. Do not walk into danger unguarded and alone; take with you the strength and the allies you need. Yet the line was spoken by a friend in disguise, so do not mistake every stranger on the road for an enemy: help may come from where you least expect it.
entries.context: In Iliad 24, as Priam drives by night to Achilles' camp to ransom Hector's body, Hermes meets him disguised as a young Myrmidon. He remarks that neither the old king nor his aged herald is young enough to fight off a man who starts a quarrel, then promises to protect him rather than harm him.

aspects.love: Do not provoke a quarrel with the one you love, but do not let yourself be trampled either. A gentle firmness will serve you better than silence or anger.
aspects.work: If a rival or a client turns hostile, you have the right to defend your interests. Make sure you are not facing them with too little support; bring a trusted colleague or adviser.
aspects.home: Those who are older or more fragile in your household need a protector now. Be the one who stands between them and trouble, as the god stood beside Priam.
aspects.health: Guard your strength rather than spending it in conflicts you did not start. If you are worn down, do not take on battles alone; ask for help.
aspects.journeys: A road taken at night, with precious cargo and few defenders, is a risky one. Go if you must, but go with a guide and keep your wits about you.

entries.greek: θαρσῶν νῦν Διόμηδες ἐπὶ Τρώεσσι μάχεσθαι·
entries.english: Take courage now, Diomedes, and fight against the Trojans.
entries.reading: The answer is to take heart and act. What you are facing calls for boldness, and the strength you need has been given to you, perhaps as an inheritance from those who came before you. Go forward with a clear eye, but know the limits of your contest and do not pick fights with powers far above you.
entries.context: In Iliad 5, Diomedes has been wounded by an arrow from Pandarus and prays to Athena. She answers him in person, telling him to fight the Trojans with confidence, for she has put his father Tydeus' fearless spirit in his breast and lifted the mist from his eyes so that he can tell gods from men.

aspects.love: Speak your heart with confidence. The courage you need to declare yourself is already within you; let it carry you past hesitation.
aspects.work: This is a time to compete boldly for what you want. You are better equipped than you fear, but choose your contests wisely and do not challenge those far out of your reach.
aspects.home: You carry the strength of your parents and forebears. Draw on what they taught you when your family needs someone to lead.
aspects.health: Even with a wound you can rise again. Take courage in your recovery, and ask for the help that clears your sight and restores your energy.
aspects.journeys: Go forward with your decision. The mist is lifting and you can now see more clearly which path is yours to take.

entries.greek: ἦ ῥά νύ τοι μεγάλων δώρων ἐπεμαίετο θυμὸς
entries.english: Truly, your heart was set on great gifts,
entries.reading: Ask yourself honestly what is drawing you on. A great reward has been promised, but rewards held out by others can lead you into places where you will be caught and used. Weigh the prize against the risk, and do not let desire for it make you careless with what you know.
entries.context: In Iliad 10, Odysseus and Diomedes capture the Trojan scout Dolon, who confesses that Hector promised him Achilles' horses and chariot for spying on the Greek ships. Odysseus smiles and says that his heart was set on great gifts indeed, horses that no mortal but Achilles can master; Dolon is soon killed after telling them what they want to know.

aspects.love: Ask whether you are drawn to this person or to what they seem to offer. Love sought for its rewards is a dangerous errand.
aspects.work: An offer that sounds too generous deserves suspicion. Be sure the one promising it can actually give it, and that you are not being sent into danger for another's gain.
aspects.home: Do not let ambition for possessions put your household at risk. What you already have may be worth more than the prize you are chasing.
aspects.health: Do not push yourself past your limits for the sake of reward. Strain undertaken for a glittering prize can cost more than it gains.
aspects.journeys: Before you set out, know why you are going. If greed is the only reason, reconsider; the road may lead into the enemy's camp.

entries.greek: νίκην καὶ μέγα κῦδος, ἀτὰρ Δαναοῖσί γε πῆμα·
entries.english: victory and great glory, but ruin for the Greeks.
entries.reading: The signs are in your favour: the line promises success and honour for you, and loss for those who stand against you. Act while the moment is with you. Remember, though, that in Homer the god's favour is given for a season, not for ever, so use your advantage well and without arrogance.
entries.context: In Iliad 8, Zeus thunders three times from Mount Ida as a sign to the Trojans. Hector calls to his men that he knows the son of Cronus has granted him victory and great glory, and ruin for the Greeks, and he boasts that he will leap their ditch and burn their ships.

aspects.love: The tide in love is with you now. Speak or act while it is, but do not let success make you careless of the other's feelings.
aspects.work: Your enterprise is favoured and your rivals will falter. Press your advantage, but do not boast before the work is done.
aspects.home: A season of good fortune comes to your house. Share it generously, for the god's favour turns, and kindness lasts longer than triumph.
aspects.health: Your strength is rising. Use it well, and do not mistake a good day for proof that you can ignore rest.
aspects.journeys: The omens favour the venture you are considering. Set out while the signs are good, but plan for the day when they change.

entries.greek: ἀλλʼ οὐ πείσονται Τρῶες καὶ Δαρδανίωνες
entries.english: But the Trojans and the Dardanians will not believe it,
entries.reading: You fear what someone may say about you, but the people who matter have seen your deeds and will not be persuaded by idle talk. Do not let the threat of a bad name drive you into a foolish stand. A wise retreat is no disgrace when your worth is already proven.
entries.context: In Iliad 8, Zeus' thunderbolt halts Diomedes' attack and Nestor urges him to turn the chariot and flee. Diomedes is anguished that Hector will boast that he ran away; Nestor replies that even if Hector calls him a coward, the Trojans and Dardanians will not believe it, nor will the widows of the men he has killed.

aspects.love: If someone speaks ill of you to the one you love, do not panic. Those who know you will judge you by what you have done, not by gossip.
aspects.work: A rival's slander will not stick, for your record speaks for you. You may step back from a fight that cannot be won without losing your standing.
aspects.home: Your family knows your true worth. Do not be driven into harsh action at home merely to prove yourself to outsiders.
aspects.health: Pride can push you to keep going when you should withdraw. Rest is not cowardice; listen to the wise voice telling you to turn back for now.
aspects.journeys: Changing course is not failure. If the signs are against you, retreat with dignity and wait for a better day.

entries.greek: εἰ δʼ ἄγε τοι κεφαλῇ κατανεύσομαι ὄφρα πεποίθῃς·
entries.english: Come, I will nod my head to you, so that you may trust me.
entries.reading: You may trust what has been promised. The line is the sign of a word that will not be taken back, given by one with the power to keep it. Go quietly and let the matter take its course; what has been pledged to you will be honoured, though perhaps not in the way or at the speed you would choose.
entries.context: In Iliad 1, Thetis clasps Zeus' knees on Olympus and begs him to give the Trojans the upper hand until the Greeks honour her son Achilles. Zeus, uneasy about Hera's anger, agrees and says he will nod his head so that she may trust him, for his nod is the greatest pledge among the gods and is never revoked.

aspects.love: The promise made to you is sincere. Trust it, and do not press for repeated proofs that would only strain the bond.
aspects.work: An agreement in your favour will hold. Once it is sealed, leave it to be carried out, and avoid stirring up those who might oppose it.
aspects.home: Pleading on behalf of someone you love may win a powerful ally. Ask humbly and honestly, then trust what you are given.
aspects.health: Assurance is a medicine of its own. Let the trustworthy word you have received ease your anxiety and allow you to rest.
aspects.journeys: The decision has been made and it will not be reversed. Go your way quietly; what you set in motion will unfold in its time.

entries.greek: οὐκ ἐάᾳ Κρονίδης ἐπαμυνέμεν Ἀργείοισιν.
entries.english: The son of Cronus will not allow you to help the Greeks.
entries.reading: This is not the moment to intervene. However strongly you wish to help or to change things, a greater power has decided against it, and to push on would bring harm to you without helping anyone. Hold back for now; the time for your part may come later.
entries.context: In Iliad 8, Hera and Athena drive out from Olympus to help the Greeks against Zeus' command. Zeus sends Iris, who stops them at the gates and tells them that the son of Cronus will not allow them to aid the Argives, and repeats his threat to lame their horses and strike them with the thunderbolt. They turn back.

aspects.love: You cannot rescue someone from a situation they must face themselves. Stand by them, but do not force your way in.
aspects.work: An authority above you has ruled against your plan. Defying it now will cost you dearly; wait and look for another way.
aspects.home: Do not take sides in a family quarrel that is not yours to settle. Your interference would only provoke the stronger party.
aspects.health: Do not drive yourself out against the warnings you have been given. Turning back now will spare you an injury that would be slow to heal.
aspects.journeys: The gate is closed for now. Turn back without shame; the journey may be possible at a later time.

entries.greek: σοὶ δʼ ἐγὼ οὐχ ἅλιος σκοπὸς ἔσσομαι οὐδʼ ἀπὸ δόξης·
entries.english: I will be no useless scout for you, nor fall short of your hopes.
entries.reading: You are ready to swear that you will not fail, and your confidence is real. But be careful what you undertake and what you ask in return: a bold promise made for a dazzling reward can lead you straight into the enemy's hands. Know the ground before you volunteer to cross it.
entries.context: In Iliad 10, at a night council of the Trojans, Dolon offers to spy on the Greek ships if Hector swears to give him Achilles' horses and chariot. He promises Hector he will be no useless scout and will not disappoint his hopes. On the way he is caught and killed by Odysseus and Diomedes.

aspects.love: Do not promise more than you can give in love, nor demand a pledge for what you have not yet done. Let trust grow before vows are made.
aspects.work: You are eager to volunteer and to name your price. Make sure the task is within your powers and the reward is not bait.
aspects.home: Before you take on a burden for your family, count the cost honestly. Good intentions are not enough on unknown ground.
aspects.health: Confidence in your body is good, but do not overestimate it. Prepare for the effort ahead instead of trusting speed alone.
aspects.journeys: Venturing alone into unfamiliar territory carries real danger. Find out what lies ahead before you set out with such haste.

entries.greek: ἔγρεο Τυδέος υἱέ· τί πάννυχον ὕπνον ἀωτεῖς;
entries.english: Wake up, son of Tydeus! Why do you sleep the whole night through?
entries.reading: This is a call to wake up. While you rest, events are moving close to you, and what needs to be done cannot wait for morning. Rouse yourself and others: the danger, or the opportunity, is nearer than you think.
entries.context: In Iliad 10, in the night after the Trojans have camped on the plain beside the Greek ships, old Nestor goes round waking the leaders. He stirs the sleeping Diomedes with his foot, asking why he sleeps all night when the Trojans are encamped so close to the ships.

aspects.love: Do not sleep through a relationship that needs your attention. Something is pressing close; wake to it before it is too late.
aspects.work: While you rest on past success, competitors are gathering at your gates. Rise early and act.
aspects.home: An older and wiser member of the family may be trying to rouse you. Listen, even if their urging feels rough.
aspects.health: Lethargy is your adversary now. Shake it off gently but firmly; a little effort today will spare you much trouble later.
aspects.journeys: The time for decision is now, not tomorrow. Get up and take the first step while there is still ground between you and the danger.

entries.greek: παύσειε κλαυθμοῖο γόοιό τε δακρυόεντος.
entries.english: that she should cease from her weeping and tearful lament.
entries.reading: Your grief has been seen. The answer offers consolation: help is being sent to quiet your weeping, and the one you fear for is not yet lost. Rest if you can; something will come to ease your heart, perhaps in a dream or through a familiar voice.
entries.context: In Odyssey 4, Penelope has learned that Telemachus has sailed secretly and that the suitors plan to ambush him; she lies sleepless and fasting. Athena makes a phantom in the form of her sister Iphthime and sends it to her room, so that Penelope might cease from her weeping, and the phantom assures her that her son will come home.

aspects.love: The sorrow you carry for someone dear will be eased. A sister or close friend may bring the comfort you need.
aspects.work: Worry has stolen your appetite and your sleep, but the outcome you fear is not certain. Steady yourself and wait for clearer news.
aspects.home: A child or loved one far from home is under protection. Let go of the worst fears and keep the hearth ready for their return.
aspects.health: Grief and fasting wear down the body. Eat, sleep and accept consolation; your heart needs rest to endure.
aspects.journeys: Someone close to you has set out on a risky venture. You cannot follow, but you can trust that they are not alone on their road.

entries.greek: οὐκ οἶδʼ· οὐ γάρ πώ τις ἑὸν γόνον αὐτὸς ἀνέγνω.
entries.english: I do not know: for no one has ever known for sure who his own father is.
entries.reading: You are asking for a certainty that no one can give. Some matters, even the closest to your own life, rest on trust rather than proof. Do not torment yourself demanding what cannot be known; act on what you do know, and on the word of those who love you.
entries.context: In Odyssey 1, Athena, disguised as the stranger Mentes, asks Telemachus whether he is truly Odysseus' son. He replies, in a bitter mood, that his mother says so but that he himself does not know, for no one has ever known for sure his own parentage, and wishes he were the son of some luckier man.

aspects.love: You cannot see into another's heart with perfect certainty. Love must rest on trust; do not destroy it by demanding proof.
aspects.work: You lack full information to decide. Admit what you do not know, and seek counsel from someone who can see more clearly than you.
aspects.home: Questions about where you come from may trouble you. Your worth is not settled by such questions but by what you make of your inheritance.
aspects.health: Do not dwell on uncertainties you cannot resolve. Bitterness about the unknown wears the spirit; turn to what you can tend today.
aspects.journeys: The answer to your question is hidden for now. Make your decision with humility, knowing that some things will become clear only as you go.

entries.greek: εἶμι μέν, οὐδʼ ἅλιον ἔπος ἔσσεται ὅττί κεν εἴπῃ.
entries.english: I will go, and the word will not be spoken in vain, whatever it says.
entries.reading: You are being called, and though you are weary and unwilling, you should go. Whatever is asked of you will not be idle or without consequence. Heed the summons even in sorrow; from it will come something that matters.
entries.context: In Iliad 24, Iris finds Thetis in her sea cave mourning the coming death of Achilles and tells her that Zeus summons her. Thetis says she is ashamed to mingle with the gods in her grief, but she will go, for whatever he says will not be said in vain. Zeus then sends her to tell Achilles to give back Hector's body.

aspects.love: Someone is calling you back into company, though you would rather stay alone with your feelings. Go; the meeting may help to heal a quarrel.
aspects.work: A summons from a superior should be answered, even if you are reluctant. What you are asked to do will carry real weight.
aspects.home: You may be the one chosen to carry a hard message within the family. Your words will be heard, so speak with care.
aspects.health: Withdrawal in grief is natural, but do not stay hidden too long. Being among others will strengthen you.
aspects.journeys: A call to set out has come, and it is not idle. Rise from where you have been resting and go where you are asked.

entries.greek: ἔσσεται ἢ ἠὼς ἢ δείλη ἢ μέσον ἦμαρ
entries.english: It will be at dawn, or in the evening, or at midday.
entries.reading: The thing you ask about will surely come, but its hour is not given to you. It may be early or late; do not try to fix it. Live and act well in the meantime, since what is fated waits for no one's permission and hurry or delay will not change it.
entries.context: In Iliad 21, the Trojan prince Lycaon begs Achilles for his life by the river Scamander. Achilles refuses, reminding him that Patroclus has died and that he too must die: a dawn, an evening or a midday will come when someone takes his life in battle. He then kills Lycaon.

aspects.love: What you hope for in love will come in its own time, morning, evening or noon. Do not set a deadline that only breeds anxiety.
aspects.work: The result you await is certain to arrive, but you cannot command its date. Keep working steadily rather than watching the clock.
aspects.home: Time touches every house. Cherish those you love now, for no one knows the hour of change.
aspects.health: All bodies are mortal, and wisdom accepts it. Let that knowledge make you value each day rather than fear it.
aspects.journeys: The moment of departure will come whether you are ready or not. Prepare now, so that when the hour strikes you are not taken by surprise.

entries.greek: ἴσχεο, μηδʼ ἔθελʼ οἶος ἐριζέμεναι βασιλεῦσιν·
entries.english: Hold back, and do not try to quarrel alone with kings.
entries.reading: Hold your tongue for now. You may have a point, but to set yourself alone against those with power, in public and with scorn, will win you only humiliation. Find a better time, a better way and better allies before you speak.
entries.context: In Iliad 2, Thersites rails at Agamemnon before the assembled army and urges the Greeks to sail home. Odysseus stands over him and rebukes him harshly, telling him to hold back and not try to quarrel alone with kings, then strikes him with the sceptre while the soldiers laugh.

aspects.love: Harsh words spoken in front of others will wound and shame. If you have a grievance with someone you love, raise it privately and gently.
aspects.work: Challenging those above you by yourself and in public will not succeed. Gather support and choose your moment.
aspects.home: Avoid setting yourself against the whole family at once. Even if you are right, a lone outburst will be laughed off.
aspects.health: Anger vented without purpose damages you more than anyone else. Restrain it and spend your energy where it can help.
aspects.journeys: Do not abandon the enterprise on a wave of resentment. Wait until you can see clearly whether going or staying is truly better.

entries.greek: ἀντίον εἶμʼ αὐτῶν· τρεῖν μʼ οὐκ ἐᾷ Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη.
entries.english: I will go to meet them: Pallas Athena does not let me be afraid.
entries.reading: Go out and meet what is coming. You have strength still in you, and the wisdom that guides you does not allow you to be ruled by fear. Steady yourself and face the matter directly; hanging back now would be the greater danger.
entries.context: In Iliad 5, Sthenelus sees Aeneas and Pandarus charging and urges Diomedes to retreat in the chariot. Diomedes refuses: he will not shrink from the fight but will go to meet them on foot, for Pallas Athena does not let him be afraid.

aspects.love: Do not shrink from a difficult conversation with the one you care for. Go to meet it openly; wisdom will steady you.
aspects.work: A strong challenge is coming at you in your work. Face it on your own feet, with a clear plan, and do not run.
aspects.home: When trouble comes towards your household, be the one who steps forward. Your calm will steady the others.
aspects.health: Your vigour is still steady. Meet the demands before you without fear, but keep a friend at your side, as Diomedes kept Sthenelus.
aspects.journeys: Advice to retreat comes from caution, not wisdom, this time. Go forward towards what you must face.

entries.greek: ἐχθρὰ δέ μοι τοῦ δῶρα, τίω δέ μιν ἐν καρὸς αἴσῃ.
entries.english: His gifts are hateful to me: I value him no more than a splinter.
entries.reading: Some offers are not worth taking. If what is held out to you comes from someone who has wronged you and has not truly made amends, you are right to see that no gift can repair a broken trust. But beware of pride that refuses every bridge: Achilles' refusal cost him dearly in the end.
entries.context: In Iliad 9, Agamemnon sends Odysseus, Ajax and Phoenix to offer Achilles lavish gifts if he will return to battle. Achilles answers Odysseus that Agamemnon's gifts are hateful to him and that he values the man at no more than a splinter; he will not fight for him again.

aspects.love: Presents cannot replace an apology. If someone who hurt you offers things instead of honesty, you may decline them.
aspects.work: A deal offered by someone who has cheated you before should be refused or examined with great care. Your self-respect is not for sale.
aspects.home: When a family wound is offered only gifts as balm, it will not heal. Seek words of truth, and be ready to accept them when they come.
aspects.health: Bitterness held too long becomes a weight of its own. Protect your dignity, but do not let resentment poison your peace.
aspects.journeys: You are free to walk away from a broken partnership. Before you do, consider whether your refusal could later cost you something you love.

entries.greek: μοῦνον τηλύγετον πολλοῖσιν ἐπὶ κτεάτεσσι,
entries.english: an only son, born late, heir to great wealth.
entries.reading: You are, or will be, held dear. The line speaks of the kind of love a parent gives to a long-awaited only child, generous and protective. Receive such care with gratitude, and remember that those who raised and sheltered you have a claim on your heart in return.
entries.context: In Iliad 9, old Phoenix reminds Achilles of his past: after fleeing his own father he came to Peleus, who welcomed him and loved him as a father loves an only son, born late and heir to great wealth, and made him rich. Phoenix then recalls how he raised the infant Achilles, as part of his plea for Achilles to relent.

aspects.love: You are loved more dearly than you may realise. Accept that love without suspicion, and return it.
aspects.work: A patron or mentor may treat you with great generosity. Honour their trust by working faithfully for them.
aspects.home: A home may be found among people not of your blood. The family that takes you in can become as true as the one you were born to.
aspects.health: You are cared for; let yourself be looked after when you need it, as a well-loved child is.
aspects.journeys: If you must leave one home, another may welcome you warmly. The road away may lead you to a place where you are treasured.

entries.greek: νῦν μὲν δὴ μάλα πάγχυ κακὸς κακὸν ἡγηλάζει,
entries.english: Look at that: here is one wretch leading another.
entries.reading: Others may judge you by the people you walk with, and judge harshly. Do not be stung into a rash reply. The insult says more about the one who gives it than about you; keep your dignity, for appearances are deceiving and your time to be recognised may come.
entries.context: In Odyssey 17, the swineherd Eumaeus is leading Odysseus, disguised as a beggar, into town. At the spring they meet the goatherd Melanthius, who insults them, crying that here is one wretch leading another, for god always brings like to like. He then kicks Odysseus, who restrains himself.

aspects.love: Others may sneer at the one you love or at your friendship. Stand by them; scorn from outsiders is no measure of a true companion.
aspects.work: Do not be discouraged if you are underestimated or lumped together with those thought lowly. Bide your time and let your work speak.
aspects.home: A loyal member of your household may be mocked for their kindness to you. Defend their honour, and do not repay insult with violence.
aspects.health: Insults and slights can lodge in the body as tension. Let them pass through you; self-control is a kind of strength.
aspects.journeys: On the road you may meet those who abuse travellers. Keep walking, keep your temper, and remember where you are going.

entries.greek: καί κε τὸ βουλοίμην, καί κεν πολὺ κέρδιον ἦεν
entries.english: That is what I would wish, and it would have been far better.
entries.reading: The line looks back with regret at something that should never have begun. Ask whether you are about to start something you will wish you had left alone. If it is already done, face its consequences squarely rather than hiding from them.
entries.context: In Iliad 3, Paris shrinks back into the Trojan ranks on seeing Menelaus. Hector rebukes him, wishing that Paris had never been born or had died unmarried; that, he says, is what he would wish, and it would have been far better than being a disgrace and a thing despised.

aspects.love: A union begun in haste or at another's expense may bring more sorrow than joy. Think hard before you bind yourself.
aspects.work: If an undertaking can still be abandoned, it may be better to abandon it. Do not let charm or vanity draw you into it.
aspects.home: Harsh words between siblings carry truth and pain. Listen to the rebuke from your family, even if it stings.
aspects.health: Do not hide from what frightens you. Facing it, however hard, will be less harmful than the shame of avoiding it.
aspects.journeys: Before you set out, ask whether you are doing so for good reason. Some voyages bring ruin on a whole house.

entries.greek: τῷ κέ τοι ἀγλαΐας γε διασκεδάσειεν ἁπάσας,
entries.english: Then he would scatter all your fine show to the winds.
entries.reading: Display and swagger will not last. Someone who struts while doing harm is living on borrowed time, and the rightful order will return. If you are the one tempted to show off, beware; if you are the one wronged, take heart, for the reckoning is near.
entries.context: In Odyssey 17, after Melanthius has insulted and kicked the disguised Odysseus, Eumaeus prays to the nymphs of the spring that Odysseus may come home. Then, he tells Melanthius, his master would scatter all the fine show that the goatherd so insolently parades about town while the flocks are ruined.

aspects.love: Do not be dazzled by a suitor's fine show. Look at how they treat the humble, for that is their true character.
aspects.work: Neglecting your duties while you parade your success will catch up with you. Tend the flock before you flaunt the fleece.
aspects.home: If someone is exploiting your household in your absence, their time is short. Pray, prepare, and be ready to set things right.
aspects.health: Fine appearances can hide neglect. Tend to the foundations of your wellbeing, not only the outward show.
aspects.journeys: The rightful master may soon return. If you are far from home, your coming will restore order there.

entries.greek: ἀλλʼ ἤτοι τάδε πάντα καταφλέξω πυρὶ κηλέῳ
entries.english: But I will burn all these things in blazing fire,
entries.reading: The answer points to letting go. Things kept for a purpose that can no longer be fulfilled become only a burden of grief. Release them, and turn your loss into honour for what was loved, rather than leaving it to decay.
entries.context: At the end of Iliad 22, Andromache laments Hector, whose body lies naked by the Greek ships. She thinks of the fine clothes woven for him that lie in the palace and says she will burn them all in blazing fire, since he will never be wrapped in them, so that they may be an honour to him before the Trojans.

aspects.love: What was lost in love can be honoured, but not recalled. Let a ritual of farewell mark the ending, and keep the memory with respect.
aspects.work: Plans and materials prepared for a project that will not happen should be cleared away. Make room for what can still be built.
aspects.home: Possessions kept for someone who is gone can weigh down a house. Give them a fitting end, as an act of love.
aspects.health: Grief needs an outlet. Let tears and remembrance do their work, rather than holding everything locked away.
aspects.journeys: A decisive act of release may be the change you need. Burn the bridge only if it truly leads nowhere, and do it with reverence.

entries.greek: οὐδέ κεν ὧς ἔτι θυμὸν ἐμὸν πείσειʼ Ἀγαμέμνων
entries.english: not even so would Agamemnon win over my heart,
entries.reading: There are wounds that no payment will mend. If you are being asked to sell your agreement, you may rightly refuse until the true wrong is acknowledged. Be clear with yourself about what you are really waiting for, so that your refusal does not harden into a punishment of yourself.
entries.context: In Iliad 9, Achilles rejects the embassy sent by Agamemnon. Listing riches beyond count, he declares that not even so would Agamemnon win over his heart until he has paid back in full the outrage that grieves him.

aspects.love: Affection cannot be bought. If someone tries to win you with wealth alone, your heart is right to stay unmoved.
aspects.work: Your loyalty is worth more than a payment. Make clear what you need in order to return to the table, and hold to it.
aspects.home: A family quarrel cannot be settled with presents. What is needed is for the hurt to be acknowledged openly.
aspects.health: A heart that is deeply grieved needs more than distraction. Give yourself time and honest acknowledgement of what wounded you.
aspects.journeys: Do not let a generous offer push you into a decision your heart rejects. Stay where your conscience stands.

entries.greek: ἔσθλʼ ἀγορεύοντες, κακὰ δὲ φρεσὶ βυσσοδόμευον.
entries.english: speaking kind words, but plotting evil deep in their hearts.
entries.reading: Watch those who speak kindly to you now. Fair words may be covering intentions that are far from fair. Keep your own counsel, stay close to the friends who have been loyal from the start, and let actions rather than speeches tell you who is with you.
entries.context: In Odyssey 17, Telemachus, newly home from his voyage, walks into the assembly place. The suitors throng around him speaking kind words, but plotting evil deep in their hearts; he avoids them and sits with Mentor and the old friends of his father.

aspects.love: Flattery is not affection. Be slow to trust one whose sweet words are not matched by kind deeds.
aspects.work: Colleagues who praise you to your face may be working against you. Keep your plans to yourself and rely on proven allies.
aspects.home: Those who crowd into your home with friendly faces may not wish it well. Stay close to the old friends of your family.
aspects.health: Pleasant habits can conceal harm. Look beneath the surface of what seems to do you good.
aspects.journeys: Returning from a venture, you may be greeted warmly by people who hope you fail. Hold your course and choose your company carefully.

entries.greek: οὔ τοι ἀπόβλητʼ ἐστὶ θεῶν ἐρικυδέα δῶρα
entries.english: The glorious gifts of the gods are not to be thrown away.
entries.reading: Do not despise what has been given to you. Whatever gift or talent has come your way, it was not of your choosing and should not be thrown aside out of shame or because others mock it. Yet own your gifts honestly, and be ready to stand behind them when it counts.
entries.context: In Iliad 3, after Hector scorns him for his good looks and Aphrodite's favour, Paris replies that the glorious gifts of the gods are not to be thrown away, for no one can choose them for himself. He then offers to settle the war by single combat with Menelaus.

aspects.love: The love that has come to you is a gift; do not cast it away out of fear of what others will say. But be prepared to defend it honourably.
aspects.work: A talent you have been given may be underrated by others. Value it and use it, rather than apologising for it.
aspects.home: Accept the blessings of your household with gratitude, whatever form they take. They are not yours to spurn.
aspects.health: Your body and its gifts are to be cared for, not resented. Accept what you have been given and make the most of it.
aspects.journeys: An opportunity has been placed before you that you did not seek. Do not throw it away; take it up, and be ready to stand by your choice.

entries.greek: δαιμόνιοι, μαίνεσθε καὶ οὐκέτι κεύθετε θυμῷ
entries.english: Fools, you are mad, and you no longer hide what is in your hearts.
entries.reading: Others are showing their true nature openly, and their behaviour is past hiding. You need not match their madness. Name it calmly and with courage, as Telemachus did, and let their own excess work against them.
entries.context: In Odyssey 18, Eurymachus hurls a footstool at the disguised Odysseus; it misses and strikes the wine-steward, and the suitors break into uproar. Telemachus rebukes them: they are mad and can no longer hide that they have had too much food and wine; some god is stirring them, and they should go home to bed.

aspects.love: Someone's true feelings have now been revealed by their behaviour. See them for what they are, and do not make excuses for them.
aspects.work: Unruly conduct among your colleagues has come into the open. Speak plainly and firmly, and let the reckless discredit themselves.
aspects.home: If your home has been overrun by quarrelling and excess, it is time to say so. A calm, firm word can send the troublemakers away.
aspects.health: Excess in food and drink is clouding judgement. Know when enough is enough, and go home to rest.
aspects.journeys: This is not a moment for rash action. Let the folly around you spend itself before you make your move.

entries.greek: τοῦ μὲν φθίνοντος μηνός, τοῦ δʼ ἱσταμένοιο,
entries.english: as one month wanes and the next begins.
entries.reading: Change is coming at a turning of time, as one month ends and another begins. Watch for it at a threshold, when the old phase is fading. What has long been awaited may be closer than those around you believe.
entries.context: In Odyssey 14, the disguised Odysseus swears to the doubting swineherd Eumaeus that Odysseus will return within this very year, as one month wanes and the next begins, and will punish those who dishonour his wife and son. Eumaeus does not believe him.

aspects.love: A reunion or a turn in love may come at the change of the month. Keep faith a little longer.
aspects.work: Look for a shift in your affairs at the turn of the month. Have your accounts in order when it comes.
aspects.home: An absent member of the household may return sooner than expected. Prepare the house quietly for the change.
aspects.health: As the moon wanes and renews, so may your strength. Give yourself until the new month before you judge your progress.
aspects.journeys: The time for the change you are considering is at the threshold between one month and the next. Choose that turning for your step.

entries.greek: οὐκ ἄν τοι χραίσμῃ…
entries.note: One of two lines that begin the same way: Iliad 11.387 or 3.54.
entries.english: It would be no help to you…
entries.reading: What you are relying on will not help you. Whether it is charm, distance, or some trick that kept you safe from a direct trial, it will fail when the real test comes. Look for strength of a sounder kind, or avoid the contest altogether.
entries.context: The papyrus line begins with words found in two places in the Iliad, so the identification is uncertain. At Iliad 11.387 Diomedes, shot in the foot by Paris, taunts him that his bow and arrows would be no help to him in open combat; at Iliad 3.54 Hector tells Paris that his lyre and Aphrodite's gifts would be no help when he lay in the dust. Both are said to Paris.

aspects.love: Charm and good looks will not sustain a relationship through hard times. Look for deeper qualities in yourself and in the other.
aspects.work: The tactic you depend on will not serve you in an open contest. Strengthen your real skills before the test.
aspects.home: Outward show will not protect your household. What it needs is honest effort and courage.
aspects.health: A quick remedy or a show of strength will not help. Seek what truly builds health, patiently.
aspects.journeys: Keeping your distance has kept you safe so far, but it will not carry you through what lies ahead. Prepare for a direct meeting, or choose another road.

entries.greek: μήτε τι τὸν ξεῖνον στυφελίζετε μήτε τινʼ ἄλλον
entries.english: Do not mistreat the stranger, nor anyone else
entries.reading: The answer is a warning against mistreating those weaker than you or at your mercy, whether strangers, guests or those who serve. Show decency to everyone under your roof. The humble person before you may be far more than he seems.
entries.context: In Odyssey 18, after Telemachus has rebuked the suitors for their brawling, the suitor Amphinomus calls on them not to answer a just rebuke with anger. He tells them not to mistreat the stranger or any of the servants in Odysseus' house, but to pour a libation and go home.

aspects.love: Treat even those you do not yet know with courtesy; one of them may become dear to you.
aspects.work: Respect those who work for you or under you. Decency to the lowest in the house is the mark of a good master.
aspects.home: Make your home a place where guests and helpers are safe. Hospitality given now will be honoured.
aspects.health: Be gentle with yourself as you would be with a stranger in need. Harshness, even towards yourself, does harm.
aspects.journeys: When you travel, you will be the stranger. Show others the courtesy you hope to receive.

entries.greek: αἰσχρόν τοι δηρόν τε μένειν κενεόν τε νέεσθαι.
entries.english: It is shameful to wait long and go home empty-handed.
entries.reading: To give up now would be the worse disgrace. You have waited long and suffered much, and it would be a shame to come away with nothing. Bear it a little longer, until it becomes clear whether the promise made to you will be kept.
entries.context: In Iliad 2, after Agamemnon's test of the army sends the Greeks rushing for the ships, Odysseus addresses the assembly. He admits that nine years is a long time to wait, but says it is shameful to wait long and go home empty-handed, and urges them to stay and see whether Calchas' prophecy of victory comes true.

aspects.love: You have invested much in this bond. Do not walk away just as it may be about to bear fruit; give it a little more time.
aspects.work: You have laboured long on this enterprise. To abandon it now would waste all that effort; persevere until the result is clear.
aspects.home: Separation from home weighs on you, and that is understandable. Hold on a while longer, so that you do not return with nothing to show.
aspects.health: Endurance is needed for a little longer. Keep your spirits up; the end of your trial may be nearer than it feels.
aspects.journeys: Do not rush for the ships. Stay where you are until you can see whether the promised outcome will come.

entries.greek: μὴ παῖδʼ ὀρφανικὸν θήῃς χήρην τε γυναῖκα·
entries.english: Do not make your child an orphan, and your wife a widow.
entries.reading: Consider those who depend on you before you take a dangerous step. Courage is not only in the charge; it is also in protecting what you love. Weigh whether the risk you are drawn to is truly yours to take.
entries.context: In Iliad 6, Andromache meets Hector at the Scaean gate with their infant son. Having lost her father and brothers to Achilles, she tells Hector that he is everything to her and begs him to stay on the wall and not make his child an orphan and his wife a widow. Hector answers that shame will not let him hold back.

aspects.love: The one who loves you is pleading with you. Hear their fear, and let it shape what you do.
aspects.work: Do not stake everything on a gamble when others depend on your earnings. Defend your position rather than charging into danger.
aspects.home: Your family needs you present and whole. Stay close to them now, and guard the place where they are weakest.
aspects.health: Do not take risks with your safety for the sake of pride. Those who love you need you well.
aspects.journeys: Before you make a bold decision, consider who will bear its cost. Choose the course that protects those who rely on you.

entries.greek: ἔσται ταῦτα Σκάμανδρε διοτρεφές, ὡς σὺ κελεύεις.
entries.english: It shall be so, Scamander, nursling of Zeus, just as you command.
entries.reading: Yield where it is right to yield, but do not give up your purpose. You can grant a reasonable demand courteously and still go on toward the thing you must do. Be gracious in the small concession and steady in the large aim.
entries.context: In Iliad 21, the river Scamander, choked with the bodies of Trojans Achilles has killed, rises in human form and tells him to drive them out of his stream. Achilles answers that it shall be so, Scamander, nursling of Zeus, as he commands, but says he will not stop killing Trojans until he has met Hector.

aspects.love: Give way to your partner on the matter they ask of you, gracefully. You need not abandon what matters most to you to do so.
aspects.work: Accept the conditions laid down by a powerful party, but keep your eyes on the goal you set yourself.
aspects.home: Respect the wishes of an elder or of the spirit of the place you live in. Concession in small matters keeps the peace at home.
aspects.health: Listen when your body tells you that you are overburdening it. You can ease the strain without abandoning your purpose.
aspects.journeys: Your route may need to change, but your destination need not. Bend with the current and keep going.

entries.greek: δυσμενέσιν μὲν χάρμα, κατηφείην δὲ σοὶ αὐτῷ;
entries.english: a joy to your enemies, and a shame to yourself?
entries.reading: Consider where your course is leading. What you are doing may give your rivals cause to rejoice and leave you with nothing but disgrace. If you have caused trouble for others, the honourable thing is to face it yourself and not leave others to pay.
entries.context: In Iliad 3, Hector rebukes Paris for slipping away from Menelaus. He reminds him that he brought Helen from a far land, a great harm to his father, his city and his people, a joy to their enemies and a shame to himself, and asks whether he will not stand and face Menelaus.

aspects.love: A love that wrongs others will bring grief to many and shame to you. If you have chosen it, then stand by it with courage.
aspects.work: Your actions may be giving your competitors cause for delight. Correct your course before the damage grows.
aspects.home: What you do reflects on your whole family. Think of your parents and kin before you act.
aspects.health: Do not make choices that please your adversaries and harm yourself. Look after your wellbeing with dignity.
aspects.journeys: Consider the consequences of carrying something home from far away. Some prizes bring a war behind them.

entries.greek: τοῦδʼ αὐτοῦ λυκάβαντος ἐλεύσεται ἐνθάδʼ Ὀδυσσεύς.
entries.english: Within this very year, Odysseus will come home.
entries.reading: The return you hope for is promised within the year. It may seem unlikely to others, and you may have stopped believing it yourself, but the line answers with an oath. Keep your house in order and your faith steady until the time comes.
entries.context: In Odyssey 14, Odysseus, disguised as a wandering Cretan, swears by Zeus, the table of hospitality and Odysseus' own hearth that Odysseus will come home within this very year. The swineherd Eumaeus, who has been deceived by travellers' tales before, refuses to believe him.

aspects.love: Someone you long for may return to you within the year. Keep faith, though others tell you it is foolish.
aspects.work: What you are working for will bear fruit within the year. Keep tending your affairs faithfully.
aspects.home: Your household will be made whole again within this year. Prepare for the return and guard what is precious until then.
aspects.health: Recovery and renewal are promised within the year. Trust the slow work of time.
aspects.journeys: The journey home, or the decision you wait for, will be settled within the year. Be ready when it comes.

entries.greek: οὐδὲν σοί γʼ ὄφελος, ἐπεὶ οὐκ ἐγκείσεαι αὐτοῖς,
entries.english: They are no use to you, since you will not lie wrapped in them.
entries.reading: What you are holding on to can no longer serve you. Keeping it out of habit or grief only adds weight. Let it go, or find a way to turn it to honour, since it will not do what it was made for.
entries.context: In Iliad 22, Andromache mourns Hector, killed by Achilles and lying unburied by the Greek ships. Of the fine clothes woven for him, she says she will burn them, for they are no use to him since he will not lie wrapped in them; instead they shall be a mark of honour before the Trojans.

aspects.love: A hope kept for a love that has ended cannot warm you. Lay it aside with tenderness.
aspects.work: Resources tied up in a lost cause bring no return. Release them and put your effort where it can bear fruit.
aspects.home: Keepsakes of one who is gone may become a source of pain. Honour them, but do not let them fill the house with sorrow.
aspects.health: Holding on to what is lost will weigh on your spirit. Allow yourself to mourn, and then to set it down.
aspects.journeys: Plans made for a future that will not come should be released. Turn to the path that remains open.

entries.greek: τῷ δέ κε νικήσαντι γυνὴ καὶ κτήμαθʼ ἕποιτο·
entries.english: Let the woman and the treasure go to the one who wins.
entries.reading: Settle the matter by a fair and open trial, and agree in advance to abide by the result. A long, wearing dispute may be ended by a single clear decision. Accept beforehand that the prize goes to the one who wins, and be ready for that to be either party.
entries.context: In Iliad 3, the herald Idaeus summons Priam to the plain to swear oaths with the Greeks. He explains that Paris and Menelaus will fight for Helen, and that the woman and the treasure will go to the winner, while everyone else makes peace. Priam shudders, but goes.

aspects.love: If two hearts are contending for one person, let the matter be decided openly and honestly, and let the others make peace.
aspects.work: A dispute over property or contract may be best resolved by a fair process. Agree to the terms in advance, and hold to them.
aspects.home: A long family quarrel can be ended by a single agreed settlement. Bring the parties together and let the decision stand.
aspects.health: Long strain weakens you. Bring the matter that troubles you to a conclusion, so that you can rest.
aspects.journeys: Instead of endless deliberation, set a clear test for your decision and abide by its outcome.

entries.greek: οὐκ ἀγαθὸν πολυκοιρανίη· εἷς κοίρανος ἔστω,
entries.english: Rule by many is no good thing: let there be one ruler.
entries.reading: Too many voices are trying to steer. The answer calls for a single clear authority: decide who leads, whether that is you or another, and then let the others follow. Divided command will bring confusion; order will bring strength.
entries.context: In Iliad 2, after Agamemnon's test causes the army to flee for the ships, Odysseus goes through the ranks restraining them. He tells common soldiers who shout that they cannot all be kings, that rule by many is no good thing, and that there should be one ruler, to whom Zeus has given sceptre and law.

aspects.love: Too many counsellors are crowding into your relationship. Listen to your own heart and your partner, not to every voice around you.
aspects.work: A project with too many leaders will founder. Settle who makes the final decision, and support them.
aspects.home: A household needs clear arrangements. Decide who is responsible for what, and quarrels will ease.
aspects.health: Conflicting advice is confusing you. Choose one wise guide and follow that counsel steadily.
aspects.journeys: Do not try to follow every opinion about which way to go. Choose one course and commit to it.

entries.greek: εἰδώλων δὲ πλέον πρόθυρον, πλείη δὲ καὶ αὐλή,
entries.english: The porch is full of ghosts, and the courtyard full of them too,
entries.reading: This is a grave warning. Something is wrong that those around you are laughing off, and you should not join their laughter. Look closely at the signs, change course while there is time, and do not remain where disaster is gathering.
entries.context: In Odyssey 20, Athena stirs the suitors to wild, unnatural laughter at their feast. The seer Theoclymenus sees a vision of their doom: night about their heads, walls dripping with blood, and the porch and courtyard full of ghosts hurrying to the darkness below. The suitors only laugh at him.

aspects.love: If a relationship is surrounded by darkness that others ignore, trust your unease. Do not stay out of politeness.
aspects.work: There are signs of serious trouble in the enterprise you are part of. Take them seriously, even if your companions mock the warning.
aspects.home: Something in your house is not right. Look at it honestly before it grows worse.
aspects.health: Do not laugh off warning signs about your wellbeing. Attend to them with care and seek counsel.
aspects.journeys: Leave a place where ruin is gathering. Like the seer, walk out while others feast.

entries.greek: ἠράμεθα μέγα κῦδος· ἐπέφνομεν Ἕκτορα δῖον,
entries.english: We have won great glory: we have killed the noble Hector.
entries.reading: The line proclaims a victory. What you have struggled for has been achieved, or soon will be, and you may rightly take honour from it. But look at what Achilles did next and do not let triumph turn into cruelty: how you treat a fallen rival will be remembered too.
entries.context: In Iliad 22, Achilles has just killed Hector. He calls the Greeks to sing the victory song and return to the ships, saying they have won great glory and killed noble Hector, whom the Trojans prayed to as a god. He then ties Hector's body to his chariot and drags it in the dust.

aspects.love: You may win the heart you seek, or the argument you are in. Do not humiliate the other in victory.
aspects.work: A great success is at hand. Celebrate it, but deal honourably with the competitor you have overcome.
aspects.home: Your household may rejoice in an achievement. Let the celebration be generous, not boastful.
aspects.health: You have overcome a great trial. Do not let the relief turn into recklessness; rest and recover.
aspects.journeys: The decisive moment has gone your way. Now decide how you will use your victory, for that choice will define you.

entries.greek: ὡς καὶ ἐμοὶ τόδε ἔργον ἀέξεται, ᾧ ἐπιμίμνω.
entries.english: so my work too grows and prospers, the work I keep at.
entries.reading: Keep at your work. The task you have stayed with faithfully is growing under your hands, and the gods bless steady effort. Be patient and loyal to what you have been entrusted with; its rewards may come later, and from an unexpected quarter.
entries.context: In Odyssey 14, the swineherd Eumaeus receives Odysseus, disguised as a beggar, in his hut. He speaks of his absent master, who would have rewarded his faithful work with a house and land, as a kind master does for a servant whose labour the god makes prosper, so too his own work grows, the work he keeps at.

aspects.love: Love tended faithfully over time grows strong. Keep showing your care in small daily ways.
aspects.work: Your steady work is increasing. Keep at it; it is noticed, even by those who are absent.
aspects.home: A household cared for with loyalty thrives. Your devotion to your home is bearing fruit.
aspects.health: Daily habits kept up patiently will strengthen you. Persist in the good routines you have begun.
aspects.journeys: This is not a time to wander but to remain at your post. The rewards of staying will come.

entries.greek: οὐδʼ εἴ μοι τόσα δοίη ὅσα ψάμαθός τε κόνις τε,
entries.english: not even if he gave me gifts as many as the grains of sand and dust.
entries.reading: No amount of payment will buy what you are really after, and no amount should buy you. If you are being offered compensation, ask whether the true wrong has been answered. If you are the one offering, understand that riches alone will not mend this.
entries.context: In Iliad 9, Achilles answers the embassy sent by Agamemnon with a sweeping refusal: not even if Agamemnon gave him gifts as many as the grains of sand and dust would he win him over before paying back the bitter outrage.

aspects.love: If you have wronged someone you love, gifts will not mend it. Only honest acknowledgement can begin to.
aspects.work: No fee or settlement will satisfy a partner whose honour has been insulted. Address the insult first.
aspects.home: Do not try to buy back a family member's goodwill. Offer the respect that was denied.
aspects.health: Peace of mind cannot be bought. Look for its real source rather than piling up comforts.
aspects.journeys: No reward should tempt you into a decision your deepest self refuses. Stand firm.

entries.note: Only the opening survives: "So he spoke, praying…", words that begin several lines in Homer.

entries.greek: μηκέτι παῖδε φίλω πολεμίζετε μηδὲ μάχεσθον·
entries.english: Fight no more, dear sons, and stop your battle.
entries.reading: The time for fighting is over. Both sides have proven their worth, and to go on would only bring harm. Accept the truce with honour, exchange what courtesy you can, and rest; night has fallen on this quarrel.
entries.context: In Iliad 7, Hector and Ajax fight a long duel. As night falls and they are about to close with swords, the heralds Idaeus and Talthybius hold their staffs between them, and Idaeus tells them to fight no more, for Zeus loves them both and both are warriors. The two exchange gifts and part.

aspects.love: End the quarrel with the one you love. Both of you have made your point; let the day close in peace.
aspects.work: A rivalry has gone on long enough. Make an honourable truce, and even exchange tokens of respect.
aspects.home: Let the children or relatives who are at odds be parted kindly. Both are loved, and the fighting must stop.
aspects.health: You have been pushing hard. Night has come: stop, rest and recover your strength.
aspects.journeys: Lay down a struggle that cannot be won today. The road ahead will be clearer after a night's rest.

entries.greek: ἄλκιμος ἔσσʼ, ἵνα τίς σε καὶ ὀψιγόνων ἐὺ εἴπῃ.
entries.english: Be brave, so that those born in years to come may speak well of you.
entries.reading: Find your courage. What you do now will be told of later, and it is a time to act as one who will be well spoken of by those who come after. Leave behind childish things and take up your part with resolve.
entries.context: In Odyssey 1, Athena, disguised as Mentes, counsels the young Telemachus to seek news of his father and to deal with the suitors. She reminds him of the fame Orestes won by avenging his father, and urges him, tall and fine as he is, to be brave so that people in later times will speak well of him.

aspects.love: Act in love with courage and honour, as one whose conduct will be remembered with respect.
aspects.work: Take on the responsibility that has come to you. Your work now will build a name that lasts.
aspects.home: Step up for your family. It is time to protect your home as an adult, not wait for others to do it.
aspects.health: Strength of spirit supports the body. Take heart and stand tall.
aspects.journeys: The voyage or decision before you is your coming of age. Set out bravely.

entries.greek: στήλῃ κεκλιμένος ἀνδροκμήτῳ ἐπὶ τύμβῳ
entries.english: leaning against a pillar on a tomb built by men's hands.
entries.reading: Beware of the one who strikes from hiding. A threat may be aimed at you from a sheltered place, by someone who will not face you openly. Keep watch on your flanks, and do not be so intent on your prize that you leave yourself exposed.
entries.context: In Iliad 11, Paris takes aim at Diomedes with his bow, leaning against a pillar on the tomb of Ilus, the ancient elder of Troy. While Diomedes is stripping the armour from a fallen enemy, Paris shoots him through the foot.

aspects.love: Be wary of a rival who works against your love from the shadows. Guard what is precious to you.
aspects.work: While you are busy collecting the rewards of success, someone may strike at you unseen. Watch your back.
aspects.home: Old memories and old monuments can shelter new dangers. Be alert to quarrels rooted in the past.
aspects.health: Do not become so absorbed in your goals that you ignore small hurts. Attend to them before they lame you.
aspects.journeys: On the road, keep alert for hidden dangers, especially when you pause to rest or gather your gains.

entries.greek: ἔρχεο· πάρ τοι ὁδός, νῆες δέ τοι ἄγχι θαλάσσης
entries.english: Go: the road lies open before you, and your ships are close to the sea.
entries.reading: You are free to go. Nothing holds you here against your will, and the means of departure are close at hand. But know that others will stay and see the thing through, so be sure that leaving is truly what you want, not what discouragement tells you.
entries.context: In Iliad 9, Agamemnon, despairing after defeat, proposes that the Greeks sail home. Diomedes rebukes him: if his heart is set on going, let him go, the road is open and his ships stand by the sea; the rest of the Greeks will stay until Troy is taken, and even if they leave, Diomedes and Sthenelus will fight on.

aspects.love: You are free to leave this relationship if your heart truly wishes. Make sure the wish is not born of a passing despair.
aspects.work: The door is open for you to leave this position. Others will carry the work on; decide whether you would rather be among them.
aspects.home: Your home is near and the way to it is clear. If it is time to return, go.
aspects.health: If you need to step back and recover, the way is open. Do not push on from pride alone.
aspects.journeys: The ships are at the shore: you can make your move whenever you choose. Make sure it is courage, not defeat, that sends you.

entries.greek: ψευστήσεις, οὐδʼ αὖτε τέλος μύθῳ ἐπιθήσεις.
entries.english: You will be proved a liar, and you will not bring your words to pass.
entries.reading: A promise or boast is being made that will not come true. Be wary of declaring what will happen before it does, and test the oaths you are asked to swear. Cunning may be at work behind a plausible claim; examine it before you commit yourself.
entries.context: In Iliad 19, Agamemnon, making peace with Achilles, tells how even Zeus was blinded by Ate. When Zeus announced that a man of his blood born that day would rule his neighbours, Hera, planning deceit, told him he would prove a liar and not fulfil his word, and tricked him into an oath that let her delay Heracles' birth.

aspects.love: Promises made in love may not be kept. Look for deeds, and do not bind yourself with oaths on the strength of words.
aspects.work: A claim or forecast will not be fulfilled. Do not commit yourself to an agreement until you understand its terms fully.
aspects.home: Be wary of announcing family plans too soon. Hidden opposition may undo them.
aspects.health: Do not stake your peace on a single promise of a cure. Keep your expectations measured.
aspects.journeys: The plan as declared will not come to pass as stated. Leave room for change before you set out.

entries.greek: μήτηρ δʼ αὖθʼ ἑτέρωθεν ὀδύρετο δάκρυ χέουσα
entries.english: And on the other side his mother wept and wailed, shedding tears.
entries.reading: Listen to the voices of those who love you, even if you cannot do as they ask. Their tears are not weakness but wisdom of the heart. Weigh their plea seriously before you go out to meet your danger.
entries.context: In Iliad 22, Hector waits alone outside the walls of Troy for Achilles. Priam has begged him from the wall to come inside, tearing his grey hair; then on the other side his mother Hecuba weeps and wails, baring her breast and pleading with him to fight from within the walls. Hector does not yield.

aspects.love: Someone who loves you deeply is grieving over your choices. Let their tears soften your resolve.
aspects.work: Those who depend on you fear for the risk you are taking. Consider defending from within rather than going out alone.
aspects.home: Your parents' fear for you comes from love. Honour it by listening, even if you must decide otherwise.
aspects.health: Heed the counsel of those who care for you about your wellbeing. Their worry may see what you cannot.
aspects.journeys: Before you go out to meet your trial, hear those who plead with you to stay. Their pleas deserve an answer.

entries.greek: οὐδʼ εἰ πεντάετές γε καὶ ἑξάετες παραμίμνων
entries.english: not even if you stayed here five years, or six, to ask
entries.reading: There is no point in lingering to learn every detail of past sorrows. Some histories are too long to hear in full, and staying to ask would keep you from your own task. Take what wisdom you need and go home.
entries.context: In Odyssey 3, Telemachus visits Nestor at Pylos to ask news of his father. Nestor recalls the sufferings of the Greeks at Troy and the heroes who died there, saying that not even if Telemachus stayed five years or six to ask could he hear all their woes; he would grow weary and go home first.

aspects.love: Do not dwell endlessly on the past hurts of a relationship. Learn what you must and turn to the present.
aspects.work: Further enquiry will not yield much more. Gather the essential facts and return to your work.
aspects.home: Your home needs you more than the old stories do. Do not let nostalgia keep you away.
aspects.health: Rehearsing old pains wears you down. Let them rest and give your strength to today.
aspects.journeys: You have lingered long enough. It is time to bring your enquiry to a close and go home.

entries.greek: ὣς φάτο, καὶ Παιήονʼ ἀνώγειν ἰήσασθαι.
entries.english: So he spoke, and ordered Paeon the healer to heal him.
entries.reading: You come to the oracle wounded, perhaps by a fight you chose yourself, and this line answers that care is coming. Even one who has brought trouble on himself may be tended and made whole, though a rebuke may come with the remedy. Accept the reproach without bitterness and let the healing do its work; then consider whether you need to return to the quarrel that hurt you.
entries.context: In Iliad 5, Ares, wounded by Diomedes with Athena's help, flees to Olympus and complains to Zeus. Zeus scolds him as the most hateful of the gods for his love of strife, but because Ares is his own son he orders Paeon, the gods' healer, to cure him, and the wound closes at once.

aspects.love: A quarrel has left a wound between you and someone close; the one you hurt or who hurt you may still be willing to send for healing. Accept care even when it comes with a frank word about your part in the strife.
aspects.work: A setback at work was partly of your own making, yet help is available if you ask for it. Take the remedy offered and learn from the rebuke rather than resenting it.
aspects.home: Within the family, a stern parent or elder may scold and still protect you because you are their own. Let the bond of kinship do its mending work.
aspects.health: This is a favourable sign for recovery: seek out the skilled healer and follow the treatment. Rest from the fray that injured you while the cure takes hold.
aspects.journeys: Before you set out again, withdraw and recover fully, as Ares went up to Olympus to be healed. A change undertaken while still wounded would only reopen the hurt.

entries.greek: ταῦτά τοι, ὦ δύστηνε, τελευτήσω τε καὶ ἔρξω.
entries.english: All this, unhappy one, I will carry out and do for you.
entries.reading: The answer is a promise: what is owed will be done. If your question concerns a duty to someone absent, departed or easily forgotten, the oracle asks you to honour it fully and not leave it half-finished. A pledge given gently to one who cannot repay you is among the most binding of all. Speak your promise plainly, then carry it out.
entries.context: In Odyssey 11, at the edge of the Underworld, the ghost of Elpenor, the young comrade who fell from Circe's roof and was left unburied, begs Odysseus to return to Aeaea, burn his body with his armour and raise a mound with his oar upon it. Odysseus answers with this line, promising to do it all.

aspects.love: Someone needs you to remember them and to honour what you owe them, even if they are far away. Answer them gently and keep the promise you make.
aspects.work: An unfinished obligation to a former colleague or partner should be settled properly. Do the work thoroughly, so that nothing is left undone to trouble you later.
aspects.home: Care for the memory and the remains of those who came before you; a family duty to the departed asks for your attention. Honouring it will bring a quiet peace to your house.
aspects.health: Lay to rest something that still haunts you, so that it no longer follows you. A rite of farewell, however simple, can lighten the heart.
aspects.journeys: Before you go further, you may need to return somewhere to complete a task you left behind, as Odysseus returned to Aeaea. The way forward will be clearer once it is done.

entries.greek: πῶς ἐθέλεις ἅλιον θεῖναι πόνον ἠδʼ ἀτέλεστον,
entries.english: How can you wish to make my labour vain and come to nothing?
entries.reading: Something you have worked long and hard for seems about to be set aside, and your indignation is understandable. The oracle names the fear that effort will come to nothing, and gives you leave to say so openly to whoever holds the power to undo it. Yet remember that the one who speaks here is driven by anger, not wisdom; argue for the worth of your labour, but ask yourself whether its aim is still a good one.
entries.context: In Iliad 4, after the duel between Paris and Menelaus, Zeus teasingly proposes that the war might end in friendship and Troy be spared. Hera, who has toiled to gather the Greek army against Priam, protests furiously with this line, and Zeus gives way and lets the war resume.

aspects.love: You may feel that someone is undoing the care and effort you have put into a relationship. Tell them so, but ask whether your efforts were aimed at harmony or at winning.
aspects.work: Long toil on a project may be threatened by a decision from above. Make your case clearly to the one in authority; your sweat gives you the right to be heard.
aspects.home: A family plan you have worked to bring about may be overturned by another's whim. Speak plainly, but do not let your resentment poison the household.
aspects.health: Do not let anger at wasted effort exhaust you further. Guard your strength, for bitterness wears the body as much as labour does.
aspects.journeys: A long preparation may seem to have been for nothing, but the matter is not yet settled. Press your view, then accept that the final choice may not lie with you.

entries.greek: ὄψιμον ὀψιτέλεστον, ὅου κλέος οὔ ποτʼ ὀλεῖται.
entries.english: Late it comes, and late it is fulfilled, but its fame will never die.
entries.reading: What you hope for will not come quickly. The sign is slow in its fulfilment, but when it arrives it will be worth the waiting and long remembered. Do not take delay for refusal; hold your course through the long years as the Greeks held theirs. Patience here is not passivity but endurance with a purpose.
entries.context: In Iliad 2, as the Greek army nearly abandons the war, Odysseus reminds them of the portent at Aulis, where a serpent devoured eight sparrow chicks and their mother and was turned to stone. He recalls how the seer Calchas declared it a sign from Zeus, late in coming and late in fulfilment, meaning that they would fight nine years and take Troy in the tenth.

aspects.love: Love or friendship may come late, or take long to ripen, but what grows slowly here is meant to endure. Do not abandon it for something quicker.
aspects.work: Success in your work or trade will be slow in arriving, perhaps years in the making. Keep faith with the long effort; its reward is lasting reputation.
aspects.home: A hope for your family will be fulfilled, but in its own season. Let the household hold steady through the waiting years.
aspects.health: Healing or strength may return slowly; measure your progress in seasons, not days. Steady patience will serve you better than haste.
aspects.journeys: A long road lies ahead before the goal is reached, yet the sign points to its completion. Do not turn back in the ninth year when the tenth holds the prize.

entries.greek: πρίν κεν ἀνιηθεὶς σὴν πατρίδα γαῖαν ἵκοιο.
entries.english: You would grow weary and go home to your own country first.
entries.reading: The oracle answers that some troubles cannot be fully told or fully understood, and that searching out every detail would only wear you down. Do not exhaust yourself raking over the past or demanding a complete account of what went wrong. Take what you need to know, honour what was lost, and turn for home while you still have the strength.
entries.context: In Odyssey 3, Telemachus at Pylos asks old Nestor for news of his father. Nestor begins by saying that the sufferings of the Greeks at Troy are so many that if Telemachus stayed five or six years to hear them all, he would grow weary and sail home before the telling was done.

aspects.love: Do not demand that a loved one recount every hurt of the past; some stories are too heavy to tell in full. Listening with patience is enough.
aspects.work: Endless review of old failures will only weary you. Take the lesson you need and give your energy to the work at hand.
aspects.home: Family memories may hold more sorrow than can be spoken. Honour them, but do not let them keep you from home and from the people waiting there.
aspects.health: Rehearsing old pains can tire the spirit. Give yourself leave to set some memories down, as an old man might, and to rest.
aspects.journeys: If you are seeking answers far afield, know when you have heard enough. The time will come to stop asking and to head home.

entries.greek: ἐλθεῖν, ὄφρʼ ἔνθεν θυμοφθόρα φάρμακʼ ἐνείκῃ,
entries.english: to go there, and bring back poisons that destroy the life,
entries.reading: Others may be talking about your plans and imagining the worst of them, as idle and guilty people often do. Do not be drawn into answering their mockery; their fear tells you more about their conscience than about your purpose. Go about your errand quietly and openly, and let the outcome speak for you. If you yourself are tempted to harm in secret, the oracle warns against it.
entries.context: In Odyssey 2, Telemachus announces that he will sail to Pylos and Sparta for news of his father. The suitors mock him at their feast, one jeering that he may go to fertile Ephyra to fetch deadly poisons and drop them in the wine bowl to destroy them all.

aspects.love: People around you may whisper about your intentions and assume the worst. Let your conduct, steady and honest, answer them better than any argument.
aspects.work: Rivals may mock your ambitions while secretly fearing them. Pursue your plans openly and do not stoop to underhand means.
aspects.home: Unruly guests or members of the household may be gossiping about you. Keep your counsel and attend to setting your house in order.
aspects.health: Beware anything that harms by slow and hidden means, in body or in spirit. Choose what nourishes, and avoid what poisons, however pleasant it seems.
aspects.journeys: Your departure may be misread by those who stay behind. Go anyway, as Telemachus did; the journey is right even if others jeer.

entries.greek: ἆνερ ἀπʼ αἰῶνος νέος ὤλεο, κὰδ δέ με χήρην
entries.english: Husband, you have died young and left me a widow
entries.reading: This is a line of mourning, and it asks you to face a loss honestly rather than hurry past it. Something has ended before its time, and those left behind carry the weight of it. Give your grief its proper voice and place, as the Trojans did; but notice that Andromache grieves also for the child, for what must still be cared for. Tend what remains.
entries.context: In Iliad 24, Priam brings Hector's body home to Troy. As the singers lead the dirge, Andromache, holding Hector's head in her hands, begins her lament with these words: he has died young and left her a widow in the halls, with their son still an infant.

aspects.love: A bond may have ended too soon, by death, distance or circumstance. Let yourself mourn it truly, and speak your love even now.
aspects.work: A venture or position has been cut off before it could mature. Acknowledge the loss honestly before you build something new on its foundations.
aspects.home: Someone in the household is left vulnerable by a loss, perhaps a child or a widowed relative. Gather round them and share the weight.
aspects.health: Grief is a burden on the body; let it be expressed rather than locked away. The company of others who mourn can steady you.
aspects.journeys: A great change is forced upon you by loss. Do not decide everything at once; first give the sorrow its due season.

entries.greek: ᾗ περ δὴ φρονέω τε καὶ ὡς τετελεσμένον ἔσται,
entries.english: as I truly think, and as it will surely come to pass.
entries.reading: The oracle counsels plain speech. Say what you truly think and what you know will happen, without softening it to please others or hiding one thing while saying another. A clear refusal or a clear consent spares everyone the wearing murmur of persuasion. Be sure, though, that your certainty is earned and not merely stubbornness.
entries.context: In Iliad 9, Odysseus leads an embassy to Achilles, offering Agamemnon's gifts if he will return to battle. Achilles begins his reply by saying he must speak out bluntly, as he truly thinks and as things will be, because he hates the man who hides one thing in his heart and says another. The identification of this line in the papyrus is probable but marked as uncertain.

aspects.love: Say honestly what you feel and what you want; a heart that hides one thing and speaks another cannot be trusted. Clear words now spare pain later.
aspects.work: In negotiation, give a plain answer rather than letting others wear you down with offers. Make sure your firmness rests on sound judgement, not pride.
aspects.home: Family members may keep pressing you from every side. State your position once, clearly and kindly, so the murmuring can stop.
aspects.health: Be truthful with yourself and with any healer about how you really are. Honest reckoning is the first step to cure.
aspects.journeys: If you have already decided, say so and stop entertaining persuasion. But remember that Achilles' certainty was later overturned by grief.

entries.greek: μή μοι οἶνον ἄειρε μελίφρονα πότνια μῆτερ,
entries.english: Do not bring me honey-sweet wine, my lady mother,
entries.reading: A kind offer is being made to you, perhaps rest, ease or indulgence, and the oracle advises you to decline it for the present. The comfort is not wrong, but taking it now would loosen your strength when you most need it. Thank the giver warmly, keep your mind on the task, and leave the sweetness for when the work is done.
entries.context: In Iliad 6, Hector returns from battle to Troy to ask the women to pray to Athena. His mother Hecuba offers him honey-sweet wine to pour to Zeus and to restore his strength; Hector refuses with this line, saying it would weaken him and make him forget his courage, and that he will not pour libations with unwashed hands.

aspects.love: Affection offered at the wrong moment can distract you from a pressing duty. Receive the tenderness gratefully and return to it when your task is done.
aspects.work: This is not the time for rewards or indulgence; stay sharp and finish what you have begun. Celebration can wait for the end of the labour.
aspects.home: A parent's loving offer of comfort is to be honoured, even if you must decline it now. Explain yourself gently so that no hurt is left behind.
aspects.health: Abstain from what dulls or weakens you, especially strong drink, while you need all your strength. Clear-headedness is your best defence.
aspects.journeys: Do not linger at the halfway house of comfort. Make your visit brief and go back to where you are needed.

entries.greek: ὕστατα καὶ πύματα νῦν ἐνθάδε δειπνήσειαν·
entries.english: Let this be the last time, the very last, that they dine here.
entries.reading: Those who have been taking more than their due will not do so much longer. The oracle answers with Penelope's wish that a wrong which has gone on for too long should come to its end. Do not let yourself be consumed by those who use you; draw a line, and believe that it can be held. If you are the one who has been taking, take this as a warning.
entries.context: In Odyssey 4, the herald Medon comes to tell Penelope that the suitors are plotting to ambush and kill Telemachus on his way home. Before he can speak, she bitterly asks whether they have sent him to order her maids to prepare a feast, and wishes that this might be the very last time they dine in the house.

aspects.love: If someone has been taking from you without giving, the oracle wishes that it end. Do not keep setting the table for those who only consume.
aspects.work: Those who draw on your resources without right will not go on doing so for long. Protect what is yours and watch for any plot against you.
aspects.home: Unwelcome guests or demands are draining the household. Hold fast, guard the young ones, and trust that the end of the intrusion is near.
aspects.health: Wasteful habits that consume your strength should come to their final meal. Let this be the last time you indulge what harms you.
aspects.journeys: Someone dear to you is travelling and may be in danger from those who resent them. Keep watch, send word if you can, and pray for their safe return.

entries.greek: οὐ χρὴ παννύχιον εὕδειν βουληφόρον ἄνδρα
entries.english: A man who must give counsel should not sleep the whole night through.
entries.reading: If others depend on you, this is no time to rest easy. The oracle rouses you: a decision is waiting and the responsibility is yours. Rise, gather your thoughts and act.
