Yet weigh carefully the voice that wakes you; in Homer this message was a deception, so test any sudden urging before you stake everything on it.
entries.context: In Iliad 2, Zeus sends a deceptive Dream to Agamemnon in the likeness of Nestor. Standing over the sleeping king, the Dream rebukes him that a counsellor responsible for so many should not sleep all night, then falsely promises that he can take Troy that very day.

aspects.love: Do not drift in complacency in a relationship that needs your attention. Wake, take counsel, and act with care, but test any rumour before you believe it.
aspects.work: Responsibility for others rests on you, and you cannot afford to sleep through it. Rise early, think it through, and beware of plans that promise too easy a victory.
aspects.home: Those in your charge look to you for decision. Be alert, but do not let a single dream or rumour drive the whole household into rashness.
aspects.health: The line speaks of broken rest; guard your sleep, but do not use it to avoid what must be faced. A troubled mind needs both rest and resolution.
aspects.journeys: A sudden urging to act may come to you as if in a dream. Weigh it with trusted advisers before you commit; not every bright promise is sent in good faith.

entries.greek: δαιμόνιʼ οὐ μὲν καλὰ χόλον τόνδʼ ἔνθεο θυμῷ,
entries.english: Strange man, it is not right to nurse this anger in your heart.
entries.reading: You are holding on to a grievance while others bear the cost of your withdrawal. The oracle, speaking with Hector's sharpness, tells you that this anger is not fitting and that you are needed. Whatever slight you are nursing, put it down and take up your part again. A hard word from someone who cares may be the kindest thing you hear.
entries.context: In Iliad 6, Hector finds his brother Paris idling in his chamber, polishing his armour beside Helen, while the Trojans die around the walls in a war fought on his account. Hector rebukes him with this line and urges him back into battle.

aspects.love: You may be sulking while someone who loves you waits for you to return. Put aside the grudge; pride is a poor companion.
aspects.work: Others are labouring hard on a matter that is partly your responsibility. Leave the comfortable room and take up your share.
aspects.home: A brother or sister may be telling you hard truths. Hear them; the rebuke comes from someone who has the family's welfare at heart.
aspects.health: Brooding anger saps the body and the will. Let it go, and movement and purpose will return.
aspects.journeys: Do not withdraw from a struggle you started. The right decision now is to rejoin the field, not to hide from it.

entries.greek: τίς δʼ οἶδʼ εἴ κέ ποτέ σφι βίας ἀποτίσεται ἐλθών,
entries.english: Who knows whether he may come one day and repay their violence?
entries.reading: No one can say that the present injustice will last. The oracle offers hope without a promise: the one who has been wronged may yet return and set things right, alone or with help. Do not resign yourself, but neither rush into revenge; wait, prepare, and be ready to act when the time and the help arrive.
entries.context: In Odyssey 3, Telemachus tells Nestor of the suitors' outrages and laments that the gods have given him no power to punish them. Nestor answers with this line: who knows whether Odysseus may one day come home and pay them back for their violence, alone or with all the Achaeans.

aspects.love: If you have been wronged by someone, the matter is not yet closed; justice may come in time. Wait with dignity rather than bitterness.
aspects.work: Those who exploit you now may yet be called to account, perhaps with the help of allies you do not expect. Prepare quietly and gather support.
aspects.home: An absent member of the family may return and restore order. Keep the household together until then.
aspects.health: Do not let a sense of injustice gnaw at you; hope and patience are better for body and spirit. Keep your strength for when it is needed.
aspects.journeys: Seek out wise elders, as Telemachus sought Nestor, before you decide your course. Their counsel may show that the tide can still turn.

entries.greek: ἄξομαι ἀμφοτέροις ἀλόχους καὶ κτήματʼ ὀπάσσω
entries.english: I will find wives for them both, and give them possessions.
entries.reading: Faithfulness that has gone unseen is about to be recognised. The oracle answers with a master's promise to those who stayed true when others did not: there will be home, companionship and a share in what is restored. If you have been loyal, take heart; if you depend on the loyalty of others, remember to reward it generously.
entries.context: In Odyssey 21, Odysseus, still disguised, takes the faithful swineherd Eumaeus and cowherd Philoetius outside and reveals himself to them. He promises that if the gods let him overcome the suitors, he will give each of them a wife, possessions and a house near his own, and treat them as Telemachus' companions and brothers.

aspects.love: Faithful love or friendship will be recognised and rewarded. If someone has stood by you, tell them openly what they mean to you.
aspects.work: Loyal service will be repaid; if you lead others, reward the ones who stayed true through hard times. Generosity now binds them to you.
aspects.home: Those who kept your house in your absence deserve a place close to you. Bring them in as kin, and the household will be stronger.
aspects.health: Trust those who have cared for you faithfully; their steady presence is a kind of medicine. Let them share in your recovery.
aspects.journeys: A homecoming or a long-awaited return is near. Reveal yourself first to those you can trust, and enlist their help.

entries.greek: τόξου πειρώμεσθα καὶ ἐκτελέωμεν ἄεθλον.
entries.english: Let us try the bow, and see the contest through.
entries.reading: A test lies before you, and the oracle tells you to take it up and carry it to the end. Prepare well and make proper trial, rather than giving up at the first stiff resistance. But be honest about whether the task truly suits you; some bows are not for every hand, and preparation cannot replace the strength that is needed.
entries.context: In Odyssey 21, the suitor Leodes has failed to string Odysseus' great bow. Antinous scorns him and orders the goatherd Melanthius to light a fire and bring a cake of fat, so that the young men can warm and grease the bow, try it again and finish the contest.

aspects.love: A trial of a relationship is before you; prepare well and see it through rather than quitting at the first difficulty. Be honest about whether you are suited to the task.
aspects.work: A demanding test or competition awaits. Prepare your tools, practise, and try again, but know that preparation cannot make up for real strength.
aspects.home: A household task that has defeated others falls to you to attempt. Make ready with care, and do not boast before you succeed.
aspects.health: Warm and loosen yourself before any strenuous effort, as the bow was warmed. Steady preparation prevents injury.
aspects.journeys: Do not abandon the venture halfway; finish what you have begun. But watch who directs the contest, for not every master of ceremonies has your interest at heart.

entries.greek: οὐ γάρ τις νέμεσις φυγέειν κακόν, οὐδʼ ἀνὰ νύκτα.
entries.english: There is no shame in running from ruin, even by night.
entries.reading: The oracle permits you to step back from danger, and says there is no shame in escaping a harm rather than being caught by it. But be careful: in Homer this counsel came from a leader losing heart, and it was sharply rebuked. Withdraw if the situation is truly hopeless, yet do not let weariness disguise itself as prudence when others need you to stand firm.
entries.context: In Iliad 14, with the Trojans breaking through the Greek wall, Agamemnon despairs and proposes launching the ships at night and fleeing, saying there is no blame in escaping ruin even by night. Odysseus immediately rebukes him for the suggestion, and Diomedes urges the leaders back to the battle.

aspects.love: There may be no shame in leaving a situation that is truly harmful to you. Yet do not abandon a bond simply because it has become difficult.
aspects.work: Retreat from a failing venture can be wise, but test the proposal against the counsel of bolder colleagues. Odysseus would remind you that flight can betray those who rely on you.
aspects.home: If your home is threatened, you may rightly move your people to safety. Make sure the decision is shared, not taken in a moment of despair.
aspects.health: Stepping back from danger to protect your health is no weakness. Rest, regroup, and return when you are able.
aspects.journeys: A night departure or sudden change of plan is permitted, but not commanded. Seek a second opinion before you set out.

entries.greek: παντοίης ἀρετῆς μιμνήσκεο· νῦν σε μάλα χρὴ
entries.english: Remember all your courage. Now, above all, you must
entries.reading: The moment you have been preparing for, or fearing, has come, and there is no avoiding it now. Call up every strength and skill you possess and bring them to bear. This is a line of decisive confrontation; it does not tell you who will prevail, only that you must meet the test wholly and not halfway.
entries.context: In Iliad 22, Hector, facing Achilles at last before the walls of Troy, asks that the winner return the loser's body. Achilles refuses any pact and, with this line, tells Hector to remember all his prowess, for now he must be a spearman and bold warrior, since there is no escape left to him.

aspects.love: A decisive conversation can no longer be postponed. Bring all your honesty and courage to it, and do not hide behind half-measures.
aspects.work: A critical test of your skill is upon you. Draw on every lesson you have learned; this is the time to show your full worth.
aspects.home: A hard confrontation within the family must be faced. Stand firm, and speak with all the strength you have.
aspects.health: Rally your whole strength for the struggle ahead. Courage of spirit sustains the body when it is tested.
aspects.journeys: There is no way around the decision now; it must be met head-on. Choose with your whole heart and stand by your choice.

entries.greek: χήρην ἐν μεγάροισι· πάϊς δʼ ἔτι νήπιος αὔτως,
entries.english: a widow in the halls; and the child is still only a baby.
entries.reading: A loss has fallen, and the oracle turns your eyes to whoever is most vulnerable in its wake. Grief is right, but so is attention to the small and dependent ones who cannot fend for themselves. Ask who now needs your protection, and give it. Do not let sorrow make you forget the living.
entries.context: In Iliad 22, Andromache, hearing the cries from the wall, runs out and sees Achilles dragging Hector's body behind his chariot. When she recovers from her faint she laments that Hector has gone to the house of Hades, leaving her a widow in the halls and their son still a baby.

aspects.love: In the wake of a loss, the one who remains needs comfort and protection. Be present for them, even if you cannot mend what has broken.
aspects.work: When a leader or provider falls, those who depend on them are exposed. Step in to safeguard the vulnerable before you think of your own advancement.
aspects.home: A child or dependent may be left without their protector. Make their care your first concern.
aspects.health: Shock and grief can overwhelm the body; let others support you when you falter. Recovery begins when you allow yourself to be held.
aspects.journeys: A great change has been forced upon your household. Do not plan far ahead yet; secure the safety of the little ones first.

entries.greek: ἀλλὰ σὺ μὲν μή πω καταδύσεο μῶλον Ἄρηος
entries.english: But do not go into the struggle of war just yet.
entries.reading: Your cause may be just and your resolve strong, but the oracle says: do not plunge in yet. You are not properly equipped for this struggle, and what you need is on its way. Wait until it reaches you, then act. Haste now would waste the very courage that will be needed later.
entries.context: In Iliad 18, Achilles, grieving for Patroclus, vows to return to battle at once to kill Hector. His mother Thetis agrees the cause is good, but reminds him that Hector now wears his armour, and tells him not to enter the fighting until she returns at dawn with new arms from Hephaestus.

aspects.love: Your feelings may urge you to declare yourself at once, but the oracle bids you wait a little. Let things be made ready before you speak.
aspects.work: You are eager to enter the contest, but your tools or resources are not yet in place. Wait until what you need arrives, and you will be far stronger.
aspects.home: Listen to the counsel of a parent or elder who asks you to hold back until morning. Their delay is love, not doubt.
aspects.health: Do not rush back into strenuous activity before you are restored. Wait for the right moment and the right support.
aspects.journeys: A departure should be postponed until you are fully equipped. Set out at dawn, not in the dark.

entries.greek: αἶψα γὰρ ἐν κακότητι βροτοὶ καταγηράσκουσιν.
entries.english: For in hardship, mortals grow old before their time.
entries.reading: The oracle speaks with compassion about the toll of long trouble. You or someone close to you may be worn beyond their years by what they have endured, and this is no failing but the common lot of mortals. Treat that weariness with tenderness, and offer the simple care that restores. Recognition may be nearer than you think.
entries.context: In Odyssey 19, Penelope asks the old nurse Eurycleia to wash the feet of the disguised beggar, unaware that he is Odysseus. She remarks that Odysseus must by now look as this man does, for in misfortune mortals quickly grow old; moments later, Eurycleia recognises her master by his scar.

aspects.love: Someone you love may have been aged by their troubles; look for the familiar person beneath the weariness. Recognition and tenderness may be close.
aspects.work: Long hardship in your work has taken its toll. Acknowledge the strain, and seek conditions that let you recover your vigour.
aspects.home: An elder in the household carries the marks of long service; honour them with simple kindness. They may know you better than you think.
aspects.health: Stress and misfortune age the body before its time. Ease your burdens where you can, and accept care from those who offer it.
aspects.journeys: A return after long absence may find you changed and others not knowing you. Be patient as they learn to see you again.

entries.greek: οὐκ ἔσθʼ οὗτος ἀνὴρ διερὸς βροτὸς οὐδὲ γένηται,
entries.english: That man is not alive, and never will be born,
entries.reading: You have arrived somewhere strange and fear you will be unwelcome, but the oracle reassures you: no enemy waits here. Those you are afraid of are more likely to help than to harm. Approach openly and with courtesy, accept the hospitality offered, and let your fear settle.
entries.context: In Odyssey 6, the shipwrecked Odysseus appears, naked and salt-caked, before the princess Nausicaa and her maids, who flee in fright. Nausicaa calls them back, telling them that no man lives or will ever be born who could come to the land of the Phaeacians bringing war, for they are dear to the gods.

aspects.love: You fear rejection, but the person you approach is not an enemy. Come forward openly; welcome is more likely than you suppose.
aspects.work: In a new workplace or market, those you meet are well disposed. Present yourself with courtesy and you will be received.
aspects.home: Strangers in your home are not a threat but an opportunity for kindness. Offer them what hospitality you can.
aspects.health: Your fears may be larger than the danger. Let reassurance calm you, and accept the help that is near.
aspects.journeys: You are arriving in a land that will treat you well. Go on into the city and ask for guidance.

entries.greek: ναὶ δὴ ταῦτά γε τέκνον ἐτήτυμον οὐ κακόν ἐστι
entries.english: Yes, my child, this is true; it is no bad thing
entries.reading: The oracle affirms that what you mean to do is right: to stand by those who are struggling is no bad thing. But the line goes on to a caution, for a good cause still needs the proper means. Be sure you are equipped before you act, and accept advice from those who love you about when and how to begin.
entries.context: In Iliad 18, Achilles declares that he will go back to battle and avenge Patroclus even if it costs him his life. Thetis replies with this line, agreeing that it is good to defend his hard-pressed comrades from destruction, but warns that his armour is now in Hector's hands.

aspects.love: Your wish to stand by a friend in trouble is good and true. Make sure you have what you need to help them before you rush in.
aspects.work: Coming to the aid of colleagues in difficulty is honourable. Secure your equipment and support first, or your help may fail.
aspects.home: A mother's counsel is to be heeded: she agrees with your purpose but warns you of what you lack. Accept her help.
aspects.health: Your desire to act is sound, but your strength must be restored first. Wait for what will protect you.
aspects.journeys: The cause that calls you away is worthy. Prepare properly, and set out only once you are armed for the road.

entries.greek: οὔ οἱ νῦν ἔτι γʼ ἔστι πεφυγμένον ἄμμε γενέσθαι,
entries.english: Now there is no way left for him to escape us,
entries.reading: The oracle answers that the matter is settled: what you have been pursuing can no longer slip away. Pause, catch your breath, and trust that the outcome is now in hand. Yet consider the cost of victory and how you will carry it; what is won in Homer here is also the beginning of a great grief.
entries.context: In Iliad 22, after Zeus weighs the fates and Hector's sinks, Apollo abandons him. Athena comes to Achilles and tells him that now Hector cannot escape them, even if Apollo grovels before Zeus, and bids him stand and rest while she persuades Hector to fight.

aspects.love: A matter of the heart has reached its decisive point. Rest a moment, then act, mindful that every victory has another side.
aspects.work: The deal or contest is all but won; what you have pursued cannot now escape you. Handle the final stage with care and without cruelty.
aspects.home: A long family struggle is coming to its end. Take a breath before the last step, and think of how you will live with the result.
aspects.health: Stand and breathe, as Athena bade Achilles; recovery of your breath and strength comes before the final effort.
aspects.journeys: The way is settled and the outcome assured. Proceed, but remember that triumph can bring its own sorrows.

entries.greek: χαλκοῦ τε χρυσοῦ τʼ ἀπολυσόμεθʼ, ἔστι γὰρ ἔνδον·
entries.english: We will ransom them with bronze and gold, for there is plenty inside.
entries.reading: Something dear to you is missing or in someone else's power, and the oracle says it may yet be recovered if you are willing to pay its price. You have resources enough, and this is the time to use them. But the line carries uncertainty, for Priam does not yet know whether his sons live; prepare for both outcomes and hope wisely.
entries.context: In Iliad 22, Priam begs Hector from the walls not to face Achilles alone. He speaks of his sons Lycaon and Polydorus, whom he cannot find in the city, and says that if they are alive among the Greeks he will ransom them with bronze and gold, of which there is plenty in the house; he does not know that both are already dead at Achilles' hands.

aspects.love: Someone dear may feel lost to you, but the bond may yet be bought back by generosity and effort. Give freely, though the outcome is not certain.
aspects.work: You have the resources to recover what is lost; use your wealth wisely to redeem it. Do not hoard when spending can restore.
aspects.home: A father's anxious love for absent children speaks here. Do all you can for those who are missing, and keep the rest of the family from rash danger.
aspects.health: Invest in your recovery, whatever it costs; health once lost may be regained. But prepare yourself gently for news you may not want.
aspects.journeys: Before you face a dangerous road, listen to those who beg you to stay safe. Their pleading comes from love and loss.

entries.greek: πῖνέ τε, μηδʼ ἐρίδαινε μετʼ ἀνδράσι κουροτέροισιν.
entries.english: Drink, and do not quarrel with men younger than yourself.
entries.reading: The oracle repeats a warning given by an insolent man: stay quiet, enjoy what you have, and do not challenge those who think themselves your betters. Read it with care, for in Homer the one warned was in the right and the one warning was soon to fall. It counsels you not to pick a quarrel needlessly, but it does not ask you to give up your rightful claim; bide your time.
entries.context: In Odyssey 21, the disguised Odysseus asks to try the bow. Antinous, alarmed, scolds him as a drunken beggar, recalls how the Centaur Eurytion was maimed for drunken folly, threatens to ship him to the cruel King Echetus, and ends by telling him to drink in peace and not compete with younger men.

aspects.love: Someone may try to keep you in your place by telling you that you are too old or too humble to compete. Stay calm, but do not believe them.
aspects.work: A rival who feels threatened may belittle you to keep you from the contest. Avoid a public squabble and let your skill decide the matter when the moment comes.
aspects.home: Overbearing people in your house may tell you to sit quietly and accept your lot. Keep your peace for now; the master of the house is not always the one who shouts.
aspects.health: The line warns against drinking to excess and against heated quarrels. Moderation in both will protect you.
aspects.journeys: Do not let threats of exile or hardship scare you away from what is yours. Wait patiently for your chance, rather than fleeing or fighting at the wrong moment.

entries.greek: πῇ φεύγεις μετὰ νῶτα βαλὼν κακὸς ὣς ἐν ὁμίλῳ;
entries.english: Where are you running, turning your back like a coward in the crowd?
entries.reading: You may be tempted to turn and run while someone near you is in danger. The oracle calls you back sharply: flight leaves your back exposed and your companion abandoned. Stand your ground, at least long enough to help one who cannot save himself. Courage here is measured by loyalty, not by victory.
entries.context: In Iliad 8, Zeus turns the battle against the Greeks, and Nestor is trapped when Paris shoots one of his horses. As Hector charges at him, Diomedes shouts to Odysseus with this line, asking where he is fleeing and urging him to stay and save the old man; Odysseus does not hear and runs on to the ships, so Diomedes rescues Nestor alone.

aspects.love: A friend or partner needs you to stay when things become frightening. Do not turn your back; your presence may be all that saves them.
aspects.work: When a project goes badly, do not abandon the colleague left exposed. Stand with them, and others may follow your example.
aspects.home: An elder in your family may need protection at a perilous moment. Be the one who turns back to help.
aspects.health: Panic urges flight, but steadiness serves you better. Breathe, stand, and face what frightens you.
aspects.journeys: Before you hurry away from a difficulty, ask who you are leaving behind. A decision to stay may be the braver one.

entries.greek: αἲ γὰρ ἐμοὶ τοιόσδε πόσις κεκλημένος εἴη
entries.english: If only such a man might be called my husband,
entries.reading: The oracle speaks of admiration and longing: someone has come into your life who seems far greater than you first supposed. Your hopes may be stirring, and they are honourable ones. Yet hold them lightly, for not every admired stranger is free to stay. Show kindness and welcome, and let what is meant to be unfold.
entries.context: In Odyssey 6, after Odysseus has bathed in the river and Athena has made him tall and handsome, Nausicaa marvels at the change. She tells her maids that he who seemed so wretched now looks like a god, wishes aloud that such a man might be her husband and stay among them, and orders them to give him food and drink.

aspects.love: A person may have caught your heart unexpectedly, appearing far nobler than at first sight. Cherish the feeling, but remember that their path may lead elsewhere.
aspects.work: Someone who seemed unremarkable may prove to be of great worth. Treat newcomers with respect; first impressions deceive.
aspects.home: You may wish that a newcomer would settle among your family. Offer generous welcome, without pressing them to stay.
aspects.health: Care and rest can transform a person who was exhausted and battered. Give yourself the bath and the meal, and see how you are renewed.
aspects.journeys: A guest you meet may be passing through toward their own home. Help them on their way, and the meeting will still have been a blessing.

entries.greek: οὐρανῷ ἐστήριξε κάρη καὶ ἐπὶ χθονὶ βαίνει·
entries.english: Her head strikes the heavens while she walks upon the earth.
entries.reading: This is a warning about how quarrels grow: they begin small and soon fill the sky. If you are on the edge of a dispute, know that once it is set going it will not stay modest. Ask yourself whether it is worth the groaning it may bring, and if you can, quench the spark before it becomes a blaze.
entries.context: In Iliad 4, after the truce is broken, the armies advance into battle for the first time in the poem. The narrator describes the gods who drive them on, among them Strife, sister and comrade of Ares, who rises small at first but soon has her head in the heavens while she walks the earth, spreading conflict and grief among men.

aspects.love: A small irritation between you and someone close could swell into a great rift. Speak gently now, before it reaches the sky.
aspects.work: A minor dispute with a colleague or customer can quickly escalate. Address it early and with calm, or it will consume everyone's effort.
aspects.home: Watch for the first stirrings of discord in the house. What begins with a cross word can soon fill every room.
aspects.health: Anger that seems minor at first can grow until it dominates your thoughts and body. Do not feed it.
aspects.journeys: A decision taken in a spirit of contention will grow larger than you intend. Choose your course from peace, not from strife.

entries.greek: ἀλλʼ οὐ Ζεὺς ἄνδρεσσι νοήματα πάντα τελευτᾷ·
entries.english: But Zeus does not bring every plan of men to fulfilment.
entries.reading: The oracle answers soberly: not all that you intend will come to pass. You may have made confident promises, perhaps to others, which the gods will not fulfil. Accept that some outcomes lie beyond your power, and let this teach humility in what you promise. Grief at a broken hope is natural, but do not blame yourself for what was never yours to command.
entries.context: In Iliad 18, Achilles mourns over the body of Patroclus and laments to the Myrmidons. He recalls promising Patroclus' father Menoetius that he would bring his son home with a share of the plunder from Troy, and says with this line that Zeus does not fulfil all men's plans, for both of them are fated to die at Troy.

aspects.love: A promise you made about the future of a relationship may not be kept, through no fault of yours. Grieve, and be gentler in what you vow.
aspects.work: Your plans and forecasts may not come out as you hoped. Prepare for a different result and do not stake everything on a single outcome.
aspects.home: Assurances given to a parent or family member may prove beyond your power. Be honest with them about what you can and cannot do.
aspects.health: Not every plan for recovery goes as hoped. Accept the limits of what can be done, and find peace within them.
aspects.journeys: A return or a goal you have promised may not be reached. Choose your course knowing the outcome is not entirely in your hands.

entries.greek: νεῦσε δέ οἱ λαὸν σόον ἔμμεναι οὐδʼ ἀπολέσθαι.
entries.english: He nodded his promise that the people would be safe and would not perish.
entries.reading: This is a line of mercy. Your earnest plea, made in distress, has been heard, and the oracle promises that what you most fear, total ruin, will not come. Not every loss will be averted, but your people will be spared. Take heart, and watch for the sign that confirms it.
entries.context: In Iliad 8, with the Greeks driven back to their ships by Hector, Agamemnon weeps and prays to Zeus to let at least his men escape with their lives. Zeus pities him and nods his promise that the army will be saved, and at once sends an eagle with a fawn in its talons, which it drops by his altar.

aspects.love: A sincere appeal you have made for someone you love has been heard. The bond will survive this trial.
aspects.work: Though the venture is under great pressure, it will not be destroyed. Hold steady; relief is coming.
aspects.home: Your household is under protection; those you fear for will be kept safe. Give thanks, and continue to watch over them.
aspects.health: A good omen for those who have prayed for recovery. The danger will pass, though there may still be hardship.
aspects.journeys: Your plea for a safe way through has been granted. Look for a clear sign before you move, then go forward with courage.

entries.greek: μὴ ὄφελες λίσσεσθαι ἀμύμονα Πηλεΐωνα
entries.english: You should never have pleaded with the noble son of Peleus,
entries.reading: You may have been begging someone to change their mind, offering more and more to win them over. The oracle says that this only hardens a proud heart. Stop pleading; leave them to come or go as they will, and turn to what you can do yourself. Your strength is better spent on your own resolve.
entries.context: In Iliad 9, the embassy returns from Achilles with his refusal to fight. In the silence that follows, Diomedes tells Agamemnon that he should never have begged Achilles with countless gifts, since he was proud enough already and is now prouder, and urges the Greeks to rest and fight on without him.

aspects.love: Pleading with someone who holds themselves aloof only feeds their pride. Let them go their way; if they return, it must be by their own choice.
aspects.work: Repeated offers to an unwilling partner or client will not win them. Withdraw the offer and rely on your own team.
aspects.home: A family member who refuses reconciliation will not be moved by gifts. Leave the door open, but stop knocking.
aspects.health: Do not exhaust yourself trying to change what will not change. Conserve your strength for what lies within your power.
aspects.journeys: Do not wait upon another's consent before you go forward. Rest tonight, and at dawn take up the work yourself.

entries.greek: οἶνός σε τρώει μελιηδής, ὅς τε καὶ ἄλλους
entries.english: The honey-sweet wine has gone to your head, as it does to others,
entries.reading: The oracle speaks a warning about excess. Something sweet has gone to your head, whether wine, praise or ambition, and it may make you bold beyond your sense. Take only what is fitting. But note that in Homer these words were flung by a scornful man at one who was wiser than he looked; check whether the accusation fits you before accepting it.
entries.context: In Odyssey 21, the disguised Odysseus asks the suitors to let him try the bow, to test whether his old strength remains. Antinous, fearing he may succeed, rebukes him with this line, saying the sweet wine has harmed him as it harms anyone who gulps it without measure, and begins the tale of the Centaur Eurytion.

aspects.love: Intoxication, whether of drink or infatuation, can lead you to say or do what you will regret. Keep a clear head in matters of the heart.
aspects.work: Do not let early success make you reckless. Measure is the mark of a capable worker.
aspects.home: Excess at the table can bring quarrels into the house. Keep feasts temperate, and the household peaceful.
aspects.health: This is a plain warning against drinking greedily or without measure. Take care of yourself with moderation.
aspects.journeys: Decide nothing important while your judgement is clouded. Wait until you are sober in mind and body.

entries.greek: ἔρξον ὅπῃ δή τοι νόος ἔπλετο, μὴ δʼ ἔτʼ ἐρώει.
entries.english: Do as your mind is set on doing, and hold back no longer.
entries.reading: The oracle gives you leave: do what you have resolved, and hold back no longer. Hesitation has had its time, and those whose word counts are no longer standing in your way. Act decisively, but know the weight of what you set in motion, for this permission in Homer sealed a great man's fate.
entries.context: In Iliad 22, as Achilles chases Hector around the walls of Troy, Zeus wonders aloud whether to save Hector. Athena objects that his death is long fated, and Zeus yields, telling her with this line to act as she intends and delay no longer; she darts down from Olympus to the plain.

aspects.love: If you have long been resolved on a course in love, the way is now open. Act, but act with care for the other person.
aspects.work: Your superiors have stepped aside and the decision is yours. Proceed with what you have planned, without further delay.
aspects.home: A family elder has given way to your wishes. Use that freedom responsibly, for the consequences will touch everyone.
aspects.health: If you have decided on a course of treatment or a change in your way of life, begin it now. Lingering doubt only wastes strength.
aspects.journeys: You have permission to go; the hesitation is over. Set out swiftly, knowing that the decision cannot be easily undone.

entries.greek: ἄμφω γὰρ πέπρωται ὁμοίην γαῖαν ἐρεῦσαι
entries.english: For both of us are fated to redden the same earth.
entries.reading: The oracle speaks of a bond so close that two lives must follow the same course. Whatever you are asking, it reminds you that you are not alone in your fate; another walks the same road, for good or ill. Honour that companionship, and do not pretend that one of you can escape while the other suffers.
entries.context: In Iliad 18, Achilles laments over Patroclus to the Myrmidons. He says that he promised Menoetius to bring Patroclus home, but that both of them are fated to redden the same earth at Troy, since he too will never return to his father Peleus or his mother Thetis.

aspects.love: You and another are bound to share one destiny. Let this make you faithful companions rather than rivals.
aspects.work: Your fortunes are tied to those of a partner or colleague. Rise or fall, you will do it together; plan accordingly.
aspects.home: The fate of one family member is linked with yours. Stand by them, for you cannot be separated by what is to come.
aspects.health: The line touches mortality; it asks you to hold close those who share your path and to make good use of the time you have.
aspects.journeys: The road ahead may not lead back home. Choose it knowingly, and choose companions you would be glad to fall beside.

entries.greek: βάλλʼ οὕτως, αἴ κέν τι φόως Δαναοῖσι γένηαι
entries.english: Keep shooting like this, and you may become a light to the Greeks.
entries.reading: What you are doing now is working; carry on in the same way. The oracle praises steady skill and promises that it may bring you honour and make you a light to others. Remember, too, those who raised you and took you in; your success can bring them glory as well.
entries.context: In Iliad 8, the archer Teucer, sheltering behind the shield of his half-brother Ajax, shoots down Trojan after Trojan. Agamemnon, delighted, encourages him with this line to keep shooting, so that he may become a light to the Greeks and bring glory to his father Telamon, who brought him up in his house though he was not his wife's son.

aspects.love: The care you are giving is right and is being noticed. Continue, and your love will be a light to those around you.
aspects.work: Your steady effort is bearing fruit and has caught the eye of those in authority. Keep to your method; reward and recognition will follow.
aspects.home: Make your family proud, especially those who took you in and raised you. Your success honours them as much as you.
aspects.health: Your present routine is serving you well. Persevere with it, and stay close to those who protect you.
aspects.journeys: This is not a time to change course. Continue as you are, and the road will open of itself.

entries.greek: ὡς οὐκ ἔσθʼ ὃς σῆς γε κύνας κεφαλῆς ἀπαλάλκοι,
entries.english: So there is no one who could keep the dogs from your head,
entries.reading: This is one of the oracle's hardest answers. What you hope to buy your way out of cannot be bought; no price or promise will change the mind of the one you face. Do not waste yourself in pleading, and do not trust in wealth to save you here. Look instead to what you can still do with dignity, and to the help that may come later from unexpected quarters.
entries.context: In Iliad 22, Hector lies mortally wounded and begs Achilles to accept ransom from his parents and return his body to Troy for burial. Achilles refuses with savage contempt, saying that no one will keep the dogs from Hector's head, not even if ten or twenty times the ransom were brought, or his weight in gold.

aspects.love: Someone's heart is closed to you at present, and no gift or plea will open it. Do not humble yourself further; preserve your dignity.
aspects.work: A hard bargain is not open to negotiation, however much you offer. Stop bidding, and protect what you still have.
aspects.home: A family feud has hardened beyond the reach of payment or persuasion for now. Leave it, and trust that time, as with Priam later, may soften what anger has fixed.
aspects.health: Some things cannot be reversed by any expense. Accept what is beyond remedy, and turn your care to comfort and peace.
aspects.journeys: Do not stake a decision on buying your way out of a dangerous position. Choose a course that does not depend on another's mercy.

entries.greek: οὐ μέν με κτενέεις, ἐπεὶ οὔ τοι μόρσιμός εἰμι.
entries.english: You will not kill me, for I am not fated to die by you.
entries.reading: You are pursuing something that is not yours to overcome. The oracle tells you plainly that it will not fall to you, however hard you chase, and that your efforts are drawing you away from where you are truly needed. Stop and look around: the work that matters may be back where you left it.
entries.context: At the start of Iliad 22, Apollo, who in the guise of the Trojan Agenor has lured Achilles away from Troy so that the routed Trojans can escape into the city, reveals himself and mocks Achilles, telling him with this line that he cannot kill him, for he is not fated to die. Achilles, furious at the deception, races back toward the walls.

aspects.love: You may be chasing someone who will never be yours. Let go of the pursuit, and turn back to those who are close at hand.
aspects.work: A goal you are straining after is not within your reach, and the chase is costing you real opportunities. Return to the task that matters.
aspects.home: While you pursue a distraction, events at home are moving without you. Go back before the gates are shut.
aspects.health: You cannot defeat what is beyond mortal power by sheer effort. Rest, and spend your strength where it can do good.
aspects.journeys: The road you are racing along leads nowhere useful. Turn around; your real purpose lies behind you.

entries.greek: ἐνθάδε κʼ αὖθι μένων σὺν ἐμοὶ τόδε δῶμα φυλάσσοις
entries.english: Stay here with me instead, and guard this house,
entries.reading: You are being offered comfort, safety and perhaps a kind of permanence if you will remain where you are. The offer is generous and sincere, but the oracle asks whether it would cost you what you most long for. If your heart is set on another home, honour that longing even though the road is hard. Choose with your eyes open to both the gift and the price.
entries.context: In Odyssey 5, the nymph Calypso, ordered by the gods to let Odysseus go, shares a last meal with him. She warns that if he knew the sorrows awaiting him before he reached home, he would stay with her, keep her house and become immortal, however much he yearned for his wife; Odysseus still chooses to leave.

aspects.love: Someone offers you devotion and security, but your heart may belong elsewhere. Do not stay out of comfort alone; be honest with them and with yourself.
aspects.work: A secure and generous position is offered on condition that you give up a deeper ambition. Weigh whether its ease is worth the loss.
aspects.home: The longing for your true home is not to be dismissed, even when another place is pleasant. Let it guide you.
aspects.health: Rest and recovery in a sheltered place have their season, but staying too long can become a gentle captivity. Know when you are well enough to go.
aspects.journeys: You are warned that the road ahead holds hardship. Go if your purpose is true, but leave with gratitude, not haste.

entries.greek: εἶκε, γέρον, προθύρου, μὴ δὴ τάχα καὶ ποδὸς ἕλκῃ.
entries.english: Get away from the doorway, old man, before you are dragged off by the foot.
entries.reading: Someone is trying to drive you away from a place where you have every right to be. They speak with bluster, but the oracle hints that they are weaker than they appear. Do not be cowed by threats from a loud and empty challenger; stand your ground calmly, and the matter may turn quickly in your favour.
entries.context: In Odyssey 18, a burly but feeble beggar of Ithaca named Arnaeus, nicknamed Irus, arrives at the palace and tries to chase the disguised Odysseus away from the doorway with this threat. The suitors set them to fight for sport, and Odysseus fells Irus with a single blow.

aspects.love: A rival may try to elbow you out with noise and swagger. Stay where you are; their boldness is mostly show.
aspects.work: Someone who guards a position jealously may threaten you. Do not yield the threshold; your quiet strength is greater than their bluster.
aspects.home: In your own house, someone may treat you as an intruder. Hold firm with restraint, and do not use more force than the situation requires.
aspects.health: Do not let a loud fear drive you from what sustains you. When faced squarely, it may prove to have little power.
aspects.journeys: Being told to move on does not mean you must go. Consider whether you belong where you stand before you surrender it.

entries.greek: βέλτερον ὃς φεύγων προφύγῃ κακὸν ἠὲ ἁλώῃ.
entries.english: Better to run and escape from trouble than to be caught.
entries.reading: The oracle grants that it is better to escape harm than to be taken by it. If you face a danger you cannot overcome, there is wisdom in getting clear. But weigh who is speaking: in Homer this counsel came from a disheartened king and was firmly rejected by wiser companions. Flee real ruin, not mere difficulty.
entries.context: In Iliad 14, as the Trojans press the Greeks back to their ships, Agamemnon proposes launching the ships by night and sailing away, concluding with this line that it is better to flee and escape disaster than to be caught. Odysseus rebukes him angrily, and Diomedes rallies the leaders to return to the battle.

aspects.love: If a relationship has become truly dangerous to you, leaving is better than being trapped. If it is only hard, stay and work with others to save it.
aspects.work: Escaping a failing enterprise may be prudent, but do not make that judgement alone and in despair. Consult those who will tell you the truth.
aspects.home: Getting your household out of harm's way is a worthy aim. Ensure that the danger is real and not a counsel of fear.
aspects.health: Remove yourself from what is harming you before it takes hold. Prevention is better than being caught.
aspects.journeys: A swift departure may be the safest course, but listen to the voices that argue against it before you decide.

entries.greek: μηδέ τῳ ἐκφάσθαι μήτʼ ἀνδρῶν μήτε γυναικῶν,
entries.english: and tell no one, neither man nor woman,
entries.reading: The oracle counsels silence. Do not reveal your purpose or your trouble to anyone yet, man or woman; endure in secret what must be endured. Your time is not yet come, and to speak too soon would undo the plan. Patience and discretion are your shield now, and you are not without divine help.
entries.context: In Odyssey 13, Odysseus wakes on Ithaca, and Athena reveals herself to him. She promises to help him hide the Phaeacians' gifts and to plan the suitors' downfall, and warns him that he must endure many sorrows in his own house, telling no one, man or woman, that he has come home, but suffering in silence the insolence of men.

aspects.love: Keep your feelings or intentions private for now. The moment for revealing them will come, and it will be stronger for having waited.
aspects.work: Guard your plans closely; disclosure would expose you to those who would thwart you. Work quietly and gather your resources.
aspects.home: Even within the household, be sparing with what you reveal. Bear slights patiently until order can be restored.
aspects.health: You may have a burden that you cannot yet share; carry it with care, and find a trusted source of strength to sustain you.
aspects.journeys: You have arrived, or are about to, but should not announce yourself. Observe first, then act.

entries.greek: πυρῶν ἢ κριθῶν· τὰ δὲ δράγματα ταρφέα πίπτει·
entries.english: of wheat or barley, and the cut handfuls fall thick and fast.
entries.reading: This line is an image of reapers meeting from either end of a rich man's field, the sheaves falling thick, a picture the poet uses for armies cutting each other down. It warns that a struggle, once joined in earnest, will bring heavy losses on both sides. If you are entering a contest, count its cost; if you are reaping a real harvest, work steadily, for there is much to gather.
entries.context: In Iliad 11, as Agamemnon's great day of fighting begins, the Trojans and Greeks charge into each other. The poet compares them to two lines of reapers moving towards each other across a wealthy man's field of wheat or barley, with the cut handfuls falling thick, so that neither side thinks of flight.

aspects.love: Two people locked in a contest of wills will both lose much. Seek a way to work together in the same field rather than against each other.
aspects.work: Abundant work lies before you, and steady hands will bring in a great harvest. But a fierce rivalry would consume the profits of both parties.
aspects.home: A family that labours together prospers, while one that turns on itself is cut down. Choose cooperation.
aspects.health: Heavy labour must be balanced with rest; do not let the pace of reaping exhaust you.
aspects.journeys: A decision to engage in open conflict will bring loss on every side. Weigh carefully whether the field is worth the cost.

entries.greek: ὁπποῖόν κʼ εἴπῃσθα ἔπος, τοῖόν κʼ ἐπακούσαις.
entries.english: Whatever word you speak, that word will you hear in return.
entries.reading: The oracle reminds you that whatever words you send out will come back to you in the same coin. Insults breed insults; courtesy invites courtesy. If you are caught in a war of words, stop trading taunts and turn to deeds, or to peace. Be careful what you say, for you will hear it again.
entries.context: In Iliad 20, Aeneas faces Achilles in battle. After Achilles taunts him, Aeneas recites his lineage and says they should stop exchanging insults like children, for the human tongue is supple and full of words, and the kind of word one speaks is the kind one hears in return; he then hurls his spear.

aspects.love: Harsh words to someone you love will return to you in kind. Speak gently, and you will be answered gently.
aspects.work: In disputes with rivals or customers, insults will only multiply. Let your work answer for you rather than your tongue.
aspects.home: Quarrels in the family feed upon themselves. Be the first to stop the exchange of blame.
aspects.health: Bitter speech, even inwardly, wounds the speaker. Choose words that heal your own spirit as well as others'.
aspects.journeys: Before you set out on a course of confrontation, remember that every challenge will be answered. Choose words you can bear to hear repeated.

entries.greek: οὐκ εἴασχʼ Ἑλένην δόμεναι ξανθῷ Μενελάῳ,
entries.english: would not let Helen be given back to fair-haired Menelaus.
entries.reading: This line tells of a man who took gold to keep a wrong in place, and of the price his sons later paid. The oracle warns you against being bought, or against counselling others for gain against what is right. Whatever profit you make by blocking justice may fall heavily on those you love. Choose honesty, even when it costs you.
entries.context: In Iliad 11, during Agamemnon's onslaught, the narrator describes how he kills Peisander and Hippolochus, sons of Antimachus. Antimachus was the Trojan who, having taken Paris' gold and splendid gifts, most strongly opposed giving Helen back to Menelaus; his sons now beg for their lives and are refused.

aspects.love: Do not let gifts or advantages persuade you to stand in the way of what is right between people. The cost may fall on others you care for.
aspects.work: Refuse any reward offered to keep you silent or to block a fair settlement. Corrupt gain brings ruin on the whole house.
aspects.home: The choices of a parent can fall heavily on the children. Act so that your family will not pay for your greed.
aspects.health: A conscience burdened by wrongdoing weighs on the body. Set the matter right and be free of it.
aspects.journeys: A decision taken for money against justice will not end well. Choose the path you could defend before all.

entries.greek: ἦ τι μεταστρέψεις; στρεπταὶ μέν τε φρένες ἐσθλῶν.
entries.english: Will you change your mind a little? The hearts of good men can be turned.
entries.reading: The oracle asks you gently: will you change your mind a little? A noble heart is not rigid, and to yield to wise counsel is no defeat. If you are standing on your pride, consider giving way, especially to those older or with a rightful claim. If you are seeking to persuade someone else, speak to the good in them.
entries.context: In Iliad 15, Zeus sends Iris to order Poseidon to withdraw from the battle. Poseidon angrily insists that he is Zeus' equal in honour. Iris asks whether she must carry this harsh reply back, or whether he will relent a little, since the hearts of the noble can be turned and the Furies always side with the elder; Poseidon yields.

aspects.love: Relent a little in a quarrel with someone dear; it costs you less than you fear and may gain much. The noble heart can bend.
aspects.work: A stubborn position may be weakening your cause. Moderate your demand, and acknowledge the authority you cannot defeat.
aspects.home: Respect for elders keeps a household whole. Soften your stance towards a parent or older sibling, even if you feel equal to them.
aspects.health: Rigidity of mind can become rigidity of body. Allow yourself to change your habits or your treatment if wiser counsel advises it.
aspects.journeys: Do not cling to a plan merely because you have declared it. A wise change of course is a sign of strength.

entries.greek: αὐτὰρ ἐγὼ τὸ μὲν οὔ ποτʼ ἀπίστεον, ἀλλʼ ἐνὶ θυμῷ
entries.english: But I never doubted it; in my heart I knew
entries.reading: The oracle speaks with a protector's reassurance: someone who watches over you never doubted that you would come through, though you have lost much on the way. What has seemed like abandonment was a waiting for the right time. Take courage; the help you need is at your side, and your homecoming, in whatever form, was always foreseen.
entries.context: In Odyssey 13, on Ithaca, Athena reveals herself and praises Odysseus' caution. She says that she never doubted but knew in her heart that he would return home after losing all his companions, but that she did not wish to fight her father's brother Poseidon, who was angry with him for blinding his son.

aspects.love: Someone has kept faith in you all along, even when they seemed absent. Their love has been quieter than you knew.
aspects.work: A mentor or patron believed in your success from the start. Their support now becomes visible; accept it.
aspects.home: You are nearer to home than you realised. Those who love you have trusted that you would return.
aspects.health: You will come through this, though you may lose something along the way. Grieve the losses, and give thanks for what survives.
aspects.journeys: The long wandering is ending, and the destination was always certain. Be wary still, but go forward with confidence.

entries.greek: Εὐρύμαχʼ, οὐχ οὕτως ἔσται· νοέεις δὲ καὶ αὐτός.
entries.english: Eurymachus, it will not be so; and you know it yourself.
entries.reading: The oracle answers that things are not as bleak as you suppose, and that you already half know it. A failure that seems final may simply have come on the wrong day. Set the matter aside for now and return to it at a better time. But be wary of comfortable excuses; in Homer this reassurance only delayed a reckoning.
entries.context: In Odyssey 21, after Eurymachus fails to string the bow and laments the shame of the suitors' weakness, Antinous answers with this line, insisting it will not be so. He says that it is a holy festival of Apollo, so no one should be bending bows; they should set it aside and try again the next day.

aspects.love: A setback in love may not be the end you dread. Give it time, but do not invent excuses to avoid an honest reckoning.
aspects.work: A failed attempt may be put down to poor timing rather than incapacity. Try again when conditions favour you, and prepare honestly in the meantime.
aspects.home: Do not despair at a household problem that seems insoluble today. Rest and return to it, but face the true cause.
aspects.health: One poor result does not decide your health. Rest, and test yourself again at a better hour.
aspects.journeys: Postponing a decision may be right, but delay is not the same as resolution. Use the time to see clearly.

entries.greek: ἆ δειλὲ ξείνων, ἔνι τοι φρένες οὐδʼ ἠβαιαί·
entries.english: Wretched stranger, you have not a scrap of sense in you.
entries.reading: You may be dismissed, as the beggar was, as someone without sense or standing. The oracle bids you bear the insult calmly; those who scorn you may simply fear what you can do. Do not answer contempt with anger, and do not doubt your own judgement because others mock it. If you are the one tempted to scorn, remember who that beggar truly was.
entries.context: In Odyssey 21, the disguised Odysseus asks to try the bow to test his old strength. The suitors are indignant, fearing he will succeed, and Antinous berates him with this line, calling him a wretched stranger without a scrap of sense who ought to be content to dine among his betters.

aspects.love: Someone may belittle you or your feelings. Do not let their contempt shake your sense of worth.
aspects.work: You may be dismissed as unqualified by those who fear competition. Keep your composure; your ability will speak at the right time.
aspects.home: In your household, the person treated as least may be the most deserving of honour. Show respect to all.
aspects.health: Do not take others' scorn into your heart; it is a poison that harms only the one who swallows it.
aspects.journeys: Do not let mockery drive you from a step you are right to take. Ask again, and wait for one who will give you the chance.

entries.greek: τῷ δʼ ἕτερον μὲν ἔδωκε πατήρ, ἕτερον δʼ ἀνένευσε·
entries.english: The father granted him one thing, and refused him the other.
entries.reading: Your prayer will be partly answered. The oracle tells you that one thing you ask for will be given and another refused. Consider carefully which of your hopes matters most, and do not assume that because one part succeeds the whole will follow. Prepare for the part that may be denied.
entries.context: In Iliad 16, as Patroclus leads the Myrmidons into battle, Achilles pours a libation and prays to Zeus that Patroclus will drive the Trojans from the ships and return safely. Zeus hears him and grants the first request but refuses the second: Patroclus saves the ships but is killed by Hector.

aspects.love: Some of what you hope for in love will come to you, but not everything. Treasure what is given, and guard well the person you fear for.
aspects.work: A venture may achieve its immediate aim while failing in another way. Plan for success and for loss at once.
aspects.home: A wish for a family member will be partly granted. Do not send them into danger on the strength of the half that is promised.
aspects.health: Healing may be granted in one respect and not another. Give thanks for the gain and attend carefully to what remains.
aspects.journeys: The first stage of your undertaking will succeed; the return is less certain. Do not go further than your purpose requires.

entries.greek: ἀλλʼ εἰς οἶκον ἰοῦσα τὰ σʼ αὐτῆς ἔργα κόμιζε
entries.english: But go to your room, and see to your own work,
entries.reading: The oracle turns you back to what is truly yours to do. Some matters are not in your hands, and fretting over them will not move them; your own work, done well, is the ground you can stand on. Go home to your tasks, keep your household in order, and let the larger struggle be carried by those whose part it is.
entries.context: In Iliad 6, Hector speaks to his wife Andromache at the Scaean Gate, after she has begged him not to return to battle. He tells her that no one escapes their fate, and sends her home to her loom and her maids, saying war is the concern of men; it is the last time they meet alive.

aspects.love: Love that is real does not need you to stand at every gate; trust the bond and give each other room to do what each must.
aspects.work: Return to the work in front of you and do it with care; the outcome of the larger contest does not rest on your worrying.
aspects.home: Order your household and direct those who help you; a well-kept home is its own defence in uncertain days.
aspects.health: Fear for others can wear you thin; ease your mind with steady, familiar labour of the hands.
aspects.journeys: This is not the moment to go out to meet the danger yourself; stay, and keep what is yours in good repair.

entries.greek: τῷ νῦν μηδὲ σὺ ταῦτα τεῇ εἴπῃσθα γυναικί.
entries.note: The papyrus has its own wording here, blending Odyssey 8.548 and 11.224.
entries.english: So now, do not you tell these things to your wife either.
entries.reading: Not every truth is to be carried home and spoken at once. The oracle counsels discretion: there are things you have learned that are better held for now, even from those closest to you, until the right hour comes. Weigh whom a word will help before you speak it.
entries.context: The papyrus line differs from the standard text, blending Odyssey 8.548 and 11.224, so its exact source is uncertain. At 8.548 King Alcinous urges the weeping Odysseus not to hide his identity from his Phaeacian hosts; at 11.224 the ghost of his mother Anticleia tells Odysseus to learn all she has said so that he may later tell it to his wife.

aspects.love: Even with those you love most, some news is better kept until it can be shared without wounding.
aspects.work: Hold your plans close for now; speaking of them too soon may cost you the advantage.
aspects.home: Not every burden from outside the house needs to be laid upon your family tonight.
aspects.health: Give yourself room to absorb what you have learned before you put it into words.
aspects.journeys: Make your decision quietly; announce it only when it is settled and you can stand behind it.

entries.greek: λάϊνον ἕσσο χιτῶνα κακῶν ἕνεχʼ ὅσσα ἔοργας.
entries.english: you would be wearing a tunic of stone, for all the harm you have done.
entries.reading: This is a hard answer, and an honest one. Harm that has been done is not forgotten simply because others have been too patient or too afraid to name it. Look squarely at what your choices have cost those around you, and make what amends you can before the reckoning is made for you.
entries.context: In Iliad 3, Hector rebukes his brother Paris, who has shrunk back from facing Menelaus, the husband of Helen. He says that if the Trojans were not so timid, Paris would long ago have been stoned to death ('wearing a tunic of stone') for all the harm he has brought on the city; stung, Paris agrees to fight Menelaus in single combat.

aspects.love: If you have wronged someone close to you, a charming manner will not mend it; only honest amends will.
aspects.work: Charm and good looks do not make up for work left undone or debts unpaid; settle what you owe.
aspects.home: Consider what your choices have brought upon your family, and set about repairing the damage.
aspects.health: A troubled conscience is heavy to carry; facing what you have done is the first step towards relief.
aspects.journeys: Before you set out on anything new, answer for the trouble left behind by the last venture.

entries.greek: ἠρῶ ἀθανάτοισι γενειήσαντα ἰδέσθαι.
entries.english: I prayed to the immortals to see him grown, with a beard on his chin.
entries.reading: Something you once longed for has already come to pass, though grief may have kept you from seeing it. The oracle bids you lift your eyes from old sorrow and notice what has grown while you were mourning. Give thanks for the answered prayer, and meet it with a clear face.
entries.context: In Odyssey 18, the housekeeper Eurynome speaks to Penelope, who wishes to go down and warn her son about the suitors. Eurynome urges her to wash away her tears, since Telemachus is now grown, as she always prayed to the gods she might see him; Athena then makes Penelope beautiful before she appears to the suitors.

aspects.love: Someone you have cared for has grown into who you hoped they would be; let yourself see it and rejoice.
aspects.work: Labour you have long invested is bearing its fruit; recognise the result instead of only counting the cost.
aspects.home: A child or younger relative has come into their own; honour that change and speak with them as an equal.
aspects.health: Wash away the marks of long grief; the oracle bids you care for yourself again.
aspects.journeys: The season of waiting has turned; a change you prayed for is already here.

entries.greek: εὔχεο δʼ Ἀπόλλωνι Λυκηγενέϊ κλυτοτόξῳ
entries.english: And pray to Apollo, the wolf-born, famed for his bow,
entries.reading: Prayer and good intentions can be used to dress up a deed that ought not to be done. Before you act, ask whose voice is urging you on, and whether the vow you make is a cover for something you would not otherwise choose. Piety does not make a broken promise sound.
entries.context: In Iliad 4, Athena, disguised as the Trojan Laodocus, persuades the archer Pandarus to shoot at Menelaus during a sworn truce, telling him to vow a hecatomb of firstborn lambs to Apollo the wolf-born. Pandarus is persuaded, wounds Menelaus, and the broken truce sets the war going again.

aspects.love: Be wary if someone urges you to a bold act for their sake while promising rewards; love does not ask you to break faith.
aspects.work: A tempting offer may require you to break an agreement; no vow of later virtue makes that right.
aspects.home: Do not let an outsider persuade you to act against the peace of your own people.
aspects.health: Ask whether the pressure you feel is your own desire or another's voice in your ear.
aspects.journeys: Before you take a decisive shot, be sure you are not being used to break someone else's truce.

entries.greek: οὐδὲ λύκοι τε καὶ ἄρνες ὁμόφρονα θυμὸν ἔχουσιν,
entries.english: Wolves and lambs are never of one mind,
entries.reading: Some divisions cannot be bridged by fair words. If one side means you harm, no agreement will make you of one mind, and you should not stake your safety on a promise the other has no wish to keep. Know clearly who stands against you, and do not mistake a truce for friendship.
entries.context: In Iliad 22, Hector, at last standing to face Achilles outside the walls of Troy, proposes that the victor return the other's body. Achilles refuses: as there are no oaths between lions and men, and wolves and lambs are never of one mind, so there can be no pact between the two of them.

aspects.love: Do not seek closeness with someone whose intentions towards you are hostile; kindness will not change their nature.
aspects.work: Some rivals cannot be partners; make no binding deal with one who means to ruin you.
aspects.home: If a quarrel in the family has hardened into enmity, protect yourself before seeking peace.
aspects.health: Guard yourself against influences that are simply bad for you; there is no bargaining with them.
aspects.journeys: Choose your path knowing who stands against you; do not count on promises from that side.

entries.greek: ἀλλʼ ἤτοι μὲν ταῦθʼ ὑποείξομεν ἀλλήλοισι,
entries.english: But in this, let us give way to one another,
entries.reading: The answer is compromise. Neither of you will have everything; each must give a little so that the matter can move at all. Agree on what can be agreed and let the rest go, for a quarrel between equals only wears both down.
entries.context: In Iliad 4, during a council on Olympus, Hera bargains with Zeus over the fate of Troy. She allows him to destroy her own favourite cities if he wishes, and asks in return that they give way to one another, he to her and she to him; Zeus agrees and sends Athena to break the truce.

aspects.love: Between equals, love lasts when each gives way in turn; let the next yielding be yours.
aspects.work: A deal can be struck if both parties accept less than everything; find the terms you can share.
aspects.home: Household quarrels between partners are settled by trading concessions, not by winning.
aspects.health: Let go of the strain of having your own way in everything; it is wearing you down.
aspects.journeys: A decision made jointly will hold better than one forced; agree first, then act.

entries.greek: ἐν δʼ Ἔρις ἐν δὲ Κυδοιμὸς ὁμίλεον, ἐν δʼ ὀλοὴ Κήρ,
entries.english: Strife and Uproar were in the thick of it, and deadly Doom,
entries.reading: The oracle shows a scene of open conflict, where quarrel and confusion move among the combatants and no one is spared. This is a warning: the matter you ask about is close to discord, and those who enter it may not come out as they went in. Think hard before joining a fight, and do not be the one who stirs it.
entries.context: In Iliad 18, Hephaestus forges new armour for Achilles and works scenes of the whole world onto his shield. In one, a besieged city's warriors ambush herdsmen at a river; as the two sides fight, the figures of Strife, Uproar and deadly Doom move among them, dragging the wounded and the dead.

aspects.love: Be careful of entering a dispute between others; strife spreads to those who stand near.
aspects.work: Competition is fierce around you; do not be caught unguarded while others lie in wait.
aspects.home: Keep watch over what is yours; trouble may come suddenly to a home that thinks itself safe.
aspects.health: Conflict and confusion take their toll on the body; withdraw from the fray when you can.
aspects.journeys: The path ahead runs through contested ground; go carefully, and with companions.

entries.greek: ψεύδεά τʼ ἀρτύνοντας ὅθεν κέ τις οὐδὲ ἴδοιτο·
entries.english: making up lies about things no one could ever see.
entries.reading: Look carefully at the stories you are being told, and at the ones you tell. There are many who build a fine tale out of things no one can check. Trust the speaker whose words and deeds have weight together, and be that kind of speaker yourself.
entries.context: In Odyssey 11, Odysseus pauses in telling the Phaeacians of his wanderings. King Alcinous replies that they do not take him for a cheat, like the many men the earth breeds who make up lies no one could verify; his words have grace and good sense, like a bard's, and Alcinous asks him to continue.

aspects.love: Value the one whose words match their heart; a smooth story is not the same as honesty.
aspects.work: Check the claims made to you in trade; many build fine tales out of things that cannot be verified.
aspects.home: Tell your own story at home truthfully, so that those who hear it can trust it.
aspects.health: Do not feed yourself comforting falsehoods; look at your situation as it truly is.
aspects.journeys: Before you set out on another's word, seek something you can see for yourself.

entries.greek: εἴ τι νόος ῥέξει· πόλεμον δʼ οὐκ ἄμμε κελεύω
entries.english: if thinking can achieve anything; but I do not urge us to fight.
entries.reading: When things have gone badly, the first instinct is to plunge back in. The oracle counsels otherwise: sit down, take counsel, and see whether clear thinking can achieve what force cannot. Not every battle is yours to fight while you are wounded.
entries.context: In Iliad 14, the Greek wall has been breached and the fighting has reached the ships. Old Nestor meets the wounded leaders Agamemnon, Diomedes and Odysseus and urges them to consider whether any plan might help, but advises that they should not enter the battle themselves, since wounded men cannot fight.

aspects.love: When love is under strain, talk before you act; a hasty word may do more harm than good.
aspects.work: A setback calls for a plan, not a rush; gather counsel before you commit your resources again.
aspects.home: If the family is wounded by some recent blow, sit together and think; do not throw yourselves back into battle.
aspects.health: You are not in a state to strive hard; rest and let the mind do the work for now.
aspects.journeys: Delay the decision until you have thought it through; force without a plan will not serve.

entries.greek: οὐδέ τις ἔστʼ ἀλκή· φυγέειν κάρτιστον ἀπʼ αὐτῆς.
entries.english: There is no defence against it: the best thing is to flee from it.
entries.reading: Not every danger is meant to be fought. Some forces are beyond your strength, and lingering to prove your courage will only cost more. The oracle says plainly: pass by quickly, accept the loss you cannot prevent, and save what can be saved.
entries.context: In Odyssey 12, the goddess Circe warns Odysseus about the monster Scylla. When he asks whether he might fight her off, Circe rebukes him: Scylla is an immortal evil, and there is no defence against her; the best course is to row past as fast as he can.

aspects.love: If a bond is destructive and cannot be changed, the bravest course may be to leave it.
aspects.work: Some losses cannot be prevented; cut them quickly rather than spending more to fight what you cannot beat.
aspects.home: Do not stand and argue with a danger in the house that will not listen; move away from it.
aspects.health: There is no wisdom in testing yourself against what overwhelms you; step back and preserve your strength.
aspects.journeys: Pass quickly through the narrow place; lingering there will cost you more.

entries.greek: νηπύτιε τί νυ τόξον ἔχεις ἀνεμώλιον αὔτως;
entries.english: Little fool, why carry a bow when it is as useless as the wind?
entries.reading: You hold something of real power and are not using it. Whether out of reluctance, respect or fear, you are carrying a bow you never draw. The oracle asks you to decide either to use your strength or to set it down honestly, for holding it idle invites scorn.
entries.context: In Iliad 21, during the battle of the gods, Apollo declines to fight his uncle Poseidon over mere mortals and withdraws. His sister Artemis taunts him for running away and asks why he carries a bow as useless as the wind; Hera then turns on her.

aspects.love: If you hold back from showing your affection, it is as good as having none; speak or let it go.
aspects.work: You have skills you are not using; put them to work or stop claiming them.
aspects.home: In family disputes, decide whether you will stand up or step aside, but do not merely make a show.
aspects.health: Strength unused grows weak; take up the practices that keep you able.
aspects.journeys: Do not carry provisions for a road you never mean to take; either set out or set them down.

entries.greek: καὶ γάρ τʼ ἠΰκομος Νιόβη ἐμνήσατο σίτου,
entries.english: For even lovely-haired Niobe remembered to eat,
entries.reading: Grief has its due, but the living must still be fed. The oracle bids you, in the midst of sorrow, to tend to your body and the simple needs of the day; this is not a betrayal of what you have lost. Rest, take nourishment, and mourn again tomorrow with strength enough to bear it.
entries.context: In Iliad 24, Achilles has agreed to return Hector's body to King Priam. He invites the grieving father to share a meal, recalling that even Niobe, whose twelve children were killed by Apollo and Artemis, remembered to eat; they eat together, and afterwards gaze at one another in wonder.

aspects.love: Sharing a simple meal with someone, even a former adversary, can be the beginning of peace.
aspects.work: Do not neglect your daily needs while dealing with great matters; the work will wait for one meal.
aspects.home: Gather the household at the table, even in sorrow; the shared meal holds a family together.
aspects.health: Eat, sleep, and attend to the body; grief is easier to bear when you are not also starving.
aspects.journeys: Before a hard journey home, take nourishment; you will need strength for the morning.

entries.greek: χαλκόν τε χρυσόν τε ἅλις ἐσθῆτά τε δόντες,
entries.english: giving him bronze and gold in plenty, and fine clothes,
entries.reading: After hardship there is generous reward. The oracle promises that help will come from strangers who will honour you, and that you will be sent on your way better provided than before your losses. Endure the last stretch of the hard road, for the gifts at its end are real.
entries.context: In Odyssey 5, Zeus sends Hermes to tell the nymph Calypso to release Odysseus. He foretells that after twenty days on a raft Odysseus will reach the Phaeacians, who will honour him like a god and send him home with bronze, gold and clothing, more than he would have brought from Troy.

aspects.love: Kindness may come from strangers who will honour you and send you on; accept it with grace.
aspects.work: Wealth may come to you not from what you won, but from what is freely given; receive it well.
aspects.home: After many losses, you may return home better provided than you left.
aspects.health: Recovery may come with help from others; let yourself be cared for.
aspects.journeys: The last stage of the voyage is hard, but it ends among friends and with good gifts.

entries.greek: οὔ τοι ἔπειθʼ ἁλίη ὁδὸς ἔσσεται οὐδʼ ἀτέλεστος.
entries.english: your journey will not be in vain, nor go unfinished.
entries.reading: What you set out to do will not be in vain. The oracle speaks with encouragement: you have in you the steadiness of those who came before, and if you act in that spirit your effort will reach its end. Go, and finish what you have begun.
entries.context: In Odyssey 2, Telemachus, having failed to rouse the Ithacan assembly against the suitors, prays by the sea to Athena. She comes to him in the likeness of Mentor and assures him that if he has his father's spirit, his voyage to seek news of Odysseus will be neither wasted nor left unfinished.

aspects.love: What you seek in love is not a fool's errand; go with the courage of your best self.
aspects.work: Your effort will bear fruit if you work with the resolve your forebears showed.
aspects.home: Your family's spirit runs in you; let it carry you through the task you have taken on.
aspects.health: Your perseverance will see you through; do not abandon the regimen you have begun.
aspects.journeys: Set out on the journey you are contemplating; it will not be wasted.

entries.greek: εἷς οἰωνὸς ἄριστος ἀμύνεσθαι περὶ πάτρης.
entries.english: One omen is best: to fight for your country.
entries.reading: When signs are doubtful, fall back on what you know to be right: stand for your home, your people and what you hold dear. Do not wait for the heavens to make your choice for you. But remember that the man who spoke these words also refused good counsel, and paid for it.
entries.context: In Iliad 12, the Trojan Polydamas reads an eagle dropping a snake as a warning not to attack the Greek ships. Hector angrily rejects his advice, saying he cares nothing for birds and that the one best omen is to fight for one's country; he presses the attack, which in the end costs Troy dearly.

aspects.love: Stand for the one you love, but be sure your loyalty does not make you deaf to their counsel.
aspects.work: Do your duty to those who depend on you, but heed sound advice before risking everything.
aspects.home: Defend your home with resolve; yet a wise relative's warning deserves a hearing.
aspects.health: Courage is good, but stubbornness is not; listen to the signals your body gives you.
aspects.journeys: Choose the path of plain duty, but do not scorn every warning sign along the way.

entries.greek: τήν τοι ἐγὼ ῥέξω χρυσὸν κέρασιν περιχεύας.
entries.english: I will sacrifice her to you, with her horns covered in gold.
entries.reading: You are setting out on a venture that needs help beyond your own strength. Ask for it, and promise something of real worth in return, then keep your word. The oracle counsels both boldness and reverence: dare the night's work, but give thanks freely for the protection you receive.
entries.context: In Iliad 10, Diomedes and Odysseus set out by night to spy on the Trojan camp. Diomedes prays to Athena to stand by him as she stood by his father Tydeus, and vows to sacrifice to her an unbroken yearling heifer with gilded horns; Athena hears their prayers.

aspects.love: Bring your best to the one you love, freely and with reverence, and keep your promises.
aspects.work: Promise a worthy reward to those who help you, and honour that promise when the work is done.
aspects.home: Give thanks for the protection your home has enjoyed; offer something fine in return.
aspects.health: Ask for the help you need to get through the night, and be grateful when it comes.
aspects.journeys: Set out boldly, but with a prayer on your lips and a vow you mean to keep.

entries.greek: πᾶσι δέ κε Τρώεσσι χάριν καὶ κῦδος ἄροιο,
entries.english: and you would win thanks and glory from all the Trojans,
entries.reading: Someone may be offering you praise, gratitude and reward for a single bold act. Ask what the act really is, and who whispers the offer. The glory promised for breaking faith is a snare, and the thanks of others is no defence when the cost falls on you.
entries.context: In Iliad 4, Athena, disguised as Laodocus, tempts the Trojan archer Pandarus to shoot Menelaus during the truce, promising that he would win thanks and glory from all the Trojans, and rich gifts from Paris above all. Pandarus shoots and wounds Menelaus, breaking the oaths; Diomedes kills him in the next book.

aspects.love: Admiration won by betraying a trust will not last; do not purchase approval at that price.
aspects.work: A reward offered for a shady deed is no true gain; turn it down.
aspects.home: Do not seek the gratitude of one part of your family by wronging another.
aspects.health: Chasing praise can lead you into decisions you will regret; listen to your own counsel.
aspects.journeys: Before you take the bold step, ask who benefits and who pays the cost.

entries.greek: νῆα κατισχέμεναι· ἐπεὶ οὐκέτι πιστὰ γυναιξίν.
