entries.english: bring your ship in secretly; for women can no longer be trusted.
entries.reading: Return, but return with care. The oracle advises caution about announcing yourself too openly; see how things stand before you show your hand, for not everyone who should be loyal may be so. Discretion now protects the homecoming you hope for.
entries.context: In Odyssey 11, in the underworld, the ghost of Agamemnon, murdered on his return by his wife Clytemnestra, advises Odysseus to bring his ship home to Ithaca secretly rather than openly, since women can no longer be trusted. He has just conceded that Penelope is wise and loyal; the warning is born of his own betrayal.

aspects.love: Approach a reunion with care; see how the heart of the other stands before you open yours.
aspects.work: Bring your venture in quietly; reveal it only when you know the ground is safe.
aspects.home: When returning to a household after absence, observe before you announce yourself.
aspects.health: Ease back into old routines gently; do not expose yourself to strain all at once.
aspects.journeys: Make your return or your change discreetly; secrecy now protects you later.

entries.greek: οὐκ ἔστʼ οὐδὲ ἔοικε τεὸν ἔπος ἀρνήσασθαι·
entries.english: It is not possible, nor would it be right, to refuse what you ask.
entries.reading: What you ask is likely to be granted, for it comes with standing that others respect. The oracle says yes. Yet consider how you will use what is given: a favour freely won can be turned to good or to guile, and the giver trusts you with it.
entries.context: In Iliad 14, Hera asks Aphrodite for the power of love and desire, claiming she wishes to reconcile the estranged Oceanus and Tethys. Aphrodite replies that it is neither possible nor right to refuse the wife of Zeus, and gives her the embroidered band; Hera in fact uses it to beguile Zeus into sleep.

aspects.love: What you ask of the one you love is likely to be granted; ask honestly and use it well.
aspects.work: A request to a colleague or partner will be granted because of your standing; do not abuse it.
aspects.home: A family member will not refuse your request; let it be a fair one.
aspects.health: Ask for the help you need; it will not be withheld.
aspects.journeys: The way will open for you; be sure your purpose is one you could openly declare.

entries.greek: αἶψα μεταστρέψειε νόον μετὰ σὸν καὶ ἐμὸν κῆρ.
entries.english: He would quickly turn his mind to suit your heart and mine.
entries.reading: When you and the one you are bound to stand of one mind, others will follow; division between you is what gives a rival room to act. The oracle counsels unity first. Settle your differences together, and the resistance you fear may turn of its own accord.
entries.context: In Iliad 15, Zeus wakes on Mount Ida to find the Trojans routed and threatens Hera, who swears she did not set Poseidon to help the Greeks. Zeus, smiling, answers that if she would truly share his purpose, Poseidon would quickly turn his mind to suit theirs, and sends her to summon Iris and Apollo.

aspects.love: When you and your partner are of one mind, outside troubles lose their power to divide you.
aspects.work: Agree with your partners first; then others will bend to your common aim.
aspects.home: A united household can turn even a wayward member back to the common course.
aspects.health: Bring your mind and heart into agreement; inner conflict is the greatest drain.
aspects.journeys: Make the decision together with those it affects; then the way forward will clear.

entries.greek: καί οἱ σημαίνειν· ὃ δὲ πείσεται εἰς ἀγαθόν περ.
entries.english: and to guide him; and he will listen to you, for his own good.
entries.reading: You have been placed beside someone stronger or more gifted than you, and your part is to guide them. Speak your counsel plainly and in good time, for it may be heeded to their good. Do not stay silent out of deference; yours may be the very word they need.
entries.context: In Iliad 11, Nestor reminds Patroclus of the charge his father Menoetius gave him when he left for Troy: Achilles is higher in birth and far stronger, but Patroclus is older, and should advise and guide him, and Achilles would listen for his own good. Nestor urges Patroclus to persuade Achilles to return, or to fight in his armour himself.

aspects.love: In friendship, the gift you bring may be wise counsel; speak gently, and you will be heard.
aspects.work: Guide the gifted person you work beside; your experience is what they lack.
aspects.home: As an elder in the family, your advice is needed; give it, for it will be received.
aspects.health: Listen to the counsel of those who have known you long; it is meant for your good.
aspects.journeys: If you are uncertain, seek advice from one older and steadier; they will help you choose.

entries.greek: εὖχος ἐμοὶ δώσειν, ψυχὴν δʼ Ἄϊδι κλυτοπώλῳ.
entries.english: giving glory to me, and your soul to Hades of the famous horses.
entries.reading: You are facing an opponent who speaks loudly and confidently. The oracle warns that words of threat cut both ways: pride before the contest can leave even the strong exposed. Meet the challenge if you must, but let your answer be in deeds rather than boasts.
entries.context: In Iliad 5, the Lycian prince Sarpedon, son of Zeus, faces Tlepolemus, son of Heracles, after Tlepolemus has taunted him. Sarpedon answers that Tlepolemus will give him glory and his soul to Hades; they throw their spears together, and Tlepolemus is killed, while Sarpedon is badly wounded in the thigh.

aspects.love: Do not let taunts provoke you into a contest of pride with someone you care for.
aspects.work: A rival is making threats; answer with the quality of your work, not with words.
aspects.home: Family quarrels fed by boasting end with someone hurt; lower your voice.
aspects.health: Even if you prevail, a fierce contest can leave you wounded; count the cost.
aspects.journeys: Weigh carefully before accepting a challenge thrown at you; not every fight must be met.

entries.greek: νῆα ἅλις χρυσοῦ καὶ χαλκοῦ νηησάσθω
entries.english: let him load his ship with gold and bronze in plenty
entries.reading: Generous reward is promised, but it lies on the far side of the task. The oracle speaks of plenty: when the walls you labour against have fallen, you may take your fill. Yet such offers are made to win you over, so ask whether gifts can mend what was broken.
entries.context: In Iliad 9, Agamemnon, in council with the Greek leaders, lists the gifts he will give Achilles if he returns to battle, including that, if Troy is taken, he may load his ship with gold and bronze. Odysseus carries the offer to Achilles, who rejects it.

aspects.love: Lavish promises in love are made to win you back; ask whether they address the hurt itself.
aspects.work: There will be ample reward if the venture succeeds; but do not mistake promised wealth for wealth in hand.
aspects.home: Generous gifts from family may be offered to settle a quarrel; weigh them against what was lost.
aspects.health: Do not let the prospect of reward drive you to labour beyond your strength.
aspects.journeys: The prize lies at the end of the road, not at its start; go if the task itself is worth it.

entries.greek: ἀλλὰ τὸ μὲν φάσθαι, τὸ δὲ καὶ κεκρυμμένον εἶναι.
entries.english: Tell some things, but keep others hidden.
entries.reading: Not everything you know need be spoken. The oracle counsels measured openness: tell what serves, keep back what is not yet safe to share, even with those near to you. Trust is wiser when it is given in proportion.
entries.context: In Odyssey 11, the ghost of Agamemnon, murdered by his wife on his return from Troy, warns Odysseus never to be too gentle with his wife or tell her everything, but to tell some things and keep others hidden. In the next breath he grants that Penelope is wise and faithful and that Odysseus has nothing to fear from her.

aspects.love: Love thrives on trust, but not on telling everything at once; let intimacy grow in measure.
aspects.work: Share with partners what they need to know and keep the rest in hand for now.
aspects.home: In the household, be open but not careless; some matters belong to you alone for a while.
aspects.health: Speak of your troubles to those who can help, but you need not bare every wound to all.
aspects.journeys: Reveal your plans only in part until you are sure of your ground.

entries.greek: Ζεὺς ἐπὶ γιγνομένοισιν ἵει κακότητα βαρεῖαν.
entries.english: Zeus has sent heavy trouble on us from the day we were born.
entries.reading: The trouble you carry is not a mark of personal failure; it is the common lot. The oracle bids you set aside pride and take your share of the labour alongside others. Honour those who work with you, and do not hold yourself above the task.
entries.context: In Iliad 10, at night after a Greek defeat, Agamemnon sends his brother Menelaus to rouse the leaders. He tells him to call each man by name with honour and not to stand on his dignity, but to toil with them, for Zeus has laid heavy trouble on them from their birth.

aspects.love: Do not stand on your dignity with the one you love; work alongside them through the hard time.
aspects.work: Lead by working with your people, calling each by name with respect; pride will not help.
aspects.home: Hardship falls on every household; meet it together rather than blaming one another.
aspects.health: Accept that some trouble is simply the lot of mortals; it is not a judgement on you.
aspects.journeys: Go out among those who need rousing and share the task; do not wait for others to carry it.

entries.greek: οἴῳ πεπνῦσθαι, τοὶ δὲ σκιαὶ ἀίσσουσιν.
entries.english: He alone has wisdom; the others flit about like shadows.
entries.reading: Many voices will offer you guidance, but most are shadows, moving without understanding. The oracle tells you to seek out the one who has true insight, even if reaching them is hard or frightening. Go to the source, not to the crowd.
entries.context: In Odyssey 10, Odysseus asks Circe to send him home. She tells him he must first travel to the house of Hades to consult the blind Theban prophet Teiresias, to whom alone among the dead Persephone has left his wisdom, while the others flit about as shadows. Odysseus weeps at the news.

aspects.love: Do not take counsel in love from the crowd; seek the one person who truly understands your heart.
aspects.work: Find the expert who sees clearly, even if they are hard to reach; the others are guessing.
aspects.home: In family matters, consult the eldest and wisest among you rather than every passing voice.
aspects.health: Seek out a trusted, knowledgeable healer rather than heeding rumours and shadows.
aspects.journeys: Before the great decision, you must go to the one who knows the way, however daunting.

entries.greek: εἴξας ᾧ θυμῷ· τῷ δʼ οὐκέτι δῶρα τέλεσσαν
entries.english: yielding to his own heart; but they did not give him the gifts.
entries.reading: You may yet do the right thing, but if you wait until disaster is at the door, you will lose the honour and the reward you might have had. The oracle warns against stubborn delay: yield while yielding still brings thanks.
entries.context: In Iliad 9, Phoenix tells Achilles the story of Meleager, who in anger refused to defend his city until it was burning; he finally fought, yielding to his own heart, but the people never gave him the gifts they had promised. Phoenix urges Achilles not to make the same mistake and to accept Agamemnon's gifts.

aspects.love: Yield in love while yielding can still be received as a gift; later, it may count for nothing.
aspects.work: If you will help in the end, help now while it is honoured and rewarded.
aspects.home: Do not wait for the family crisis to reach the door before you act.
aspects.health: Do not leave your care until things are desperate; attend to it while it is easy.
aspects.journeys: Delay will not change your eventual choice, only its reward; decide now.

entries.greek: χαίρω σεῦ Λαερτιάδη τὸν μῦθον ἀκούσας·
entries.english: I am glad, son of Laertes, to hear what you have said.
entries.reading: Fair counsel has been given, and it is welcome. The oracle answers with approval: what has been proposed is just and fitting, and you would do well to accept it gladly and act on it. A reconciliation can be made on these terms.
entries.context: In Iliad 19, at the assembly where Achilles renounces his anger, Odysseus advises that Agamemnon should bring out his gifts, swear he never touched Briseis, and give Achilles a feast. Agamemnon replies that he is glad to hear Odysseus' words, for he has set everything out fittingly, and agrees to swear the oath.

aspects.love: A sincere attempt at reconciliation is being made; receive it gladly.
aspects.work: Fair terms have been proposed; you would do well to accept them.
aspects.home: Good counsel for the family has been spoken; act on it with a glad heart.
aspects.health: The advice you have received is sound; follow it.
aspects.journeys: The plan put before you is just and fitting; you may proceed.

entries.greek: Ζεὺς δʼ ἀρετὴν ἄνδρεσσιν ὀφέλλει τε μινύθει τε
entries.english: Zeus makes men's courage greater or less, as he pleases.
entries.reading: Courage and success are not wholly yours to command. The oracle reminds you that strength rises and falls by a will greater than your own, so do not boast of it, nor despair when it ebbs. Act with what you have today, and stop arguing about your worth.
entries.context: In Iliad 20, Aeneas, facing Achilles in battle, recites his descent from Zeus through Dardanus, Tros and Anchises. He ends by saying that Zeus increases or lessens men's prowess as he wills, and calls on Achilles to stop talking like children and fight; Poseidon later rescues Aeneas.

aspects.love: Do not measure love by pedigree or boasting; feelings rise and fall, and must be tended.
aspects.work: Success at work waxes and wanes beyond your control; do your best with what today allows.
aspects.home: Do not dwell on your family's past greatness; what matters is what you do now.
aspects.health: Your strength will vary from day to day; accept this, and do not chide yourself for it.
aspects.journeys: Stop debating your worthiness and make the move; talk will not settle the matter.

entries.greek: δεινὸς ἀνήρ· τάχα κεν καὶ ἀναίτιον αἰτιόῳτο.
entries.english: a hard man: he would soon blame even someone who is innocent.
entries.reading: Tread carefully with someone whose temper runs hot: they may blame you even when you are not at fault. The oracle counsels you to deliver your message and withdraw, rather than linger where suspicion grows. Your innocence is no shield against a harsh mood.
entries.context: In Iliad 11, Achilles sends Patroclus to Nestor's hut to learn who the wounded man is. Patroclus refuses to sit down, explaining that he must hurry back, for Nestor knows what a hard man Achilles is: he might soon blame even someone innocent. Nestor nonetheless detains him with a long speech.

aspects.love: If your partner's temper is quick, choose your moment to speak, lest you be blamed for what is not yours.
aspects.work: Your superior is demanding and quick to blame; deliver your work promptly and avoid delay.
aspects.home: A difficult family member may misjudge you; do not linger where tempers are short.
aspects.health: Do not carry the burden of another's harshness as though it were your own fault.
aspects.journeys: Carry out your errand swiftly and return; this is not the place to stay.

entries.greek: πανσυδίῃ· νῦν γάρ κεν ἕλοις πόλιν εὐρυάγυιαν
entries.english: in full force. For now you could take the city of wide streets.
entries.reading: The oracle speaks of a moment ripe for bold action: gather all your strength and move now. Yet be careful of messages that promise too easy a victory; the dream that spoke these words was sent to deceive. Prepare fully, test the ground, and do not mistake eagerness for certainty.
entries.context: In Iliad 2, Agamemnon tells the Greek council of elders of a dream in Nestor's likeness, sent by Zeus, which bade him arm the Achaeans in full force, since now he could take Troy. The dream was false, sent by Zeus to lead the Greeks into a battle that would bring them losses.

aspects.love: A sign may seem to promise success in love; be sure it is a true sign before you commit your whole heart.
aspects.work: The time may seem ripe for a decisive move; but check whether the promise is too easy to trust.
aspects.home: Gather the whole household before an important undertaking; act together, not piecemeal.
aspects.health: A sudden burst of confidence is welcome, but test it before you overexert yourself.
aspects.journeys: Bold action is called for, but confirm the message before you stake everything on it.

entries.greek: τέτλαθι δή, κραδίη· καὶ κύντερον ἄλλο ποτʼ ἔτλης.
entries.english: Endure, my heart: you have endured worse than this before.
entries.reading: You have borne worse than this and come through. The oracle bids you hold back the anger or despair rising in you, and wait; the time to act is not yet, and patience now will serve you better than an outburst. Remember what you survived before, and draw on that strength.
entries.context: In Odyssey 20, on the night before the slaughter of the suitors, Odysseus lies awake in his own house, disguised as a beggar, enraged to see his maidservants going off to the suitors. He strikes his chest and rebukes his heart, reminding it that it endured worse in the Cyclops' cave, until cunning brought him out.

aspects.love: Bear the hurt you feel now with patience; your heart has weathered worse.
aspects.work: Hold your temper with those who wrong you at work; the hour for redress has not yet come.
aspects.home: Disorder in your home is grievous, but restrain yourself; patience now will let you set it right.
aspects.health: Call on your own resilience; you have come through worse before.
aspects.journeys: Wait for the right moment to act; impulsive steps now could ruin a well-laid plan.

entries.greek: δαιμόνιʼ ἀτρέμας ἧσο καὶ ἄλλων μῦθον ἄκουε,
entries.english: Sit still, my friend, and listen to what others say.
entries.reading: This is not your moment to speak or to rush. The oracle asks you to sit quietly, hear out those with more experience, and learn before you act. Restless clamour will not change the outcome; patient listening may.
entries.context: In Iliad 2, after Agamemnon has tested the army by proposing they sail home, the troops rush for the ships. Odysseus, prompted by Athena, turns them back: he speaks gently to leaders, but strikes common soldiers with the sceptre and orders them to sit still and listen to their betters.

aspects.love: In love, listen more than you speak for now; understanding will follow.
aspects.work: Hold back from leading at present; learn from those with more experience.
aspects.home: Let the elders of the family have their say before you raise your voice.
aspects.health: Stillness is medicine; sit quietly and let your body and mind settle.
aspects.journeys: Do not rush to the ships; sit, and hear what others advise before deciding.

entries.greek: μηνιθμὸν μὲν ἀπορρῖψαι, φιλότητα δʼ ἑλέσθαι·
entries.english: to throw away his anger and choose friendship instead.
entries.reading: The answer counsels reconciliation: throw away your grudge and choose friendship. Bitterness, however justified, keeps you from the place where you are needed. Yet know too that others may hope for this change before it has truly happened; let yours be real.
entries.context: In Iliad 16, Patroclus leads the Myrmidons into battle wearing Achilles' armour. The Trojans, seeing him, believe that Achilles himself has cast off his anger and chosen friendship with the Greeks, and they waver in panic.

aspects.love: Let the old grievance go and choose friendship again; it is worth more than being right.
aspects.work: Lay down your resentment towards a colleague; working together will serve you better.
aspects.home: End the family quarrel; affection restored is a stronger shelter than any wall.
aspects.health: Anger held too long is a burden; release it and feel the weight lift.
aspects.journeys: Before deciding, put aside resentment; a choice made in anger is seldom sound.

entries.greek: ὡς ἀγαθὸν καὶ παῖδα καταφθιμένοιο λιπέσθαι
entries.english: How good it is, when a man dies, that he leaves a son behind.
entries.reading: The oracle speaks of legacy. It is good to leave behind someone who will carry your name and set right what was wrong. Whatever you build now, in children, students or work, may be what answers for you when you are gone; tend it well.
entries.context: In Odyssey 3, old Nestor tells Telemachus what he knows of the Greeks' homecomings, including Agamemnon's murder by Aegisthus. He reflects that it is good for a slain man to leave a son behind, since Orestes took vengeance on his father's killer, and he urges Telemachus to be brave as well.

aspects.love: Love that bears fruit in a new generation is a great good; cherish what grows from your bond.
aspects.work: Build work that someone can carry on after you; a worthy successor is a lasting achievement.
aspects.home: Your children and heirs are your legacy; teach them well and they will honour your name.
aspects.health: Take heart from those who will continue after you; the thought can steady you.
aspects.journeys: Choose with an eye to what you will leave behind, not only to what you will gain.

entries.greek: τῆ δέ, τόδε κρήδεμνον ὑπὸ στέρνοιο τανύσσαι
entries.english: Here, take this veil and wrap it beneath your chest,
entries.reading: In the storm, help is being offered from an unexpected quarter. The oracle tells you to let go of what can no longer carry you and take hold of the gift held out, trusting it even when the waves are high. Once you reach solid ground, give it back with thanks.
entries.context: In Odyssey 5, Odysseus' raft is battered by Poseidon's storm. The sea goddess Ino, called Leucothea, takes pity on him and tells him to strip, abandon the raft, swim for the land of the Phaeacians, and tie her immortal veil beneath his chest, promising he will not perish; he must throw it back into the sea when he reaches land.

aspects.love: Let love that is offered keep you afloat; accept the help held out to you.
aspects.work: Let go of a failing venture and take the opportunity being offered, trusting it to carry you.
aspects.home: Help may come to your household from an unexpected quarter; receive it gratefully.
aspects.health: Accept the support offered to you through this storm; you need not swim alone.
aspects.journeys: Leave behind what can no longer carry you and strike out for the shore with the help you have.

entries.greek: οὐχ ὁσίη κταμένοισιν ἐπʼ ἀνδράσιν εὐχετάασθαι.
entries.english: It is not right to boast over men who have been killed.
entries.reading: If victory comes to you, take it quietly. The oracle warns against exulting over those who have fallen, however much they deserved it. Let joy be kept in the heart, and leave the judgement to powers greater than your own.
entries.context: In Odyssey 22, after Odysseus has killed the suitors, the old nurse Eurycleia sees the bodies and begins to cry out in triumph. Odysseus restrains her, saying it is not holy to boast over slain men; the fate of the gods and their own wicked deeds destroyed them.

aspects.love: If you have won a quarrel with someone you love, keep your satisfaction to yourself.
aspects.work: Do not exult over a rival's fall; quiet success earns more respect than boasting.
aspects.home: When a family wrong is set right, celebrate quietly; gloating will reopen the wound.
aspects.health: Hold your feelings in measure, even in relief; let calm follow the storm.
aspects.journeys: When the hard choice has been made and the danger is past, move on without triumph.

entries.greek: νύκτα διʼ ἀμβροσίην, ὅτε θʼ εὕδουσι βροτοὶ ἄλλοι;
entries.english: through the immortal night, when all other mortals are asleep?
entries.reading: You are moving through the dark while others sleep, on an errand that may seem foolish or perilous. The oracle asks you to account for your purpose. Yet such a question may be put by a friend in disguise: a dangerous journey made for love can find unexpected protection.
entries.context: In Iliad 24, the aged King Priam is driving by night to Achilles' camp to ransom Hector's body. The god Hermes, disguised as a young Myrmidon, meets him on the plain and asks where he is going through the night when other mortals sleep; he then offers to guide him safely.

aspects.love: You may be taking great risks for love; be clear about what you seek, and you may find protection.
aspects.work: You are working while others rest; ask yourself why, and be sure the purpose is worth it.
aspects.home: For the sake of family you may go through the dark; a guide may meet you on the way.
aspects.health: Make sure that you rest; journeys by night take more from you than you think.
aspects.journeys: If you set out in uncertain times, go with purpose and watch for unexpected allies.

entries.greek: πῶς ἂν ἔπειτʼ Ὀδυσῆος ἐγὼ θείοιο λαθοίμην,
entries.english: How could I ever forget godlike Odysseus,
entries.reading: When you choose who will go with you into danger, choose by worth, not by rank or politeness. The oracle points to the companion of steady heart and good judgement, whom you would not forget. With such a one beside you, even fire can be passed through.
entries.context: In Iliad 10, Diomedes volunteers to spy on the Trojan camp and is told to choose any companion he wishes. He answers that he could not overlook godlike Odysseus, whose heart is eager in every toil and whom Athena loves; with him, they could return even from blazing fire.

aspects.love: Choose a companion whose heart is steady through every hardship.
aspects.work: For a hard task, pick a colleague for their worth and good judgement, not their title.
aspects.home: Look to the family member you can rely on in every trial; do not overlook them.
aspects.health: Choose companions who strengthen you; good company can carry you through fire.
aspects.journeys: Do not travel alone; take with you the one you trust most.

entries.greek: ἔλλαβε πορφύρεος θάνατος καὶ μοῖρα κραταιή.
entries.english: dark death and mighty fate seized him.
entries.reading: This is a sombre answer. It speaks of an ending that comes swiftly and cannot be turned aside. The oracle does not say this ending is yours; it asks you to recognise what is beyond your power, and to act with care where you still have choice.
entries.context: In Iliad 5, the narrator describes a series of killings in battle. The Greek Eurypylus cuts off the arm of the Trojan Hypsenor, priest of the river Scamander, as he flees, and dark death and mighty fate seize him.

aspects.love: Some endings in love come swiftly and cannot be undone; honour what was, and look to what remains.
aspects.work: A venture may end abruptly; accept what cannot be reversed and secure what you still can.
aspects.home: Hold your loved ones close; life is fragile, and its turns can be sudden.
aspects.health: This is a call to respect your limits and to care for yourself where you still have choice.
aspects.journeys: Some paths close without warning; turn your attention to the ones still open.

entries.greek: ὣς οὐκ αἰνότερον καὶ κύντερον ἄλλο γυναικός,
entries.english: So nothing is more terrible or shameless than a woman
entries.reading: The line is bitter, spoken out of a deep personal wrong. As an answer, it warns that the worst hurt comes from someone close who turns to treachery. Be alert, but do not let one betrayal poison all trust; the speaker himself admits that not all are alike.
entries.context: In Odyssey 11, the ghost of Agamemnon tells Odysseus how he was murdered at his homecoming feast by Aegisthus and his own wife Clytemnestra, who also killed Cassandra and would not close his eyes as he died. In his bitterness he declares nothing is more terrible or shameless than a woman who plots such deeds, though he goes on to praise Penelope.

aspects.love: A betrayal by someone close can sour the heart; do not let it turn you against those who are faithful.
aspects.work: Guard against treachery from a trusted associate, but do not judge all by one.
aspects.home: Watch for discord at home; but remember that loyalty also lives under your roof.
aspects.health: Bitterness from an old wound can poison the present; seek to let it heal.
aspects.journeys: Do not let one betrayal decide your whole course; weigh each person on their own conduct.

entries.greek: μὴ ἴομεν Δαναοῖσι μαχησόμενοι περὶ νηῶν.
entries.english: Let us not go and fight the Greeks beside the ships.
entries.reading: The oracle counsels restraint. A sign has been given, and the prudent course is not to press the attack you are planning. Even if the voice of caution is unwelcome, listen to it now, for in Homer those who scorned such warnings paid for it.
entries.context: In Iliad 12, as the Trojans prepare to cross the Greek trench, an eagle drops a wounded snake among them. Polydamas tells Hector the omen means they should not go on to fight the Greeks by the ships; Hector scornfully rejects the advice.

aspects.love: Do not press your suit or force a confrontation now; the signs counsel holding back.
aspects.work: This is not the moment to attack a competitor; wait until the omens are clearer.
aspects.home: Do not push a family quarrel to its crisis; the cost would fall on everyone.
aspects.health: Do not throw yourself into strenuous effort; heed the warnings and conserve your strength.
aspects.journeys: Hold back from the advance you are considering; caution is the better counsel.

entries.greek: ἄνδρʼ ἀπαμύνασθαι, ὅτε τις πρότερος χαλεπήνῃ.
entries.english: to defend yourself, when someone else starts the quarrel.
entries.reading: You fear that you are weak and exposed, without the means to defend yourself if someone turns against you. The oracle offers reassurance: the one who meets you may prove a protector rather than an enemy. Proceed carefully, but do not assume the worst.
entries.context: In Iliad 24, Hermes, disguised as a young Myrmidon, meets King Priam on his night journey to Achilles. He points out that Priam is old, and his attendant too, unable to defend themselves if anyone picked a quarrel; but he says he will do him no harm and will protect him, for Priam reminds him of his own father.

aspects.love: You fear being exposed if you open your heart; the one who meets you may prove gentle.
aspects.work: You may feel unprotected in your work; an unexpected ally may stand with you.
aspects.home: You feel vulnerable, but help may come from someone who sees in you a parent or elder.
aspects.health: In weakness, accept the protection offered; you do not have to fend for yourself.
aspects.journeys: Go forward carefully but without despair; a guide may appear on the road.

entries.greek: οὐδέ τί μιν παῖδες ποτὶ γούνασι παππάζουσιν
entries.english: No children will climb on his knees and call him 'Papa'.
entries.reading: A warning against overreaching. Those who strive against powers far greater than themselves do not live long to enjoy their homecoming. Know the limits of your strength and turn from contests you cannot win, so that you may return safely to those who wait for you.
entries.context: In Iliad 5, Aphrodite has been wounded by Diomedes and flees to Olympus. Her mother Dione comforts her and says that Diomedes is a fool not to know that whoever fights the immortals does not last long, and no children climb on his knees calling him father when he comes home from war.

aspects.love: Do not set yourself against forces far greater than your love can withstand.
aspects.work: Do not take on a struggle with those far more powerful; overreaching will cost you.
aspects.home: Choose the path that brings you home safely to your family, not the one that wins fame at any price.
aspects.health: Know your limits; to push beyond them is to risk your wellbeing.
aspects.journeys: Decline the contest that pits you against the impossible; return home instead.

entries.greek: ἔνδον μὲν δὴ ὅδʼ αὐτὸς ἐγώ, κακὰ πολλὰ μογήσας
entries.english: Here I am, I myself, home at last after many hardships,
entries.reading: After long trouble, the one you awaited has returned, or the thing you hoped for is near. The oracle speaks of recognition and arrival: reveal yourself to those who have stayed loyal, and let them know you. The hardships are behind you; now comes the work of setting the house in order.
entries.context: In Odyssey 21, Odysseus, still disguised as a beggar, tests the herdsmen Eumaeus and Philoetius and finds them loyal. He then reveals himself, saying he has come home in the twentieth year after many hardships, and shows them the scar on his leg as proof.

aspects.love: Someone long absent may return, or you yourself may come back to love after hardship; let yourself be known.
aspects.work: After long struggle you have arrived; now reveal yourself to those who have stayed loyal.
aspects.home: Homecoming is near; gather the faithful of the household and begin to set things right.
aspects.health: The long trial is ending; let yourself feel what it means to be home.
aspects.journeys: The wandering is over; prepare for the last task that comes with arrival.

entries.greek: μὴ δʼ οὕτως ἀγόρευε· πάρος δʼ οὐκ ἔσσεται ἄλλως,
entries.english: Do not talk like that. Things will not change before
entries.reading: Complaining about your tools or your luck will not alter what is coming. The oracle bids you stop lamenting and make the test: face the matter directly, with the help that is offered. Nothing will change until you do.
entries.context: In Iliad 5, the archer Pandarus complains that his arrows have failed to kill Diomedes and swears to burn his bow. Aeneas tells him not to talk that way: things will not change until the two of them face Diomedes together in Aeneas' chariot; Diomedes kills Pandarus in the attempt.

aspects.love: Stop lamenting what love has not given you; face the matter directly together.
aspects.work: Do not blame your tools; take up the challenge with your partners and test it in earnest.
aspects.home: Complaints will not change the household; join with others and face the problem squarely.
aspects.health: Despair about your condition helps nothing; take some practical step today.
aspects.journeys: Nothing will change until you make the attempt; climb aboard and go.

entries.greek: μιμνέτω αὐτόθι τεῖος ἐπειγόμενός περ Ἄρηος·
entries.english: Let him wait here for now, however eager he is for war.
entries.reading: However eager you are to act, hold back a little longer. The oracle counsels patience until the proper agreements are made and the gifts are given; acting too soon would leave the matter unsettled. Let what must be done in order be done first.
entries.context: In Iliad 19, at the assembly of reconciliation, Agamemnon agrees to swear the oath and bring out his gifts. He asks that Achilles, however eager for battle, should wait there for now, with the rest of the army, until the gifts are brought and the oaths sworn.

aspects.love: Do not rush to act on your feelings; wait until promises are made and understood.
aspects.work: Let the agreement be sealed before you leap into action; haste may leave it incomplete.
aspects.home: Hold back from acting until the family has settled the terms; order matters.
aspects.health: Rest a while before exertion; your eagerness can wait an hour.
aspects.journeys: However eager you are to set out, wait for the proper preparations.

entries.greek: μὴ δʼ ἐπαγαλλόμενος πολέμῳ καὶ δηϊοτῆτι
entries.english: And do not, glorying in war and battle,
entries.reading: When success comes, do not let it carry you beyond what you were asked to do. The oracle warns that pressing your advantage too far, flushed with triumph, may bring you up against forces you cannot withstand. Do the task, then turn back.
entries.context: In Iliad 16, Achilles sends Patroclus into battle in his armour, instructing him to drive the Trojans from the ships and then return. He warns him not to be carried away by the glory of war and lead the attack on Troy, lest a god, especially Apollo, should intervene; Patroclus goes too far and is killed.

aspects.love: When love is going well, do not push for more than is wise; let it unfold in its own time.
aspects.work: Achieve what you set out to do, then stop; overreaching in success can undo you.
aspects.home: Do the task the family entrusted to you and return; do not go beyond it in pride.
aspects.health: Do not exhaust yourself through the rush of a good day; stop while you are strong.
aspects.journeys: Go as far as you must and then turn back; the ground beyond is dangerous.

entries.greek: μή ποτε τῆς εὐνῆς ἐπιβήμεναι ἠδὲ μιγῆναι,
entries.english: that I never went up to her bed or lay with her,
entries.reading: The oracle speaks of a pledge to set right a wrong, sworn in earnest before witnesses. If someone offers you such an oath, weigh it: it may be the true beginning of amends. If you are the one making it, swear only what you can keep in full.
entries.context: In Iliad 9, Agamemnon tells the Greek council the gifts he will give to win back Achilles, including the return of Briseis, and says he will swear a great oath that he has never gone to her bed or lain with her. Odysseus later repeats the offer to Achilles, who refuses it.

aspects.love: If faithfulness has been doubted, a sincere oath may restore trust; mean every word.
aspects.work: Make any undertaking binding and honest; your reputation rests on it.
aspects.home: A family dispute may be eased by a solemn pledge; let it be one you can keep.
aspects.health: A clear conscience is a source of strength; keep your promises to yourself as well.
aspects.journeys: Before moving on, give or receive a pledge that settles the past.

entries.greek: χείλεα μέν τʼ ἐδίηνʼ, ὑπερῴην δʼ οὐκ ἐδίηνε.
entries.english: He wets his lips, but never wets the roof of his mouth.
entries.reading: You are being given just enough to wet your lips, not enough to satisfy. The oracle speaks of help that is grudging or partial. Do not mistake a little pity for real support; seek those who will truly share their table, and when you can, give more fully than you have been given.
entries.context: In Iliad 22, Andromache, lamenting Hector's death, imagines the life of their son Astyanax as an orphan. He goes begging among his father's friends, and one, out of pity, holds out a small cup, wetting his lips but not his palate, while another drives him from the feast.

aspects.love: Do not settle for affection that only wets your lips; seek a love that truly sustains you.
aspects.work: Small handouts will not sustain you; seek work that provides properly.
aspects.home: Show those in need in your family more than token kindness; give enough to feed.
aspects.health: Do not live on scraps; nourish yourself properly in body and spirit.
aspects.journeys: Do not depend on others' grudging pity for the way ahead; find your own means.

entries.greek: θάρσει· μή τοι ταῦτα μετὰ φρεσὶ σῇσι μελόντων.
entries.english: Take heart: do not let these things trouble your mind.
entries.reading: Do not let this worry weigh on your mind; the matter is in capable hands. The oracle offers reassurance and promises that what you need will be made ready. Yet it does not promise to change every fate, only to give you what help can be given.
entries.context: In Iliad 18, Thetis comes to the smith-god Hephaestus to beg new armour for Achilles. Hephaestus tells her to take heart and not let it trouble her: he will make armour to amaze all who see it, though he wishes he could also hide Achilles from death.

aspects.love: Take heart; what you fear in love is being cared for by someone with skill and goodwill.
aspects.work: Do not fret; the work you need will be done well by capable hands.
aspects.home: Let go of the worry for your family's immediate needs; help is at hand.
aspects.health: Set your mind at rest; good care is being prepared for you.
aspects.journeys: You may proceed with confidence; you will be well equipped, though not every outcome is in your power.

entries.greek: τοῦτον δʼ οὐ δύναμαι βαλέειν κύνα λυσσητῆρα.
entries.english: But this mad dog I cannot hit.
entries.reading: You have succeeded against many, yet one adversary stays out of reach. The oracle bids you recognise that this one is not yours to bring down now, however often you aim. Turn your effort elsewhere, or wait for a better hour; persisting may only cost you more.
entries.context: In Iliad 8, the Greek archer Teucer, shooting from behind Ajax's shield, tells Agamemnon that he has lodged eight arrows in Trojan warriors but cannot hit Hector, that 'mad dog'. He shoots again and misses, killing another Trojan instead; soon after, Hector strikes Teucer down with a stone.

aspects.love: There may be one heart you cannot reach, however often you try; do not exhaust yourself on it.
aspects.work: You have succeeded in much, but one obstacle resists; redirect your effort for now.
aspects.home: One difficult member of the family may be beyond your influence; protect the rest.
aspects.health: Persisting against what will not yield may wear you out; rest and save your strength.
aspects.journeys: One door will not open; choose another way.

entries.greek: τέττα, σιωπῇ ἧσο, ἐμῷ δʼ ἐπιπείθεο μύθῳ·
entries.english: Sit quietly, friend, and do as I say.
entries.reading: Do not answer every rebuke. The oracle counsels silence and patience, and trust in a steadier voice. A leader's harsh words may simply be a spur to action, and the wise course is to let them pass and show your worth in deeds.
entries.context: In Iliad 4, Agamemnon reproaches Diomedes for holding back from battle. Diomedes' companion Sthenelus angrily answers back, but Diomedes tells him to sit quietly and do as he says, explaining that he does not blame Agamemnon for urging the Greeks to fight, since the glory or the grief of the war will be his.

aspects.love: Do not answer every sharp word in love; patience will show your heart more clearly.
aspects.work: Let your superior's criticism pass; your work will speak for you.
aspects.home: In the family, hold your tongue when a rebuke is meant as encouragement.
aspects.health: Calm silence will serve you better than an anxious defence.
aspects.journeys: Trust the steadier counsel beside you; sit quietly and follow it.

entries.greek: οὐκ ἀρετᾷ κακὰ ἔργα· κιχάνει τοι βραδὺς ὠκύν,
entries.english: Wicked deeds do not prosper: the slow catch up with the swift,
entries.reading: Wrongdoing does not thrive for long, and what seems quick and clever is often caught by what is patient and skilful. If you have been wronged, you need not race to repay it; steady work and good craft will bring the matter to light. If you are tempted to take a shortcut that is not honest, the answer warns you that it will be found out.
entries.context: In Odyssey 8 the bard Demodocus sings of Ares and Aphrodite caught in the net forged by Hephaestus. The gods gather to look, and one says to another that the slow, lame smith has caught Ares, the swiftest of the gods, by his craft.

aspects.love: If someone has been unfaithful or deceitful with you, it will come to light without your chasing it. Do not build love on concealment, for it is caught in the end.
aspects.work: A slower, more careful competitor may outlast a quick and clever one. Trust honest craft over haste in your dealings.
aspects.home: Secrets kept inside a household do not stay hidden. Deal openly with your family, and wrongs will have less room to grow.
aspects.health: Steady, patient care will overtake a sudden setback. What you build slowly in your body and habits is more lasting than any quick cure.
aspects.journeys: On a road where others seem to race ahead, keep your own steady pace. The decision made with care catches the one made in a hurry.

entries.greek: κληῗσαι μεγάροιο θύρας πυκινῶς ἀραρυίας,
entries.english: to lock the tight-fitting doors of the hall,
entries.reading: Before the decisive moment, make things fast. Close what should be closed, set trusted people in their places, and keep your intentions to those who have proved faithful. The answer counsels quiet preparation: the work that follows will go better if nothing is left open behind you.
entries.context: In Odyssey 21, Odysseus, having just revealed himself to the swineherd Eumaeus and the cowherd Philoetius, gives his orders before the slaying of the suitors. He tells Eumaeus to bring him the bow and to tell the women to lock the tight-fitting doors of the hall and stay at their work whatever they hear.

aspects.love: Guard what is private between you and those you love. Not every confidence should be opened to the whole house.
aspects.work: Before a decisive move in your work, close the gaps: settle the accounts, secure the agreements, and tell only those you trust.
aspects.home: Make your home secure and put the trusted ones in their places. A household that is well ordered can weather a storm inside its walls.
aspects.health: Shut the door on what drains you, at least for a time. Rest and protection come before the effort that lies ahead.
aspects.journeys: Do not set out until what you leave behind is secured. A great change goes better when every door behind you is fastened.

entries.greek: ἆ δείλʼ οὐδέ τί τοι θάνατος καταθύμιός ἐστιν
entries.english: Poor wretch, you give no thought to death,
entries.reading: This is a warning given with pity rather than anger. You may be clothed in something splendid that is not truly yours, a success or a role borrowed from another, and walking forward without seeing what it will cost. Look honestly at where your present course leads before you trust its brightness.
entries.context: In Iliad 17, Zeus watches from afar as Hector puts on the immortal armour of Achilles, stripped from the dead Patroclus. Shaking his head, Zeus speaks to his own heart, pitying Hector, who gives no thought to the death that is already close to him.

aspects.love: Look closely at a bond that dazzles you. Make sure you are loved for yourself and not for a borrowed splendour.
aspects.work: A position or reward that came from another's loss may not stay with you. Consider what it will cost before you wear it proudly.
aspects.home: Something in your family may be carried forward without enough thought for its weight. Ask what it truly costs those who bear it.
aspects.health: Do not ignore warnings because you feel strong. Pay attention to what you have been avoiding thinking about.
aspects.journeys: Before taking on a role that belonged to someone else, count the cost. A bold step should not be a blind one.

entries.greek: ἦλθʼ Ὀδυσεὺς καὶ οἶκον ἱκάνεται, ὀψέ περ ἐλθών.
entries.english: Odysseus has come, he is home, though he has come late.
entries.reading: What you have long waited for arrives, though later than you hoped. Do not let the long delay make you disbelieve it when it comes. The answer is one of return and fulfilment: the absent thing, person or hope may yet stand within your doors.
entries.context: In Odyssey 23, the old nurse Eurycleia hurries upstairs to wake Penelope after the suitors have been killed. She tells her to come and see with her own eyes what she has longed for every day: Odysseus has come home, though he came late.

aspects.love: A love or friendship long absent may return. When it does, do not let the years of waiting make you cold to it.
aspects.work: Reward that has been long delayed may yet arrive. Keep faith with the work you have done.
aspects.home: Someone may come home, or a long rift may close. Be ready to recognise and receive them.
aspects.health: Recovery may be slow, but it is coming. Count the late arrival as a true one.
aspects.journeys: A long road is reaching its end. You may be nearer to your destination than you believe.

entries.greek: ἔκ τε καὶ ὀψὲ τελεῖ, σύν τε μεγάλῳ ἀπέτισαν
entries.english: he fulfils it in the end, even if late, and they pay a heavy price,
entries.reading: A promise sworn before the gods is not empty, even when nothing seems to follow from it at once. If you have been betrayed or a solemn word broken against you, the answer is that it will be answered in time, and heavily. Be patient, and do not take into your own hands what the slow turning of things will settle.
entries.context: In Iliad 4, the Trojan Pandarus has broken the sworn truce by wounding Menelaus with an arrow. Agamemnon, grieving over his brother, declares that oaths are never in vain: even if Zeus does not fulfil them at once, he fulfils them in the end, and the oath-breakers pay a great price.

aspects.love: A vow broken in love does not go unanswered, though the answer may be slow. Keep your own promises, and leave the rest to time.
aspects.work: An agreement dishonoured against you will be repaid in its season. Do not ruin yourself in haste to collect it.
aspects.home: Wrongs done within a family have long consequences that reach to children and beyond. Act now so that none are laid up for later.
aspects.health: The effects of old habits arrive late but surely. Mend what you can before the reckoning comes.
aspects.journeys: A decision made in breach of your word will cost more than it gains. Choose the road that keeps faith.

entries.greek: ἐν δʼ Ἔρις, ἐν δʼ Ἀλκή, ἐν δὲ κρυόεσσα Ἰωκή,
entries.english: In it were Strife, and Courage, and chilling Pursuit,
entries.reading: You are entering a contest, and the answer shows what goes with you into it: strife, courage and the cold rush of pursuit. Such strength is real, but it is fearsome, and it belongs to struggles that are justly undertaken. Arm yourself fully if you must, but know what you are carrying.
entries.context: In Iliad 5, Athena arms herself for battle to go with Hera against Ares and help the Greeks. Over her shoulders she throws the terrible tasselled aegis, wreathed with Rout and bearing Strife, Courage, chilling Pursuit and the Gorgon's head.

aspects.love: Strife has a way of entering love when pride is armed. Put away the aegis when you go to those you cherish.
aspects.work: Competition is fierce and you may need to go into it fully armed. Be sure the cause is just, for strife and pursuit are hard masters.
aspects.home: Do not bring the armour of battle into your own house. Keep strife and pursuit at the threshold.
aspects.health: You may be running on alarm and effort. Strength is good, but a body kept always ready for battle grows weary.
aspects.journeys: Before a major change, know what powers you are taking with you. Courage will serve you; strife will not.

entries.greek: λιμῷ δʼ οἴκτιστον θανέειν καὶ πότμον ἐπισπεῖν.
entries.english: But to die of hunger is the most pitiful way to meet one's fate.
entries.reading: When want presses hard, the worst advice sounds most reasonable. The answer warns you against a plan born of hunger or fear that asks you to break a promise or take what is forbidden. Hold to your word a little longer; the shortcut offered in desperation can cost far more than the hardship it ends.
entries.context: In Odyssey 12, Odysseus' men are stranded on Thrinacia, the island of the Sun, and their food has run out. While Odysseus sleeps, Eurylochus urges his companions to slaughter the sacred cattle of Helios, saying that of all deaths, dying of hunger is the most pitiful; the deed brings their destruction.

aspects.love: Loneliness can make a poor choice look sensible. Do not reach for what is forbidden to you because you are hungry for affection.
aspects.work: Shortage may tempt you or your colleagues to take what is not yours to take. The gain will not outlast the harm.
aspects.home: In a hard time at home, someone may urge a desperate remedy. Listen to the voice that keeps faith, even when it is quieter.
aspects.health: Treat true hunger and need with seriousness, but do not let them drive you to remedies that injure you further.
aspects.journeys: A decision taken only to escape present hardship may lead to a worse ruin. Wait for a better wind if you can.

entries.greek: κείσομʼ ἐπεί κε θάνω· νῦν δὲ κλέος ἐσθλὸν ἀροίμην,
entries.english: I shall lie still when I die. But now let me win great glory.
entries.reading: Whatever is fated will come, and there is no use in fearing it. What is yours is the present: this is the time to act, to earn the good name you want, to do the deed that matters. Do not wait for safety before you live.
entries.context: In Iliad 18, Achilles, grieving for Patroclus, tells his mother Thetis that he will go out to kill Hector, though he knows his own death will follow. If the same fate awaits him as took even Heracles, he says, he will lie still when he dies, but now he will win great glory.

aspects.love: Do not postpone love for fear of its ending. Give what you can give now, fully.
aspects.work: This is a time to put your best effort forward and earn a good name. Later can take care of itself.
aspects.home: Grief in the family may be calling you to act. Let the loss move you to honour the one who is gone.
aspects.health: Fear of what may come can steal the strength you have today. Live in the strength you have.
aspects.journeys: The decision is before you and the consequences are already known. Choose with courage rather than delay.

entries.greek: ἀλλʼ ὄρσευ πόλεμον δʼ οἷος πάρος εὔχεαι εἶναι.
entries.english: Rise up and go to war, as brave as you always boast you are.
entries.reading: You have been honoured and trusted; now it is time to show it. The answer calls you to rise and act with the courage you have always spoken of, and not to let your reputation stand in for deeds. Words have been given; the field is waiting.
entries.context: In Iliad 4, Agamemnon goes through the ranks before battle, rousing his captains. To Idomeneus of Crete he recalls the honour he always shows him at feasts, and bids him rise to war as brave as he has always claimed to be.

aspects.love: You have spoken well of your devotion; now let your actions match it. Those who love you are waiting to see it.
aspects.work: You have been well rewarded and trusted. Now rise to the task and prove you deserve it.
aspects.home: Your family has honoured you at its table. In this hour, stand up for them as you have promised.
aspects.health: You know what you are capable of. Rouse yourself to the effort that will restore you.
aspects.journeys: You have long talked of the step you would take. The moment has come to take it.

entries.greek: οὔ τί σε λωβεύω, τέκνον φίλον, ἀλλʼ ἔτυμόν τοι
entries.english: I am not mocking you, dear child; it is true,
entries.reading: Good news can seem too good to be trusted, and you may be tempted to dismiss the messenger. The answer says: this is not mockery. Hear it out, test it if you must, but do not turn away what is genuinely being offered you.
entries.context: In Odyssey 23, Penelope scolds the nurse Eurycleia for waking her with what she takes for a cruel joke. Eurycleia replies that she is not mocking her: Odysseus really has come home, and he is the stranger whom everyone mistreated. The papyrus line is identified here only probably, as Maltomini marks it uncertain.

aspects.love: A declaration of love or loyalty may seem too good to believe. It is genuine; do not reject it out of old hurt.
aspects.work: News of success or opportunity is real, though it reaches you from an unexpected quarter. Take it seriously.
aspects.home: An old and faithful member of your household brings you true word. Listen to the one who has served you longest.
aspects.health: Good news about health may be true even if you hardly dare believe it. Let hope back in.
aspects.journeys: The change you longed for has come, though it looks unlike what you imagined. Recognise it in its humble form.

entries.greek: Ἀλκμήνης δʼ ἀπέπαυσε τόκον, σχέθε δʼ Εἰλειθυίας.
entries.english: She held back Alcmene's labour, and stopped the birth-goddesses.
entries.reading: Something you expect to come forth is being held back, and another thing hurried forward in its place. This may be the work of a rival or simply of circumstance, and it can change who receives what was meant for another. Be wary of binding yourself with promises before you know all the forces at work.
entries.context: In Iliad 19, Agamemnon tells the story of how Zeus himself was led astray: Zeus swore that a child born that day would rule his neighbours, and Hera then held back Alcmene's labour and stopped the birth-goddesses, while bringing Eurystheus early to birth. Agamemnon tells this tale while making amends to Achilles.

aspects.love: Someone may be delaying or interfering in a bond that should be coming to birth. Watch for jealousy and be patient.
aspects.work: Another may be hurried into the place meant for you. Do not bind yourself with promises before you know all the facts.
aspects.home: Births and new beginnings in the family may come at their own time, early or late. Trust the process and those who care for the mother and child.
aspects.health: A matter of the body may be delayed or hastened beyond your control. Seek skilled help and do not despair at the timing.
aspects.journeys: Do not swear to a course before you know who else is moving behind it. A hasty oath can give your prize to another.

entries.greek: ἀλλʼ ἴθι ταῦτα δʼ ὄπισθεν ἀρεσσόμεθʼ εἴ τι κακὸν νῦν
entries.english: Go now; we will make amends later if any harm has been said.
entries.reading: Hard words may have passed between you and someone you respect. The answer counsels going forward with the work at hand, trusting that the harm can be made right afterwards. Do not let a quarrel halt what must be done; let it be set aside, and later repaired with good grace.
entries.context: In Iliad 4, Agamemnon has rebuked Odysseus during his review of the troops, and Odysseus answers angrily. Seeing his anger, Agamemnon smiles and takes back his words, saying he knows Odysseus' heart is kindly, and that they will make amends later for anything ill that was said.

aspects.love: A sharp word has passed between you and someone you care for. Let it be set aside now and mended with kindness soon.
aspects.work: A superior or colleague has spoken unfairly. Go on with the work, and trust that amends can be made later.
aspects.home: A quarrel at home need not stop the household's work. Leave room for apology, and offer it yourself if you can.
aspects.health: Do not carry the sting of hard words with you all day. Let them go, and your heart will be lighter.
aspects.journeys: Do not let an argument decide your path. Move forward, and settle the matter once tempers have cooled.

entries.greek: πῇ μέματον; τί σφῶϊν ἐνὶ φρεσὶ μαίνεται ἦτορ;
entries.english: Where are you rushing? Why is your heart raging with madness?
entries.reading: Stop and ask where you are hurrying, and why. A great power has already set itself against this course, and pressing on in heat will only bring harm. The answer counsels you to rein in your anger before it carries you somewhere you cannot return from.
entries.context: In Iliad 8, Hera and Athena drive out from Olympus to help the hard-pressed Greeks against Zeus' command. Zeus sends Iris, who meets them at the gates of Olympus and delivers his message: where are they rushing, and what madness is in their hearts, for Zeus will not allow them to aid the Greeks.

aspects.love: Do not rush into a love that is set against stronger wishes than your own. Ask why your heart is driving so hard.
aspects.work: You may be pressing a venture against the will of those who decide. Rein in before you are thrown.
aspects.home: A family member may be rushing out in anger. Stand at the gate, gently, and ask where they are going.
aspects.health: Rage and haste are a strain on the body. Pause and let your heart quieten.
aspects.journeys: Stop before you cross the threshold. This road has already been forbidden to you, and pressing on brings harm.

entries.greek: μὴ δή τοι κεῖνός γε λίην ἐνθύμιος ἔστω.
entries.english: Do not let him weigh too heavily on your heart.
entries.reading: Someone you care for is away from you, and you have been carrying worry for them. The answer is gentle: do not let that worry press too heavily. They are watched over, and their absence may be shaping them into more than they were.
entries.context: In Odyssey 13, Odysseus, newly landed on Ithaca, asks Athena why she did not tell Telemachus the truth about his father. Athena tells him not to be too anxious for his son: she herself sent him to Sparta to win a good name, and he sits at ease in the house of Menelaus.

aspects.love: A beloved person is away from you. Trust that they are safe and growing, and do not wear yourself out with worry.
aspects.work: A protégé or partner may be absent on a task that will serve them well. Let them gain their own reputation.
aspects.home: A child who has left home may be better cared for than you fear. Ease your heart about them.
aspects.health: Anxiety for another can harm your own wellbeing. Set some of that weight down.
aspects.journeys: Someone you sent ahead is waiting in a safe place. You may follow when the time is right without fear for them.

entries.greek: ἀλλʼ οὔ πως ἅμα πάντα θεοὶ δόσαν ἀνθρώποισιν·
entries.english: But the gods do not give men every gift at once.
entries.reading: You may be wishing you had the strength of another season of life, or every advantage together. The answer reminds you that no one is given all things at once. Use what this time of life has given you, whether vigour or wisdom, and let others supply what you lack.
entries.context: In Iliad 4, Agamemnon tells the aged Nestor he wishes Nestor's strength were as firm as his spirit. Nestor replies that he too would like to be as young as when he killed Ereuthalion, but the gods do not give everything at once; now he will serve with counsel and command, which is the right of the old.

aspects.love: You cannot be everything to someone at once. Give what this season of your life allows, and let that be enough.
aspects.work: You may not have every skill or every advantage. Offer what you do best, whether counsel or labour.
aspects.home: Each generation in a family brings its own gifts. Let the young bring strength and the old bring wisdom.
aspects.health: Your body may not do what it once did, but it has other strengths now. Honour the stage of life you are in.
aspects.journeys: No choice will bring every benefit together. Choose the one that suits what you have to give.

entries.greek: μὴ δʼ οὕτως ἀγόρευε· πάρος δʼ οὐκ ἔσσεται ἄλλως,
entries.english: Do not talk like that. Things will not change before
entries.reading: Complaining of the tools that failed you will not alter anything. The answer says that the situation will stay as it is until you meet it squarely, with the right means and the right companion. Stop lamenting and choose how you will face the thing in front of you.
entries.context: In Iliad 5, the archer Pandarus laments that his arrows have wounded Greek champions without killing them, and vows to burn his bow. Aeneas tells him not to talk like that: things will not change until the two of them face Diomedes together with horses and chariot.

aspects.love: Bemoaning past disappointments in love will not change your situation. Meet the matter face to face, with a true companion.
aspects.work: Your tools or methods may have failed you, but abandoning them in anger is not the answer. Find a partner and approach the problem differently.
aspects.home: Things at home will stay as they are until someone takes the first real step. Let it be you.
aspects.health: Complaining of your condition will not alter it. Take up a new means and act.
aspects.journeys: Nothing will change until you commit. Stop talking of breaking your bow and climb into the chariot.

entries.greek: ὣς ἔφατʼ, οὐδὲ Διὸς πεῖθε φρένα ταῦτʼ ἀγορεύων·
entries.english: So he spoke, but his words did not move the mind of Zeus.
entries.reading: You may argue your case well and still not move the power that decides it. The answer warns that the outcome you are asking for is not yours to command; a greater purpose is set on another end. Do your part honestly, but do not expect complaint to change it.
entries.context: In Iliad 12, the Trojan Asius, held back at the Greek wall by two Lapith defenders, cries out to Zeus that he is a liar for letting the Greeks hold firm. The poet says his words did not move Zeus, whose heart was set on giving glory to Hector.

aspects.love: You may plead and still not change the heart of the one who decides. Accept that their choice is not yours to make.
aspects.work: An appeal over a decision already made is unlikely to succeed. Save your strength for what can still be influenced.
aspects.home: In family matters, a greater will than yours may be at work. Do your part faithfully without bitterness.
aspects.health: Some things about your body or circumstances are not yours to command. Seek peace with them rather than rage against them.
aspects.journeys: The outcome of this decision lies elsewhere. Act well, and release what you cannot control.

entries.greek: ἀλλʼ Ὀδυσεὺς ἀνένευε καὶ ἔσχεθεν ἱέμενόν περ.
entries.english: But Odysseus shook his head and held him back, eager as he was.
entries.reading: You are close, perhaps very close, to achieving what you are straining for. But a wiser judgement asks you to hold back now, because the time is not right and your success would spoil a larger plan. Restrain yourself; the moment will come for what you can do.
entries.context: In Odyssey 21, Telemachus tries to string his father's great bow and would have done it at the fourth attempt. But Odysseus, still disguised as a beggar, shook his head and stopped him, eager though he was, so that the suitors would not be warned.

aspects.love: Hold back from a declaration or step in love that would be premature. Your readiness will be welcome later.
aspects.work: You are nearly able to do the great thing at work, but the moment is not right. Let a wiser hand decide when.
aspects.home: A parent's or elder's quiet signal may be asking you to wait. Honour it, though you are eager.
aspects.health: Do not strain to prove your strength now. Holding back preserves it for when it matters.
aspects.journeys: Pause on the threshold of this change. You are close, but the timing belongs to a larger plan.

entries.greek: πῶς ἐθέλεις ἐπὶ νῆας Ἀχαιῶν ἐλθέμεν οἶος
entries.english: How can you wish to go alone to the ships of the Greeks?
entries.reading: Those who love you fear for you, and their question is a fair one: why go alone into the place of greatest danger? Weigh their fear seriously. Yet some errands must be made in person, and if you go, go with a clear heart and the help of the gods, not in reckless grief.
entries.context: In Iliad 24, Priam tells his wife Hecuba that he means to go to the Greek ships and ransom Hector's body from Achilles. Hecuba cries out, asking how he can wish to go alone into the sight of the man who has killed so many of his sons. Priam goes, under the protection of Zeus and Hermes, and is received with respect.

aspects.love: Someone who loves you is afraid for you. Hear their fear tenderly before you decide.
aspects.work: An errand into a hostile place may need to be done in person. Prepare carefully and go with right intent.
aspects.home: Your family fears losing you as they have lost others. Speak with them before you leave and take their blessing if you can.
aspects.health: Do not go alone into a place of danger while grieving. Let others support you.
aspects.journeys: The bravest choice may also be the most frightening to those around you. Weigh it soberly, then go if it is right.

entries.greek: νυμφίον ἐν μεγάρῳ, μίαν οἴην παῖδα λιπόντα
entries.english: a bridegroom in his hall, leaving behind one daughter only,
entries.reading: A house may be left with a single heir, and that one carries everything forward. The answer speaks of loss early in life, but also of the honour that can grow from it. What seems slender and alone may become the very centre of a household.
entries.context: In Odyssey 7, Athena, disguised as a young girl of Scheria, tells Odysseus the lineage of Queen Arete. Her father Rhexenor was struck down by Apollo as a newly married man in his hall, leaving only one daughter, Arete, whom Alcinous married and honoured above all women.

aspects.love: Love may come to one who has known early loss. The one who is alone can be greatly cherished.
aspects.work: You may be the sole bearer of a legacy or responsibility. Take heart: others may come to honour and support you.
aspects.home: Your household may rest on one person. Care for them as the centre of what remains.
aspects.health: Loss in a family can be survived and outlived. Look after the one who carries the line forward.
aspects.journeys: After a sudden ending, a single path remains open. It may lead to unexpected honour.

entries.greek: ἀχλὺν δʼ αὖ τοι ἀπʼ ὀφθαλμῶν ἕλον ἣ πρὶν ἐπῆεν,
entries.english: I have taken away the mist that covered your eyes before,
entries.reading: Something has clouded your sight, and now it is being cleared. You will see more truly who stands before you and what powers are at work. Use this clarity well: it is given so that you may know which struggles are yours and which you should not enter.
entries.context: In Iliad 5, Diomedes, wounded by an arrow, prays to Athena. She fills him with his father's courage and tells him she has taken the mist from his eyes so that he can tell gods from men, warning him not to fight the gods, except Aphrodite.

aspects.love: You are beginning to see a person clearly for who they are. Use that clear sight wisely and kindly.
aspects.work: Confusion about your situation at work is lifting. You can now tell real power from mere appearance.
aspects.home: A misunderstanding at home is clearing. See your family as they truly are.
aspects.health: Clarity of mind is returning. Let it guide you to know which battles are worth fighting.
aspects.journeys: With the mist gone, you can judge which road leads where. Choose with your new sight.

entries.greek: τόξου πειρώμεσθα καὶ ἐκτελέωμεν ἄεθλον.
entries.english: Let us try the bow, and see the contest through.
entries.reading: The answer urges you to take up the test and finish it. Prepare well, warm what is stiff, make ready what resists. But know also that a trial reveals the true owner of a thing: approach it honestly, for those who try what is not theirs are shown up.
entries.context: In Odyssey 21, after Leodes fails to string the bow, the suitor Antinous orders the goatherd Melanthius to light a fire and bring a cake of fat, so the young men can warm and grease the bow and complete the contest. None of the suitors succeeds.

aspects.love: A trial lies before you in love, and it will show what is true. Do not try to win what belongs to another.
aspects.work: Take up the test before you and see it through. Prepare well, for effort without right will not succeed.
aspects.home: A matter at home must be tested and settled. Let it come to its proper conclusion.
aspects.health: Warm what is stiff and soften what resists. Gentle preparation helps the body meet its trials.
aspects.journeys: Begin the venture and finish it. The test will show whether this path is truly yours.

entries.greek: γιγνώσκω δʼ ὡς σφῶϊν ἐελδομένοισιν ἱκάνω
entries.english: I know that you two alone longed for my coming,
entries.reading: Those who truly hoped for your good are now seen for what they are. The answer asks you to recognise the few who stood by you in absence and hardship, and to reward them openly. Loyalty quietly kept deserves to be named.
entries.context: In Odyssey 21, Odysseus reveals himself to the swineherd Eumaeus and the cowherd Philoetius outside the hall. He tells them that he knows they alone among his servants longed for his return, for he has heard no one else pray for it.

aspects.love: See who has truly longed for your company and been faithful in absence. Honour them openly.
aspects.work: Reward those who have worked loyally while others did not. Their faith deserves to be named.
aspects.home: In your family, some have hoped for you more than others. Recognise and cherish them.
aspects.health: The care of a few loyal people sustains you. Let them know how much it matters.
aspects.journeys: When you return or change course, take with you those who have stood by you.

entries.greek: ἕσσω μιν χλαῖνάν τε χιτῶνά τε, εἵματα καλά,
entries.english: I will dress him in a cloak and tunic, fine clothes,
entries.reading: Someone has come to your door in need, and the answer asks you to treat them generously. Give what is decent and useful, and send them on with honour. Kindness to the unknown guest is never wasted, and may be kindness to someone greater than they appear.
entries.context: In Odyssey 16, Telemachus, at Eumaeus' hut, speaks of the beggar staying there, who is in truth his father in disguise. Not yet able to host him safely in the palace, he promises to give the stranger a cloak and tunic, a sword and sandals, and to send him wherever he wishes to go.

aspects.love: Be generous to someone who comes to you in need. Kindness to a stranger may reveal a dear one.
aspects.work: Give fair wages and proper goods. Treat those who come to you for work with respect.
aspects.home: Hospitality in your home is a sacred duty. Clothe the guest and send them on well.
aspects.health: Look to basic comforts: warm clothing and decent provision support wellbeing.
aspects.journeys: Help another on their way, and trust that the road will be kind to you too.

entries.greek: ἁψαμένη βρόχον αἰπὺν ἀφʼ ὑψηλοῖο μελάθρου,
entries.english: tying a noose high from the roof-beam above,
entries.reading: This is a grave answer, speaking of sorrow borne alone until it becomes unbearable. If you are carrying something heavy in secret, do not let it close in on you; bring it into the light and let others help you hold it. If the question concerns another, watch over them with care. Hidden grief, the answer says, is the most dangerous. If you are struggling, talk to someone today: in Australia, Lifeline answers on 13 11 14, day and night.
entries.context: In Odyssey 11, Odysseus tells of the women he saw in the underworld. Among them was Epicaste (Jocasta), who unknowingly married her own son Oedipus; when the truth came out, she went down to Hades, overcome by grief, by tying a noose from the high roof-beam.

aspects.love: A love entangled with hidden truths can bring great pain. If something weighs on your heart, speak it to someone you trust.
aspects.work: Do not let shame over a matter at work drive you into isolation. Seek counsel before despair takes hold.
aspects.home: Family secrets can wound terribly when they come to light. Approach them with care and do not let anyone bear their weight alone.
aspects.health: If you or someone close to you is overwhelmed with sorrow, reach out for help without delay: in Australia, Lifeline answers on 13 11 14. Grief is not meant to be carried in silence.
aspects.journeys: In a time of great distress, do not make decisions alone. Let others walk beside you until the darkness lifts.

entries.greek: ἡμετέρης ἀρετῆς μεμνημένος, οἷα καὶ ἡμῖν
entries.english: remembering our excellence, the kind of skill that Zeus
entries.reading: A slight or a taunt may have stung you, and you have answered it with strength. Now the answer invites you to remember not only your own excellence but the gifts of those around you. Each house and each person has their own kind of skill; honour it, and carry the memory of it to others.
entries.context: In Odyssey 8, after Euryalus insults Odysseus and Odysseus answers by throwing the discus far beyond the rest, King Alcinous calms him. He asks Odysseus to remember Phaeacian excellence when he feasts at home, the skills Zeus has given them since their fathers' time: not boxing or wrestling, but running, seafaring and dance.

aspects.love: Remember what is best in those you love and speak of it. Let a slight not overshadow their gifts.
aspects.work: Each team has its own talents. Honour others' skills alongside your own.
aspects.home: Carry home the memory of what you have learnt from others. Let your household hear of good things.
aspects.health: Rest after effort and enjoy what restores you, like music and fellowship.
aspects.journeys: As you prepare to move on, take with you a generous memory of those who received you.

entries.greek: λαῖτμα μέγʼ ἐκπερόωσιν, ἐπεί σφισι δῶκʼ ἐνοσίχθων·
entries.english: they cross the great gulf of the sea, a gift from the Earth-shaker.
entries.theme: Trust the gift you were given
entries.reading: You have a gift that carries you over great distances, a skill or a strength that was given rather than earned. The answer tells you to trust it, but also to remember its source and to be modest with strangers. Those who cross the sea safely do so by favour as well as skill.
entries.context: In Odyssey 7, Athena, disguised as a young girl, leads Odysseus through the city of the Phaeacians. She warns him that the people are wary of strangers, and that they trust in their swift ships to cross the great gulf of the sea, a gift from Poseidon the Earth-shaker.

aspects.love: Trust the gift that carries a relationship across distances. Be modest and gentle with new acquaintances.
aspects.work: Your skill can carry you through great challenges, but remember its source and treat strangers with care.
aspects.home: A gift of your family has carried you far. Remember who gave it.
aspects.health: Your strength is a gift, not something to be taken for granted. Care for it.
aspects.journeys: You may cross a great distance soon. Go with both skill and humility.

entries.greek: ἄττα, πρόσω φέρε τόξα· τάχʼ οὐκ εὖ πᾶσι πιθήσεις
entries.english: Old man, bring the bow forward; you will soon be sorry if you obey them all.
entries.reading: Many voices are shouting at you to put down what you are carrying. The answer warns that trying to please them all will end badly for you. Know whose instruction you truly owe obedience to, and carry the thing forward to where it belongs.
entries.context: In Odyssey 21, the swineherd Eumaeus is carrying the bow to the disguised Odysseus when the suitors shout at him, and he sets it down in fear. Telemachus calls out to him to bring the bow forward, warning that he will soon regret obeying everyone.

aspects.love: Do not let the voices of many decide your heart. Listen to the one whose instruction you truly trust.
aspects.work: Pressure from many sides may make you set down your task. Hold to it and bring it to its proper end.
aspects.home: In family matters, you cannot obey everyone. Choose whose word you follow.
aspects.health: Do not let the clamour of others drive you to neglect your own wellbeing.
aspects.journeys: Carry forward the decision you were entrusted with, though others shout for you to abandon it.

entries.greek: ἀλλʼ ὄρσευ πόλεμον δὲ καὶ ἄλλους ὄρνυθι λαούς.
entries.english: Rise up and go to war, and rouse the rest of the army too.
entries.reading: The time of quarrel and delay is over. The answer bids you rise to the task and to stir others to it as well, for the wrong that held things back is being made right. Accept what amends are offered, and lead.
entries.context: In Iliad 19, at the assembly where he is reconciled with Achilles, Agamemnon admits that his mind was blinded by Ate and offers boundless amends. He urges Achilles to rise and go to war, and to rouse the rest of the army too, promising all the gifts Odysseus had offered.
