aspects.love: After a quarrel, accept the amends offered. Rise up and let love move forward again.
aspects.work: The time for delay is past. Rally your colleagues and press on with the work.
aspects.home: After division in your family, it is time to come together and act as one.
aspects.health: Rouse yourself from a time of withdrawal. Movement and purpose will restore you.
aspects.journeys: The decision is made. Rise up and bring others with you.

entries.greek: οὐδὲ γὰρ οὐδὲ βίη Ἡρακλῆος φύγε κῆρα,
entries.english: For not even mighty Heracles escaped his doom,
entries.reading: No strength, however great, is exempt from what must come. The answer is not a threat but a steadying truth: knowing your limits, you may act without fear and without pretending to be more than mortal. Do what is yours to do while it is yours.
entries.context: In Iliad 18, Achilles tells his mother Thetis that he will kill Hector and accept his own death whenever Zeus wills. Not even mighty Heracles escaped his doom, he says, though he was dearest to Zeus; fate and Hera's anger overcame him.

aspects.love: No love is beyond mortality. Cherish the one you have while you have them.
aspects.work: Even the strongest enterprises have their end. Do your best work without fear of what is beyond your control.
aspects.home: Every family will know loss. Let that knowledge make you gentle with those you love.
aspects.health: Your strength is real but not limitless. Respect your limits and live fully within them.
aspects.journeys: Knowing that every road ends, choose the one worth travelling.

entries.greek: ἂψ ἐθέλω ἀρέσαι δόμεναί τʼ ἀπερείσιʼ ἄποινα.
entries.english: I am willing to make amends, and to pay a ransom beyond counting.
entries.reading: You have erred, and the answer counsels you to admit it plainly. The way forward is generous restitution, offered freely and without excuse. The one who acknowledges the fault openly keeps the hope of mending what was broken.
entries.context: In Iliad 9, with the Greeks in retreat, Nestor tells Agamemnon that he wronged Achilles. Agamemnon admits his blindness and declares he is willing to make amends and pay a ransom beyond counting, listing the gifts that the embassy will then carry to Achilles.

aspects.love: If you have wronged someone you love, admit it openly. Offer amends freely and without pride.
aspects.work: A mistake in your dealings can be repaired with generous restitution. Make it right promptly.
aspects.home: In family disputes, the one who acknowledges fault first opens the way to peace.
aspects.health: Admitting a mistake lifts a burden from your heart. Do it for your own wellbeing as well as for others.
aspects.journeys: Before going forward, make amends for what went wrong. It will clear the road ahead.

entries.greek: ὀμνυέτω δέ τοι ὅρκον ἐν Ἀργείοισιν ἀναστὰς
entries.english: Let him stand up among the Greeks and swear you an oath,
entries.reading: Before you accept a reconciliation, ask that it be made openly and bound with a solemn word. The answer favours public honesty: what is promised in front of others is harder to break. Seek an oath where trust has been damaged, and give one where you have damaged it.
entries.context: In Iliad 19, Odysseus advises Achilles about the settlement with Agamemnon. Let the gifts be brought into the assembly for all to see, he says, and let Agamemnon stand up among the Greeks and swear to Achilles that he never lay with Briseis.

aspects.love: Where trust has been damaged, let promises be made openly. A sworn word can heal a wound.
aspects.work: Agreements should be made publicly and bound with solemn words. Do not settle for private assurances.
aspects.home: In a family matter, let the promise be made before all. It will be harder to break.
aspects.health: Peace of mind may come from a clear and honest promise. Ask for it if you need it.
aspects.journeys: Before you commit to a change, ask for clear assurances. A public oath protects you.

entries.greek: ἐγγὺς ἀνήρ· οὐ δηθὰ ματεύσομεν· αἴ κʼ ἐθέλητε
entries.english: The man is close at hand; we will not look for long, if you are willing
entries.reading: You are searching widely for an answer that is already close at hand. Someone near you, perhaps one you would overlook because they are young or new, has the counsel you need. Be willing to listen to it without resentment.
entries.context: In Iliad 14, the wounded Greek leaders confer, and Agamemnon has proposed launching the ships to flee. When he asks for better advice, Diomedes speaks: the man is close at hand, they need not search long, if they will listen to him and not resent that he is the youngest among them.

aspects.love: The person who understands you may be closer than you think, even someone you have overlooked.
aspects.work: The solution to your problem is near at hand. Listen to the newer or younger voice.
aspects.home: Someone in your household has wise counsel. Do not dismiss them because of age.
aspects.health: The remedy may be simpler and closer than you imagine. Look around you.
aspects.journeys: The answer to your dilemma is close. Listen without resentment to the one who offers it.

entries.greek: ὧδε μάλʼ ἐξαπίνης καί τις θεὸς αὐτὸν ἐνείκαι;
entries.english: if he came suddenly, as if some god had brought him home?
entries.reading: Ask yourself honestly where you would stand if the one you are waiting for came back today. The answer is a test of loyalty, put quietly before the truth is revealed. Know your own heart now, so that you are ready when the moment comes without warning.
entries.context: In Odyssey 21, Odysseus, still disguised, leads the cowherd and the swineherd out of the hall and tests them. He asks what sort of men they would be if Odysseus came suddenly, as if some god had brought him: would they fight for the suitors or for him?

aspects.love: Ask yourself where your loyalty truly lies. If the one you love returned today, would you be ready?
aspects.work: Consider where you would stand if your old leader or mentor came back. Your loyalty is being quietly tested.
aspects.home: If an absent family member returned suddenly, how would you receive them? Prepare your heart.
aspects.health: Be ready for sudden change; it may come without warning, and your inner strength will matter.
aspects.journeys: An unexpected arrival may change your plans. Know your own mind beforehand.

entries.greek: ἦ δὴ ταῦτά γʼ ἑτοῖμα τετεύχαται, οὐδέ κεν ἄλλως
entries.english: Truly, these things are made ready, and not even
entries.reading: The things you feared have already come to pass, and not even a god could now make them otherwise. The answer asks you to stop arguing with what has happened and turn your mind to what can still be done. Clear sight of a hard situation is the beginning of good counsel.
entries.context: In Iliad 14, Agamemnon fears that the Greeks are turning against him as Achilles did. Nestor replies that the disaster is now accomplished beyond changing: the wall they trusted to protect the ships has fallen, and the Trojans are fighting at the ships.

aspects.love: What has happened in your relationship is done. Look forward rather than back.
aspects.work: The damage is done and cannot be undone. Now focus on what can still be saved.
aspects.home: A wall in your family may have fallen. Accept it and seek a way forward together.
aspects.health: Your condition is what it is. Clear sight of it is the beginning of good care.
aspects.journeys: The change has already happened. Turn your mind to what comes next.

entries.greek: ἀλλʼ ἐφομαρτεῖτε· πλεόνων δέ τι ἔργον ἄμεινον.
entries.english: Follow me: the work of many is better.
entries.reading: What you are attempting is too great for one person alone, however strong. The answer calls you to gather others and work together: the work of many is better. Ask for help openly, and do not shrink from leading it.
entries.context: In Iliad 12, the Lycian king Sarpedon has torn down part of the Greek battlement but cannot break through alone. He calls on his Lycians not to slacken, telling them it is hard for one man to make a path to the ships, and that the work of many is better; they press on with fresh force.

aspects.love: Love grows stronger with the support of friends and community. Do not try to carry it alone.
aspects.work: This task is too great for one person. Gather your colleagues and work together.
aspects.home: Share the work of your home. Many hands make the labour lighter.
aspects.health: Seek support from others. Wellbeing is often restored with help.
aspects.journeys: A great change needs many helpers. Ask for them openly.

entries.greek: ἐξ ἄρα δή τοι ἔπειτα θεοὶ φρένας ὤλεσαν αὐτοί.
entries.english: Then the gods themselves have surely robbed you of your wits.
entries.reading: Good advice has been given, and someone is refusing it because it is unwelcome. If you are the one rejecting sound counsel, the answer warns you to look again before you dismiss it. If you are the one giving it, know that you may be met with scorn, and that this does not make your advice wrong.
entries.context: In Iliad 7, the elder Antenor advises the Trojans to give Helen and her treasure back to the Greeks, since they have broken the truce. Paris rejects this, saying that if Antenor means it seriously, the gods themselves have destroyed his wits; he will return the treasure but not Helen.

aspects.love: If a friend tells you that what you cling to in love should be given back, do not call them witless for saying it. The thing you refuse to release may be the cause of the whole quarrel.
aspects.work: An elder or adviser has proposed a costly but honest settlement. Offering to return the goods while keeping the prize itself will not end the dispute.
aspects.home: Someone in the family has spoken an unwelcome truth in council. Answer the argument, not the person, and do not accuse them of folly for their candour.
aspects.health: When you are told that a habit must be given up, notice if your first response is scorn. That reaction is often the sign the advice has struck home.
aspects.journeys: Before you defy the sensible course in front of everyone, ask whether your stubbornness serves anyone but your own desire.

entries.greek: θάρσει, μηδέ τί τοι θάνατος καταθύμιος ἔστω.
entries.english: Take heart, and do not let death be on your mind at all.
entries.theme: Do not dwell on the end
entries.reading: Take heart, and do not let fear of the worst fill your mind; it will only cloud what you say and do. Yet the answer also asks for discernment: comfort is sometimes offered to draw out what someone wants to know. Be calm, speak truthfully, and consider who is reassuring you, and why.
entries.context: In Iliad 10, Odysseus and Diomedes capture the Trojan spy Dolon by night, and he begs to be ransomed. Odysseus tells him to take heart and not think of death, and then questions him closely about the Trojan camp; once Dolon has told all, Diomedes kills him.

aspects.love: Soothing words in love are welcome, but notice whether they come with questions that serve the speaker. Be at peace, and keep your judgement awake.
aspects.work: In a negotiation you may be told not to worry while being questioned closely. Answer truthfully, but do not give away everything for a promise of safety.
aspects.home: If a family member is frightened, reassure them as Odysseus did, but let your comfort be honest, not a means to an end.
aspects.health: Fear of death or illness may be filling your thoughts. Take heart: dwelling on the end will not keep it away, and calm serves you better.
aspects.journeys: You may be caught between sides at night, as Dolon was. Before you go out on a dangerous errand for reward, ask whether the prize is worth the risk.

entries.greek: ἐξ ὕπνου γοόωσα φίλους οἰκῆας ἐγείρῃ
entries.english: wakes her household from sleep with her weeping,
entries.reading: Before you enter a struggle beyond your measure, think of those at home who would mourn you. The answer warns against challenging powers far greater than yourself. Courage is good; but daring that forgets the people who love you is close to folly.
entries.context: In Iliad 5, the goddess Aphrodite, wounded by Diomedes, flees to Olympus and is comforted by her mother Dione. Dione warns that Diomedes should take care lest a stronger foe fight him, and his wife Aegialeia wake her household from sleep weeping for her husband.

aspects.love: Picture the one who would wake weeping if you were lost. Let that tenderness shape what risks you take.
aspects.work: A rival you have bested may be followed by one far stronger. Do not mistake one victory for invincibility in your trade.
aspects.home: Someone at home waits for you as Aegialeia waited for Diomedes. Come back to them, and do not stay away longer than you must.
aspects.health: Wounds taken in reckless contests heal, as Aphrodite's did, but they need tending. Withdraw to be comforted when you are hurt.
aspects.journeys: If the decision pits you against powers greater than yourself, remember that those who fight gods seldom come home. Choose a battle you can win.

entries.greek: ἀλλʼ ἴθι σιγῇ τοῖον, ἐγὼ δʼ ὁδὸν ἡγεμονεύσω,
entries.english: Come, go quietly, and I will lead the way.
entries.reading: A guide is offering to lead you, and the answer asks you to go quietly, without questioning everyone you meet. Keep your counsel among strangers, trust the one who shows the way, and let the right door open in its time.
entries.context: In Odyssey 7, Athena, disguised as a young Phaeacian girl, agrees to show Odysseus the way to the palace of Alcinous. She tells him to walk in silence while she leads, and not to look at or question anyone, since the people are wary of strangers.

aspects.love: A new friendship or love may be best approached quietly, without announcing yourself to everyone. Let one trusted guide bring you to the right door.
aspects.work: In a new workplace or market, keep your eyes down and your questions few at first. A kindly guide will show you where real influence lies.
aspects.home: When entering another family's house, go modestly and learn its ways before you speak.
aspects.health: Quiet walking and silence can restore you. Let yourself be led for a while rather than leading.
aspects.journeys: You are in strange country. Follow the guide who has offered to lead you, and do not stop to ask directions of everyone you pass.

entries.greek: οὔατʼ ἀκουέμεν ἐστί, νόος δʼ ἀπόλωλε καὶ αἰδώς.
entries.english: You have ears to hear, but your sense and your shame have gone.
entries.reading: You have heard the warning, but you are not taking it in. The answer rebukes the anger that makes the ears hear while the mind and conscience are absent. Stop, put down what you have picked up in fury, and consider what your rashness would bring on others.
entries.context: In Iliad 15, Ares learns that his son Ascalaphus has been killed and arms himself to avenge him against Zeus' command. Athena stops him, taking his helmet, shield and spear, and rebukes him as a madman whose ears hear but whose sense and shame have perished.

aspects.love: Anger on behalf of someone you love can make you deaf to good sense. Let a wiser friend take the spear from your hand.
aspects.work: A loss in your enterprise may push you to defy those above you. Hear the warning: acting in fury will bring harm to colleagues as well as yourself.
aspects.home: Grief in the family can turn into rage that endangers everyone. Let the one who restrains you be thanked, not resented.
aspects.health: Rage and grief together are hard on body and mind. Put down the weapons and sit again; the heart needs calm.
aspects.journeys: You have heard the warning against this course. Do not act as though you had not.

entries.greek: γηράς· ἀλλʼ οὐχ υἱὸς ἐν ἔντεσι πατρὸς ἐγήρα.
entries.english: grew old; but the son did not grow old in his father's armour.
entries.reading: You have received something from those before you, a gift, a role or a burden, and the question is how long and how well you will carry it. The answer speaks of the shortness of youth and the weight of inheritance. Honour what was handed to you, but do not assume that it will carry you as it carried them.
entries.context: In Iliad 17, Hector puts on the armour of Achilles, which he has stripped from Patroclus. The poet recalls that the gods gave it to Peleus, who passed it on to his son when he grew old; but the son would not grow old in his father's armour.

aspects.love: A love handed down or a role in someone else's story may not fit you as it fitted them. Be yourself within it.
aspects.work: You may take up equipment, a business, a reputation, from one greater than you. Use it, but do not suppose it makes you their equal.
aspects.home: What a father gives his son is not always carried into old age. Treasure the years together while you have them.
aspects.health: Youth does not last for ever. Look after yourself now, so that you may grow old in what you have been given.
aspects.journeys: Before you step into another's place, ask whether it is your own path or theirs that you are walking.

entries.greek: οἴκαδέ τʼ ἐλθέμεναι καὶ νόστιμον ἦμαρ ἰδέσθαι,
entries.english: to reach home and see the day of my return.
entries.reading: Better to endure much and come safely home than to arrive quickly and meet ruin at your own hearth. The answer counsels patience with a long road, and caution about the place you are hurrying back to. The day of return is worth waiting for, if it is reached rightly.
entries.context: In Odyssey 3, at Pylos, Telemachus despairs of his father's return. Athena, disguised as Mentor, answers that a god can easily save a man even from far away, and that she would rather suffer many hardships and then reach home and see the day of return than come home and be killed at her hearth, as Agamemnon was by Aegisthus and his wife.

aspects.love: A love long sought is worth the hardships of reaching it. Better a slow and safe return to each other than a hurried one into danger.
aspects.work: A swift success that leads into a trap is worse than slow progress. Endure the harder road at work if it brings you home safely.
aspects.home: Coming home is the great desire, but check what awaits you there. Return wisely, not hastily.
aspects.health: Recovery may be long and hard, but the day of restoration is worth the toil. Do not despair of it.
aspects.journeys: A god can bring a person home even from far away. Keep hoping, and take the longer, safer way if it is offered.

entries.greek: τὸν μὲν ἄκουρον ἐόντα βάλʼ ἀργυρότοξος Ἀπόλλων
entries.english: Silver-bowed Apollo struck him down, still with no son,
entries.reading: A line has been cut short, a plan ended before it bore fruit. The answer speaks honestly of loss that came too soon. Yet in the story this loss is not the end: what remains can still be honoured and become the root of something lasting.
entries.context: In Odyssey 7, Athena, disguised as a young girl, tells Odysseus about the family of Queen Arete. Her father Rhexenor was struck down by silver-bowed Apollo while still without a son, leaving only a daughter, Arete.

aspects.love: A marriage cut short before it could bear fruit is a grief. If you have known such a loss, let it be honoured rather than hidden.
aspects.work: A venture ended before it produced its heir or successor is not wholly lost. What it left behind may yet be the foundation of something greater.
aspects.home: A household that lost its head early can still flourish through one remaining member. Look after that one well.
aspects.health: Sudden loss strikes the young as well as the old. Grieve it fully, and then tend to the life that remains.
aspects.journeys: An unexpected ending may change the whole line of your story. Let the one who remains carry it forward.

entries.greek: ἐλπωρή τοι ἔπειτα φίλους τʼ ἰδέειν καὶ ἱκέσθαι
entries.english: then there is hope that you will see your friends and reach
entries.reading: Your hope of reaching what you long for depends on gaining the goodwill of one particular person. The answer counsels you to approach that person with respect and to win their kindness, for through them the way home may open. Know whose heart matters most, and go to them first.
entries.context: In Odyssey 7, Athena, disguised as a young girl, tells Odysseus about Queen Arete, who is honoured by all and settles quarrels with her good sense. If Arete is kindly disposed to him, she says, there is hope that he will see his friends and reach his home and native land.

aspects.love: In love, as with Arete, the favour of a wise and respected person can open doors. Win their trust honestly.
aspects.work: Your success depends on the goodwill of someone who settles disputes and is widely respected. Approach them first and with courtesy.
aspects.home: In your family, there may be a matriarch or patriarch whose kindness unlocks peace. Seek their blessing.
aspects.health: Find the person whose care and good sense can help you most. Their goodwill brings hope of recovery.
aspects.journeys: Before you seek the way home, win the favour of the one who can grant safe passage.

entries.greek: σφῶϊν δʼ, ὡς ἔσεταί περ, ἀληθείην καταλέξω.
entries.english: To you two I will tell the truth, as it will be.
entries.theme: The truth, as it will be
entries.reading: You are being told the truth now, and it comes with a promise. Those who have been loyal will share in what follows. Listen closely and trust it, for this is spoken as what will be, not as flattery.
entries.context: In Odyssey 21, after revealing himself to the swineherd and cowherd, Odysseus tells them he will speak the truth about what will happen. If the god lets him overcome the suitors, he will give each of them a wife, possessions and a house near his own, and treat them as companions of Telemachus.

aspects.love: Faithfulness in love will be repaid. The promise made to you is not flattery but truth.
aspects.work: Loyal service at work will be rewarded with partnership and a share in what is gained. Trust this word.
aspects.home: Those who have stood by the household will be given a place close to its heart.
aspects.health: A clear and honest word about your condition is being given to you. Trust it and act on it.
aspects.journeys: The truth spoken now is a promise for the future. Trust it as you prepare for change.

entries.greek: ὧδε γὰρ ἐξερέω, τὸ δὲ καὶ τετελεσμένον ἔσται·
entries.english: For I will tell you this, and it will surely come to pass.
entries.reading: Restrain yourself now, and the answer promises that what you lose will be returned to you many times over. Speak your grievance if you must, but do not draw the sword. This is said plainly, as something that will come to pass.
entries.context: In Iliad 1, Achilles is drawing his sword against Agamemnon when Athena, sent by Hera, holds him back. She tells him to stop, to reproach Agamemnon with words only, and promises that one day he will be given gifts three times as great because of this insult.

aspects.love: In a quarrel with someone you love, say what hurts, but do not strike. Restraint now will bring you far more than victory would.
aspects.work: An insult at work can be answered in words, not with drastic action. Hold back, and what you lose will be repaid three times.
aspects.home: In a family dispute, keep your hand from the sword. The peace you keep will be worth more than any revenge.
aspects.health: Holding back rage protects your own wellbeing as well as others. Let the anger pass through words, not deeds.
aspects.journeys: Do not act on impulse now. The goddess at your shoulder bids you wait, and the reward of waiting is great.

entries.greek: πέμψω δʼ ὅππη μιν κραδίη θυμός τε κελεύει.
entries.english: and I will send him wherever his heart and spirit tell him to go.
entries.reading: You are being given leave to choose your own way. The answer is generous: you will be helped and sent on, and the road you take may follow your own heart and spirit. Choose with care, since the freedom is real.
entries.context: In Odyssey 16, Telemachus speaks of the beggar in Eumaeus' hut, who is in truth his disguised father. He says he will give the stranger clothes, a sword and sandals, and send him wherever his heart and spirit tell him to go.

aspects.love: You are given freedom in love to go where your heart leads. Choose carefully, since you are truly free.
aspects.work: You may leave or move on in your work with good provision. Choose the place your heart calls you to.
aspects.home: Your family is willing to let you go, well equipped. Go where your spirit urges you.
aspects.health: Trust the instincts of your heart and spirit about what will heal you.
aspects.journeys: Your way forward is open, with the means to travel it. Let heart and spirit choose the road.

entries.greek: πλαγκτέ; τάχʼ αὖ σʼ ἐφʼ ὕεσσι κύνες ταχέες κατέδονται
entries.english: you wanderer? Soon the swift dogs will eat you among the pigs,
entries.reading: You may be scorned for doing what is right, and threatened by those who hold the room for now. The answer does not ask you to give in to them. Their jeers are loud, but they are spoken by those whose time is short; carry on with the task entrusted to you.
entries.context: In Odyssey 21, the swineherd Eumaeus carries Odysseus' bow towards the disguised Odysseus. One of the arrogant young suitors shouts at him, calling him a wretched wanderer and saying his own dogs will soon eat him among the pigs, if Apollo and the other gods favour the suitors.

aspects.love: You may be scorned by others for staying loyal to someone absent. Their jeers will not last.
aspects.work: Colleagues may mock you for carrying out an unpopular task. Carry it to the end; the outcome is not theirs to decide.
aspects.home: In a household under strain, the loudest voices may threaten the faithful. Keep your place.
aspects.health: Scorn and threats from others can wear on you. Remember that their power is shorter than they think.
aspects.journeys: You may be called a wanderer for your choice. Keep walking; their mockery has no power over your road.

entries.greek: γνοίης χʼ οἵη ἐμὴ δύναμις καὶ χεῖρες ἕπονται.
entries.english: you would learn how great my strength is, and how my hands obey me.
entries.reading: You have a strength that has not yet been seen, and you are waiting for the chance to show it in a good cause. The answer promises that, if what is hoped for comes true, your power and your hands will be equal to it. Keep faith, and be ready.
entries.context: In Odyssey 20, the disguised Odysseus swears to the loyal cowherd Philoetius that Odysseus will come home while he is there and he will see the suitors killed. Philoetius replies that he wishes Zeus would fulfil this, for then the stranger would see how great his strength is and how his hands would follow.

aspects.love: In love, you may long to prove your devotion. If the chance comes, your strength will be equal to it.
aspects.work: Your skill and strength are not yet known to all. The day may soon come when they are tested and seen.
aspects.home: You may yearn to defend your home. When the hour comes, your hands will follow your heart.
aspects.health: Your body may have reserves of strength you have not yet used. Trust them when the time comes.
aspects.journeys: If the change you hope for comes, you will be ready. Keep your strength for that hour.

entries.greek: οὔ τί σε τόνδʼ ἄξεσθαι ὀϊόμεθʼ· οὐδὲ ἔοικεν·
entries.english: We do not think he will marry you; that would not be right.
entries.reading: Someone fears not the thing itself but how it will look. The answer warns that worry about reputation can make people dismissive of the very person who deserves a hearing. Do not let fear of gossip blind you to what is happening in front of you.
entries.context: In Odyssey 21, Penelope asks that the beggar be allowed to try the bow. Eurymachus replies that the suitors do not think the stranger will marry her, which would not be fitting; rather, they are ashamed of what people would say if a beggar strung the bow that they could not.

aspects.love: Someone may dismiss a match because of how it looks to others. Do not let fear of gossip decide whom you love.
aspects.work: Fear of reputation can make people dismiss the very one who can succeed where they have failed.
aspects.home: In your home, worry about what others think may lead to injustice. Let the stranger have their chance.
aspects.health: Anxiety about appearances is a weight on the heart. Let it go.
aspects.journeys: Do not let fear of how it looks hold you back from a decision that is right.

entries.greek: ἐνθάδʼ ὁμιλέομεν, ποτιδέγμενοι ἤματα πάντα.
entries.english: We gather here, waiting day after day.
entries.reading: You have been waiting a long time for something that may never be yours. The answer asks you to look honestly at what you are waiting for and whether you have any right to it. If the prize belongs to another, the waiting itself becomes a loss; turn your hopes elsewhere.
entries.context: In Odyssey 21, the suitor Leodes fails to string the bow and declares that it will rob many champions of life and spirit. Better to die, he says, than to live and fail of the prize for which they gather in the house, waiting day after day.

aspects.love: You may have waited long for a love that belongs to someone else. Consider whether the waiting itself is wasting your life.
aspects.work: You may be lingering in a position, hoping for a prize that is not truly yours. Look elsewhere for your future.
aspects.home: Long waiting in your household can sour into idleness. Ask what you are truly waiting for.
aspects.health: Endless waiting drains vitality. Find a new hope or a new task.
aspects.journeys: The test has shown what you cannot do. Do not keep gathering at the same door; take another road.

entries.greek: κρυπτάδια φρονέοντα δικαζέμεν· οὐδέ τί πώ μοι
entries.english: to make your judgements in secret; and never yet
entries.reading: Something is being decided without you, and you feel it. The answer recognises the hurt of being kept out of counsel. Ask openly for what you need to know, but understand that not every plan is yours to share, and that demanding it may not open the door.
entries.context: In Iliad 1, Hera sees that Thetis has been plotting with Zeus and taunts him, saying he always likes to make his judgements in secret, apart from her, and has never willingly told her his thoughts. Zeus answers that she should not hope to know all his words.

aspects.love: You may feel that someone you love makes decisions without you. Speak of it openly, but do not expect to know every thought.
aspects.work: Plans may be made in secret at work. Ask for clarity, but accept that some things are not yours to know.
aspects.home: In a family, some decisions are made apart. Seek to be included, but with patience.
aspects.health: Suspicion about hidden plans can wear on your peace. Address it openly or let it go.
aspects.journeys: You may not know all that is being planned for you. Ask, but do not demand.

entries.greek: μὴ δή μοι φύξίν γε Δόλων ἐμβάλλεο θυμῷ·
entries.english: Do not think of escape, Dolon, at all.
entries.reading: The way out you are hoping for will not be given. You have come into the hands of a consequence that will not let you go, whatever you offer. The answer is stern: face what you have walked into, and if there is still a choice before you, do not repeat the course that led here.
entries.context: In Iliad 10, the Trojan spy Dolon, captured at night, has told Odysseus and Diomedes everything and begs to be spared. Diomedes, glaring at him, tells him not to think of escape, since if they let him go he would come again to spy; then he kills him.

aspects.love: If you have entered a relationship under false pretences, the consequences may be unavoidable. Face them honestly.
aspects.work: The way out of a difficult business situation may not be offered. Face what you have walked into and learn from it.
aspects.home: In your home, you may have to face the results of past choices. Do not seek to escape them by blaming others.
aspects.health: Some consequences for your health must be faced rather than escaped. Meet them with courage and seek help.
aspects.journeys: There is no escape from this path now. If there is still a choice ahead, choose more wisely next time.

translation: English translations made for this app from the Greek (Monro and Allen's Iliad, Murray's 1919 Odyssey Greek text); free to use with the app.
readings: Theme, reading, the scene in Homer and the five areas of life (love, work, home, health, journeys) are our own modern interpretation, written for this app; they are not part of the ancient papyrus.
